# Changelog

Vilan is a fast-moving alpha. Minor versions (`0.X`) may change the
language, the standard library, and the wire protocol without a
deprecation period; patch versions are fixes. Each release below links
the highlights — the [book](https://vilan-lang.org/docs/) always
tracks the latest state.

## Unreleased

<!-- family: miscompile -->
**`combine` over a source whose value is itself a tuple reads correctly: `combine((SignalCell::new((1, 2)), SignalCell::new("c"))).get()` destructured as `((x, y), l)` is `1 2 c`, where it was `x=1,2 y=c l=undefined`.** A tuple comprehension `(x in source => body)` lowered to a runtime `source.map((x) => body)` over the tuple's JS array — right while every element is one slot, and wrong the moment one is itself a tuple, because tuples store FLAT (`types.md` §5.9): a tuple-valued result NESTED in the array where the flat reader expected its slots spliced in, and a tuple-valued source element was walked one slot at a time. Every user comprehension had the same fault (`(c in cells => (7, c.get()))` read `p.0.1=7,x p.1.0=undefined`). In an instance whose layout `.map` would get wrong, the comprehension is now emitted UNROLLED: the source evaluated once, each element read at its flat offset (a slot, or a `.slice` for a multi-slot element), the body run once per element with the element binder bound to that element's type (so a call inside it specializes per element too), and a tuple-valued result spread in. Where every element and every result is one non-tuple slot the `.map` stays, byte for byte — no golden moved. The comprehension's own mapped type is now recorded once the fixpoint has typed its body, which is what the emitter reads to decide. The native backend refuses a mapped tuple by name and still does; a native-differential pin holds it to never printing a different answer. Three pins in `inference::tuples` — `combine` over a tuple-valued cell, and a user comprehension whose results are tuples and whose element is one (both red before), and the scalar control that keeps the runtime map. Tracker B397 (blocks A122's `entries()`).

<!-- family: miscompile -->
**An expression of unsuffixed literals with a fractional one in it divides as floats when nothing states its type: `1 / 4.0` is `0.25` and `3 / 2.0` is `1.5`, where they printed `0` and `1`.** A literal has no type of its own and the expression's was read off its LEFT operand, so `1 / 4.0` was `i32 / f64`: the checker admitted the mix (B148's numeric-mixing scope defers refusing it), the division verdict was truncating, and the JS build printed `0` while the native build handed rustc `1i32 / 4.0f64` and was refused. A literal-only expression containing a fractional literal now defaults as a WHOLE to `f64` — its integer literals included — in inference, in the operand checks and in the division verdict, and a literal binding it meets as an operand (`let one = 1; one / 4.0`) takes `f64` from it. `1.0 / 4` was already right and stays so; a TYPED integer beside a fractional literal (`y / 2.0` over `y: i32`, which prints `1`) is the deferred mixing family and is not touched here — reported. Found while pinning B389. Two pins in `inference::bounds` (the three shapes, red before; the fractional-left control), and the native-differential literal-position program carries both lines, byte-identical to node.

<!-- family: diagnostics -->
**The missing-member steer renders a supertrait's member at the arguments the supertrait is reached with: `impl Cell with Feed<i32> {}` under `trait Feed<T> with Base<List<T>>` is told to declare `fun read(self): List<i32>`, where it was told `i32`.** The signature was rendered with the `with` clause's own arguments, so `Base`'s `T` was bound positionally to `Feed`'s `i32` — a declaration that would itself have been refused. It now takes the declaring trait's arguments from the same supertrait walk the signature check already uses (B245). Two pins in `inference::traits`: the constructed argument (red before) and the directly implemented trait (a control). Tracker E220.

<!-- family: fix -->
**A let-bound closure whose unannotated parameter feeds a generic position resolves: `let f = |m| wrap(m); f(4)` and `let g = |m| Holder { value = m * 2 }; g(4)` run, where both were "type of variable 'f' could not be resolved".** The parameter's type comes from the closure's own call site (B13), the call site waited on the closure's type, the closure's type waited on its body, and the body waited on the parameter. A stationary fixpoint now breaks the cycle: every still-unfilled parameter of a closure a deferred call names (through `let` bindings) takes its first call site's argument type, when that is fully determined, in source order — B13's own rule, applied before the closure's type exists — and the body resolves on the next pass. It runs before B372's door, which would otherwise commit the body's calls with the parameter still open. A second call at another type is refused against the first, naming the call that typed the parameter. Four pins in `inference::generics`: both shapes and the two-types refusal (red before), and the annotated control. Tracker B392.

<!-- family: fix -->
**A `[service]` written as `export impl Door` beside a plain `impl Peer` holding its client's `[rpc] fun ping` no longer refuses its own generated call: "'ping' is provided by an `impl` in module `main` that `main` does not export" is gone.** `export impl Door` curates the module's exports, so the plain `impl Peer` is not exported — correctly — and the `[service]` expansion's generated proxy calls `ping` from GENERATED code. The call-site export gate asked `source_of` about that call, which answers the `DERIVED_SOURCE` sentinel: a "file" that declares nothing and reached nothing with `#`, so the gate turned down a non-exported block of the call's OWN module. B354 had already ruled that generated code resolves under the module whose attribute generated it (`admitting_file`), and this gate had not been brought into line: it now asks the same question of the same file, and a refusal it does raise about generated code is anchored at the attribute rather than at generated offsets. Premise verified (the item's shape refused; the unexported `impl Door` control compiled); the fix is in the admission, not in `[service]`. One pin in `inference::traits`, red before. Tracker B391.

<!-- family: fix -->
**An `impl` whose subject is refused (`impl Leaf<i32, str>` for a one-parameter `Leaf`) is reported once, at the impl, and provides nothing to anyone.** The refused subject resolved to `unknown`, and `unknown` compares equal to every type, so the block entered every type's candidate set: a call of its trait's member on an innocent type was reported "ambiguous on 'Root': both 'Root' and 'unknown' provide it" at a call site the author did nothing wrong at — and, worse, every type SATISFIED the block's trait, so `shout(5)` for `fun shout<T: Named>` and `5.name()` checked clean. The same skip the refused-field family has: impl candidacy, the bound check and the trait-argument reading all pass over a subject that did not resolve. Two pins in `inference::traits`, both red before: the repro reports ONE diagnostic, the arity refusal, and the block makes no type a `Named` by method call or at a bound. Tracker B390.

<!-- family: fix -->
**A second bound over `T` on a generic function's source parameter no longer stops the argument that determines `T` from binding it: `run<T, K, S: Source<List<T>> + DeltaFeed<T>>(source, |todo: Todo| todo.id)` over a source that is not a list source reports its two real refusals at `Todo`, in either bound order.** Binding `T` from `S`'s bounds read `DeltaFeed`'s arguments from `trait_args_for`, whose fallback hands back a blanket's arguments still abstract when the blanket does not apply (`impl type S: Source<List<type T>> with DeltaFeed<T>` over a `Source<Option<List<T>>>` mirror) — and the caller's `T` was bound to that foreign binder. It was permanent: the key closure could no longer bind `T`, and every bound was reported against an abstract `T` ("does not implement trait 'DeltaFeed<T>'", "'T' is missing the bound ': PartialEq'"). An argument carrying a binder the receiver's own type does not mention is now no evidence; a binder the receiver carries (`Box<T>` inside a generic body) still binds. This is what made A112 S3 put its `DeltaFeed` bound on the `Slot` impls instead of on `each`. Premise: reproduced with a user-declared feed over a mirror-shaped source (three errors naming `T`); std's own `each` with the second bound and the a52 program gives the same two `List<Todo>` errors with or without the fix on this tree. Three pins in `inference::bounds` — the refusal at `Todo` in both bound orders (red before, three errors naming `T`) and a real list source running under both bounds in both orders. Tracker B396.

<!-- family: fix -->
**An unsuffixed literal takes its type from its context in the five positions B370's ruling covered and its fix did not reach: the LEFT operand (`1 + n`, `0 < n`), an annotated list literal's elements (`let xs: List<u53> = [0, 1, 2]`), a `match` pattern (`match n { 0 => .. }`), a generic call's argument under an expected result (`let n: u53 = identity(5)`), and a bare `let n = 0` used later at a type.** All five were refused for every width but `i32` — the literal defaulted and then failed to match — which is the whole of what `usize` (I5 S1) needs before an index can be one without a suffix. A left literal is typed by the right operand as a right literal already was by the left, in inference and in the operand checks alike, so `1 / x` over an `f64` divides as floats; a list literal's literal elements take the numeric element type it is expected at, or a typed sibling's (`[0, n]`); a literal pattern takes the subject's type; a generic parameter only a literal argument fixes takes the numeric type the call's expectation binds it to. The fifth is new machinery: an unannotated binding whose initializer is built from literals (and other such bindings) has no type of its own until a typed USE gives it one — an argument, an annotated read, an operand beside a typed value (`i < limit`, the loop an index walks), an assignment — and it takes `i32` (`f64` with a fraction) only when none does. Such a binding waits in the constraint fixpoint; a stationary fixpoint first looks for an operand or assignment peer and then opens the default, before B372's door; a second use at another width is that use's mismatch. Not `BigInt`: an unsuffixed literal typed `BigInt` still emits a JS number (pre-existing, reported). The native backend reads each literal's settled width, recorded where a numeric context typed it — without that record `0 < n` emitted `0i32 < n` and `identity(5)` emitted `5i32` for a `u64` instance, which rustc refused. Measured: `vilan check` of kolt, 1.668 s → 1.681 s CPU (min of 7, loadavg ~35), diagnostics byte-identical. Pins: fifteen in `inference::bounds`, one per position at `i53`, `u32` and `f64`, all red before; a binding typed by a later use dividing as floats, and one used at two widths refused at the second (both red before); the untyped default and the census's thirteen passing positions at each width as controls (green before and after); and a native-differential program over the five positions, byte-identical to node and red as four rustc refusals with the recorded width removed. The book's lexical spec lists the positions, and the tour's `stamp + 1000` "trap" — already untrue for the right operand — is gone. Tracker B389 (I5 S1's blocker).

<!-- family: fix -->
**A supertrait's DEFAULT member, called on a type that implements the supertrait at other arguments, is no longer refused at a subtrait blanket's bound: `cell.twice()` on a `Base<i32>` beside `impl type S: Base<List<type T>> with Feed<T>` prints 2.** A default no impl declares is reached through every impl whose traits close over its trait — the type's own `impl Cell with Base<i32>`, and the subtrait's blanket, whose bare `S` the receiver fills as a hole. They carry one member, so one was kept, and it was the first REGISTERED: the blanket, whose bound `Cell` meets at the trait id and not at `List<T>`, so the call was refused with "'Cell' does not implement trait 'Base<List<T>>'" though `Cell`'s own impl answers it. An impl whose binders' bounds do not hold for the receiver at their arguments (B268's reading) no longer carries an inherited default while one whose bounds hold does; when none holds the list stands as before, so the bound diagnostic is kept. The same reading had a false NO of its own, harmless until now because it only ever narrowed: a bound whose argument is another of the impl's binders (`impl KeyedSource<type K: Wire + Hashable, type T: Wire + Keyed<K>>`) was checked with `K` unsubstituted, so the mirror's own impl answered "does not hold" for the mirror — its arguments are now read through what the receiver binds. This is what A112 S3's ruled `trait DeltaFeed<T> with Source<List<T>>` waited on: with it in std, `reactive-on-change.vl`'s custom `Source<i32>` (`sub`, `map`), a keyed mirror's `effect_on_change` (a `Source<Option<List<T>>>`) and the native differential's corpus leg were refused; with this fix and the switch applied the whole workspace suite passes (8313 tests, `VILAN_NATIVE_DIFFERENTIAL=1`), and the switch itself is collections-41's commit. Six pins in `inference::bounds`, four red before the fix: the item's repro, the ruled std shape as a user fixture (both blankets; `sub`/`map` on a custom `Source<i32>`, a `SignalCell<i32>` and a list-valued custom source, and the feed answered per source kind through the supertrait), the same shape refusing a `Source<i32>` as a feed with exactly one error, and a keyed-mirror miniature (red with only the argument substitution removed); the type's-impl-first ordering and the matching-arguments control were green before and stay so. B394's five soundness pins and B387's five stay green. Spec `types.md` §5.5 says the bound is read at its arguments. Tracker B395.

<!-- family: tooling -->
**`vilan fmt` measures a declaration on its OWN line: a long attribute line above a signature no longer splits the signature, and a short one no longer hides an over-budget signature from the width rule.** E219: `[deprecated("…110 characters…")] fun one(a: i32, b: i32): i32` reprinted one parameter per line, because the width rule measured the FIRST line of the item's rendering, which was the attribute. An attribute line is a line with a budget of its own that nothing breaks; the declaration's line is the one the rule is about. The printer now marks where the declaration line starts whenever it has printed attribute lines above it (a function's ordered prefix, a type's labels, `[derive]`, `[service]`/`[client_service]`, a user macro attribute) and measures from there; a statement inside a body keeps its own mark and leaves the enclosing item's alone, so a function whose body holds statements is measured by its own signature. The same bug ran the other way, and the estate had four of them: an over-budget `external fun` under a short `[extern(..)]` line was measured by the attribute and never split — `std::fs`'s `raw_read`/`raw_write`, `std::rpc`'s `reply_promise`, and one each in the `canvas` and `walkthrough` examples now split one parameter per line, the declaration width rule's shape (`vilan fmt` over the tree; the only change `fmt --check vilan crates` reports). Pins: the item's repro reprinting unchanged (a body with statements included), every attribute-carrying position (a labelled generic struct, a method under a long `[deprecated]` and `[must_use]`, a long `[derive]` line), and the control — an over-budget signature still splits under a short attribute and under a long one — red with the mark ignored and red with the body's statements clobbering it. Tracker E219.

<!-- family: feature -->
**`[deprecated("use …")]` now labels a struct, an enum, a trait, a module binding and a RE-EXPORT, with the function attribute's own warning at each use in another module — and the editor strikes a deprecated name through.** B382 (ruled R-c): A112's "deprecated `KeyedCursor` re-export" was inexpressible, and the lane did a hard rename; Order 40 measured that the renaming re-export itself already existed (`export import pkg::inner::DeltaCursor as KeyedCursor;` compiles, runs and is transparent), and that only the attribute was missing. It now leads a type's prefix (`[deprecated("use Next")] struct Previous { … }`, before `[internal]` and `[platform]`), and rides an `export import`: `export [deprecated("use pkg::inner::DeltaCursor")] import pkg::inner::DeltaCursor as KeyedCursor;` deprecates the NAME `KeyedCursor` while the item stays the item (a `KeyedCursor` literal still passes where a `DeltaCursor` is wanted). A use of a deprecated type in another module — the import, an annotation, a literal's head — warns `` `KeyedThing` is deprecated; use DeltaCursor ``, the function's warning word for word (so no new ledger row); every other module's import that reaches a deprecated re-export warns at its leaf, decided over the resolved imports (the re-export's own import names its target), and importing the item from where it is declared does not warn. The declaring module's own uses are silent, as std's are for a deprecated function. NO type alias was built (R-c: no customer; `import … as` already is one). A `[deprecated]` import that is not exported publishes nothing and is refused where it is written (the steer rides the `export`, which also kept `Import`'s already-wide payload inside `node_size`'s 96 bytes), and since the shared prefix (which admits `[platform]` on an `impl` for F27) also parsed `[deprecated]`/`[internal]` there, an `impl` carrying either is refused and pointed at its members. In the editor a deprecated declaration and every use carry the LSP's standard `deprecated` semantic-token modifier (a theme strikes it through — E213's mechanism, read off one reader, `labels::deprecated_of`, so a deprecated function and method are struck now too), and hover leads with `**deprecated** — use …`. Pins: the parse on each position and the prefix order, the formatter's reprint, the run-time meaning unchanged, the two refusals, through the binary the type warned three times from another module and never from its own, the renaming and the non-renaming re-export each warned once at the importing leaf, and a program loading the re-exporting module while importing the original from its home warned only for the name actually reached through the re-export; and in the language server the modifier at the declaration and a use (not on the replacement) and the hover's lead — red with the sweep, both refusals and the modifier each planted out. Tracker B382 (R-c, 2026-09-24).

<!-- family: feature -->
**A file can say which platform it is: `[platform("browser")];` as its first line makes everything in it require `browser` and is the platform the file is ANALYZED under — outranking inference and the `default-entry` colour — and a function's `[platform(..)]` fence now decides how its own body resolves.** The owner's case (F27): a module over `std::ui`'s `Region` that nothing reaches yet, in a package whose `default-entry` is the server, is typed under the process twin, where `region.anchor` does not exist; R2's member evidence could not reach it because `default-entry` outranks inference, and R6's note could only explain it. Now the file writes `[platform("browser")];` — the fence's attribute with a `;`, which is what tells it from a fence on the file's first function, and legal only as the file's first statement (anywhere else it is refused and told to move above the first import). It does three things. **It is the analysis platform**: `platform_color::file_platform_choices` applies it on top of the package's colour — of the legs that reach the file only those it admits type-check it, and when none does (the owner's `default-entry`, a package `target`, an unreached file) it is analyzed under the declared platform, with the reason `it declares `[platform("browser")]`` — and the language server reads the declaration off the LIVE buffer, so it takes effect before the file is saved; a bare file with no project honours it too, on the terminal as in the editor. **Everything inside requires it**: a node entry reaching `when_value` in that file is the colouring chain error (`` `when_value` requires the `browser` platform its file declares and cannot run on `node:24` `` / `reachable from the entry: main → render → when_value`), exactly as reaching a layer module's item is. **It is a fence on every function in the file**, checked on every compile, and all of them make ONE promise — an off-platform call reached from twenty of them reports once. The same attribute on an `impl` block does the second and third for the block's members; on an `impl`, a struct, an enum or a trait it also takes part in choosing the analysis platform, and so does a function's own fence: a file is analyzed under a platform every declaration in it admits whenever its colour admits none of them (declarations that share no platform are R3's twins, and the colour stands; a type requires nothing, since a requirement is on code). **In the editor**: the status bar says `analyzed as: browser — declared` (or `node — default-entry`, `— entry`, `— inferred`, …) for the active vilan file with the whole reason as its tooltip, answered by a new server request, `vilan/analysisPlatform`; R6's twin note now ends by naming the attribute (`` `[platform("browser")];` at the top of the file analyzes it under that platform ``), and a new quick fix, **Analyze this file under its platform: add `[platform("browser")];`**, inserts exactly that at the file's first line. NOT built, and reported: a server leg that LOADS a browser-declared module still type-checks it under node, so a wrong-twin field error still appears in that leg beside the chain — turning it off is R3's invariant (an item is checked only under a platform it admits), which needs its paper before codegen may run over code that did not type-check. The grammar gains `module-platform` and `platform-attr` (on `impl`, `struct`, `enum`, `trait`); spec §11.3 states the rules. Pins: the parse (the file head, the refusal at three other positions, an `impl`'s and a nominal's label), the formatter's reprint, the resolver's own rules (module-level outranking the colour and filtering a shared module's legs, items deciding only where no colour admits them, twins declaring nothing, `@process` analyzing as node), the requirement and the one-promise fence and an `impl`'s scope in `inference`, an unknown pattern reported once, the CLI end to end (the owner's module clean in file mode, a fenced body resolving under its fence, the chain from a server entry, a bare file, the note naming the attribute), the language server (declared over `default-entry`, the undeclared reason, the live buffer, the quick fix whose edit analyzes clean, the status request) and the extension's status line — red with the resolver, the seed, the one-promise key, the quick fix and the no-project path each planted out. Tracker F27 R1 (ruled 2026-09-21).

<!-- family: feature -->
**`[internal("reason")]` now labels a struct, an enum, one enum variant, a trait and a module binding, and a package can ask to be warned at their uses: `[lints] internal_use = "warn"`.** E213 shipped the label on functions, methods, externals and struct fields; E221 is the rest of the surface a reader can be steered away from. On a struct, an enum or a trait it leads the declaration (ahead of `resource`, and after an `export` or a `[derive(..)]`, as on a function); on a variant it leads the variant, as on a field; on a module binding it is a labelled `let` statement (`[internal("…")] let cache = …;`, `lazy` and `mut` included). The editor treats every kind as it treats a function: hidden from completion unless the typed prefix is an exact prefix of three characters or more (`Side::` offers `Left` and not `Auto`; `Side::Aut` offers `Auto`, sorted last with the reason as its detail), dimmed by the `internal` semantic-token modifier at the declaration and at every use — a type position included — and leading its hover. A variant reached through its enum's path (`Side::Auto`) is now painted at its LEAF: it was one token spanning the whole path, which the overlap filter dropped against the enum's own, so no enum variant in a path was ever painted by the server. A label on a LOCAL binding is refused (`` `x` is a local binding, and `[internal(..)]` labels an item on a module's surface … ``): the parser reads a labelled `let` wherever a statement stands, because a module and a function body share the production, and only the finished program knows which bindings are the module's. **`[lints]` is a new `vilan.toml` section** — in all four places a manifest key lives (the parsed `Manifest`, the language server's completion listing, the editor's JSON schema, the book) — with one lint, `internal_use`, `"allow"` by default: at `"warn"`, every import and use of an internal item in the package's own code outside the module that declares it warns `` `{name}` is internal: {reason} ``; the declaring module's own uses, std's and a dependency's stay silent, and a lint name or a level the section does not have is a manifest error rather than a silent no-op. The check runs as a post-pass over the finished program (`vilan_core::labels`), so the CLI and the language server both carry it, and every reader of a label asks the one function, `labels::internal_of`, so the editor and the lint cannot disagree about a name. NOT built: the item's "docs generator's collapsed Internal heading" — there is no docs generator in the tree (the book is hand-written, which Order 39 also found for E204), and building one is new CLI surface. Pins: the parse on every position (and a bare `[internal]`, a destructuring `let`, refused); the formatter's byte-identical reprint of every position; the program meaning nothing different at run time; the local refusal; no warning without the manifest; the lint end to end through the binary (each of five kinds warned from `main.vl`, the declaring module's own read not, and silence under `allow` and with no section); the manifest's parse, default and refusals; the `[lints]` completion; and five in the language server (bare-list hiding, the three-character return with the reason, a variant after `Side::`, the modifier on every kind at declaration and use, hover leading for a struct, a trait in a bound, a binding and a variant) — red with the lint, the refusal, the completion reads and the leaf narrowing each planted out. Tracker E221 (E213 S2).

<!-- family: tooling -->
**In VS Code a generic `<` now pairs AND its `>` types over: `List<` gets its `>`, and typing the `>` yourself moves past it instead of leaving `List<i32>>`.** E202 made the server place the `>` of a `<` opened in type position (`onTypeFormatting`), and that half could never be finished from the server: VS Code types over a closing character only when it auto-inserted it itself, and an edit cannot move the caret. A static `autoClosingPairs` entry would buy the overtype and also grow a `>` in every `a < b`, because its `notIn` filter sees only string, comment and regex scopes and the token left of the caret is the same for `List<` and `a <` — so E214's configuration route could not work (Order 40 measured it). The extension now overrides VS Code's `type` command behind a new setting, `vilan.autoClosing.generics` (on by default): every keystroke still goes through `default:type` unchanged; after a `<` it asks the server a new custom request, `vilan/opensAGenericList` (the very rule `onTypeFormatting` applies), and on a yes places the `>` itself in the `<`'s own undo step; a `>` typed onto a `>` it placed moves the caret past it — the placed set follows every edit and is forgotten once the caret leaves its line. Keystrokes queue behind a pending answer (bounded at 150 ms) so nothing typed after a `<` lands before its `>`, and a `>` is placed only before the characters the language configuration's own `autoCloseBefore` names, so `List|i32` does not become `List<>i32`. The extension declares the override in `initializationOptions` (`autoClosing.generics`, re-sent live when it is toggled), and the server's `onTypeFormatting` then stands down for `<`; a client that declares nothing keeps today's edit. It is a setting because only one extension can own `type`: turn it off to coexist with Vim emulation, and if another extension already owns the command the override stays absent, says so on the output channel and the server keeps placing the `>`. Pins: in the server, the declaration parsed, the stand-down (red with it removed), the edit kept for a client that declares nothing, and the request answering the on-type rule; the TS half is pinned textually in `vscode_extension.rs` (the setting and why, the type-through, the queue, the overtype, and the two `autoCloseBefore` lists held equal) and the request name and declaration key in `book_sync` beside the executed command — all red on the base files. Tracker E222 (ruled 2026-09-22).

<!-- family: feature -->
**`over_http_with(mount, codec, headers)`: a generated rpc client can carry a header credential on every POST, so a page that keeps its token in storage can reach a service gated by `authorize_request`.** `over_http` builds a client over `HttpTransport`, which sends nothing but the leg's media type — a cookie rides a same-origin POST on its own, but a bearer token has to be written, and there was nowhere to write it. Every `[service]` that gets `over_http` now also gets `over_http_with`, which takes the same mount and codec plus a `List<(str, str)>` of headers and builds the client over a new `std::rpc::HeaderedHttpTransport { url, headers }`; the headers are sent after the media type on every call the client makes, over the JSON codec's text frames and the binary codec's byte frames alike: `AuthClient::over_http_with("/auth/", json_codec(), [("Authorization", i"Bearer {token}")])`. It is a second transport rather than a field on `HttpTransport` because vilan has no field defaults, and a field would have broken every `HttpTransport { url }` written today. Both transports now share one `post_frame`, so B374's guarded POST-and-read is written once. `std::fetch` gains `post_bytes_with_headers(url, body, headers: List<Header>)`, which `post_bytes` and `post_bytes_typed` now call — a byte body with a media type and a credential together. **A focus SCOPE in std: `Element::tabbable` walks the tab order, and `focus_scope(root, Contain | Wrap)` traps Tab inside an overlay without `inert`.** A121 S1, from `proposal/focus-scope.md` §3-§5. **The query is a WALK and the famous selector is its documented definition**, which is not the same thing: half of that selector — every tag in it — is what `tab_index` already answers, because the host reflects the attribute with a per-tag default and knows its own focusable set; and the half a selector cannot answer honestly is the SUBTREE, since `inert` and `hidden` disable everything under them and `[inert] *` still misses a scope root that is itself inside an inert ancestor. So `is_tabbable` reads its five predicates off the element and its ancestors, in cost order: a negative `tabindex` (the author's opt-out, and every tag that is not focusable at all), `disabled` (which keeps its `tabIndex` of 0), an `inert`/`hidden` ancestor, a resolved `visibility: hidden` (which INHERITS, so one read answers for an ancestor too, and which no measurement can see because a hidden element keeps its box), and a 0x0 box, which is `display: none` anywhere above. `tabbable` answers them in TAB order — positive `tabindex` values first in ascending order, then document order, the HTML specification's sequential focus order restricted to a subtree — which is why it hands back a `List` rather than leaving the caller with a document-ordered query. `focus_first` focuses the first of them, or, when a panel holds nothing tabbable, the panel ITSELF at `tabindex="-1"`: programmatically focusable and not a tab stop, which is exactly what the hand-written `panel.focus()` fallback in every overlay was trying to be and never was — a bare `<div>` is not a focusable area, so that call has always done nothing. **The scope is two mechanisms and a stack.** The WRAP is a capture-phase `keydown` on the window that answers Tab at the ENDS of the order and does nothing in between, so the platform moves focus; focus sitting on the panel itself — where the fallback leaves it — enters the order at its near end rather than escaping. The GUARD, for `Contain` only, is a capture-phase `focusin` that pulls focus back when it arrives outside. Neither writes anything outside the panel, which is the whole point: the rest of the page stays pointer-live and stays in the accessibility tree, where `inert` would take it out of both — `inert` stays the app's own escape hatch and the doc comment says so. **Nesting is a STACK because an overlay is a portal**: a submenu opened from inside a menu mounts beside its parent's panel, not inside it, so `menu.contains(submenu)` is false and a containment test written on DOM ancestry yanks focus out of a submenu the moment it opens. The stack lives in std rather than in every driver, the guard belongs to whichever `Contain` scope is TOPMOST at event time (read from the stack in the handler, not captured at registration, which is what lets a nested scope take over and hand back), and a scope pops in its owner's `defer` — so its lifetime is its boundary's by construction. Disposal restores focus to whatever held it at install, under both honest guards: only if focus is still OURS (an app that moved focus deliberately keeps it) and only if the remembered element is still in the document (focusing a detached element sends focus to `<body>`, which is worse than leaving it). Five e2e pins over the real DOM stub — the walk with one element per reason it can be dropped and one per position in the order, the wrap at both ends and in the middle and OUTSIDE the scope (the page stays live), the guard with a nested scope taking over and handing back, and the restore with both of its guards — each proven non-vacuous by planting the mechanism away. The process twin declares the surface name for name and drops it, as `on_mount` and `autofocus` do. Tracker A121.

<!-- family: diagnostics -->
**A global host PROPERTY bound in the function form is refused where it is written, instead of emitting a call to it.** `[extern("document.activeElement")]` emits `document.activeElement()` — the function form of `[extern]` addresses a CALLABLE, which is what makes `[extern("history.pushState")]` and `[extern("Math.max")]` work — so binding a property through it ships a program that compiles clean, passes `vilan check`, and dies at the first line that reaches it with "is not a function". std paid this coin three separate times before anyone wrote it down: `__dom_window`, `__router_path` and now `__dom_active_element` are all runtime helpers that exist ONLY because the value on the other side is a property. The refusal is a TABLE and has to be — nothing in a host binding says whether the name on the other side is callable, so the honest scope is the globals whose shape the web platform and node fix, which is also the set an author actually reaches for (`document.*`, `location.*`, `window.*`, `navigator.*`, `history.state`, `screen.*`, the two storages, `process.env`/`argv`/`platform`/`std*`). A name outside the table binds exactly as before; this refuses what it KNOWS is wrong rather than guessing at what might be. The message names both spellings that work: `[extern(get, "..")]` when the property hangs off a value the program holds, and a runtime helper for a true global, which has no receiver. One ledger row, four pins — the dotted global spanning its own declaration, a bare global, an UNCALLED binding (refused at the declaration, so an unreached branch cannot ship it), and the controls, where the helper, the getter and a dotted global the table does not know all still compile. Tracker N113 (the fourth edge; A121 is what found it).

<!-- family: feature -->
**`std::dom` can read what a focus scope has to know: `tab_index`, `parent`, `has_attribute`, `computed_style`, `active_element`, `Event::related_target` — and the test DOM answers all six.** A121's prerequisite, and the slice that makes the rest of it pinnable rather than argued. `tab_index` is the DOM's own answer to "is this in the tab order" — the attribute reflected with a PER-TAG DEFAULT, so `-1` for a bare `<div>`, `0` for `<a href>`/`<button>`/`<input>`/`[contenteditable]`, the written value otherwise — which is what lets a focus walk carry no tag table of its own. `parent` is `parentElement`, the step an ancestor walk takes, because `inert` and `hidden` disable a whole SUBTREE and a selector cannot express that honestly. `has_attribute` is the read half of a boolean attribute, whose write half (`set_attribute`/`remove_attribute`) std has had since it had elements. `computed_style` is the RESOLVED value, and it exists for one predicate nothing else can make: a `visibility: hidden` element KEEPS ITS BOX, so `offset_width`/`offset_height` see it as laid out, and `visibility` inherits, so the resolved value answers for a hidden ancestor with no walk. `active_element` and `computed_style` reach the host through the two new runtime helpers (`__dom_active_element`, `__dom_computed_style`) for `window()`'s reason — a global PROPERTY has no function form — and the interpreter answers the whole `__dom_*` family as a capability MISS by design rather than as the "unknown host call" an unlisted name fell to, which read as a compiler bug to anyone who wrote `window()` in a macro. **The harness grew with them, and that half is pinned too**: the shared DOM stub reflects `tabIndex` with the specification's per-tag default, answers `parentElement` and `hasAttribute`, resolves a style through an inheritance walk for `visibility`, admits the UNIVERSAL selector `*` in the scoped `querySelectorAll` (every descendant, in document order — an enumeration, not a predicate, which is what a walk wants), and DISPATCHES `focusin` on a focus that takes, carrying `relatedTarget`. Without that last one a containment guard cannot fire at all. One pin reads all of it back through a program, so a stub that stops answering reds there rather than leaving a walk quietly finding nothing; proven non-vacuous by planting the missing per-tag default and the missing dispatch, each red on its own line. Tracker A121 (paper `proposal/focus-scope.md` §7, §8).

**A counter that could only ever read zero is gone, and what the arm it watched actually does is written down.** B365 repaired the drop-planner enrolment gate's struct-literal arm — it had been comparing a literal's own expression id against the set of struct DECLARATION ids, so it answered `false` for every program there has ever been — and wired a counter beside it, because the repair is not observable any other way: the check above the arm reads the literal's recorded type and asks the same question through `type_mentions_nominal`, so the arm can only decide a literal the solver gave a definition and no type. The counter was the instrument that would show the day one arrived. It never has. Measured rather than argued: solver-39's seven shapes, five more here (a generic wrapper, a module-level binding, an enum payload, an argument position, a helper's return), and a probe planted at the arm itself — which shows it is REACHED about twenty times per analysis of any std-importing program, always for a literal whose type does not reach a resource, and never once the thing that decided. So the counter goes, with the pin that read it and asserted nothing about it; a vacuous pin is worse than none. The arm STAYS, as the "constructed" leg of the walk's completeness argument, with all of that written at it, and B365's surviving pin says in as many words that it pins the ROUTE and would pass with the arm removed. Tracker B384.

<!-- family: performance -->
**A hover on a struct field no longer costs the workspace.** `field_at_offset` — the answer behind a hover on a field's declaration or on a struct-initializer key (E204) — walked `program.structs`, every struct in the loaded WORLD, paying a `source_of` on each before discovering it was not the open buffer's, and then walked every initializer key in the world. Hover fires on MOVE. The rows are now an offset-ordered table built with the analysis, exactly as `entity_spans` is, and the answer is a bisect. Measured in thread CPU time, release, loadavg 9–11, the old scan re-planted beside the index so both sides ran on the same build and the same box, over the item's own shape — a small open buffer inside a generated workspace of 20 and of 500 ten-field structs, the buffer held fixed so workspace size is isolated from file size — **the lookup went from 0.71 µs at 270 fields and 6.5–12.7 µs at 5,070 (9–18x the cost for 19x the fields) to 0.02–0.09 µs at both, three runs**, and the whole hover request from 3.0 µs / 10.3–12.9 µs to 2.3 µs / 3.5 µs: the field lookup was nearly all of the growth in that request. **The first measurement of this was wrong and is worth recording**, because it is how a perf item closes on the wrong number: taken over an exhibit that put all 500 structs in the entry itself, and over `document.hover` rather than the lookup, it read 23x and blamed a scan that was one percent of it. The exhibit shape and the subject both had to be the item's before the number meant anything. Pinned by a COUNT and not a clock (N116's rule, one file over): twenty workspace structs and five hundred give the open buffer the same sixteen-row table, which is the property an index has and a scan does not, and which does not move when the box is busy — red at 283 rows with the entry filter removed. The microseconds live in an `#[ignore]`d measurement beside it, where they can be read and not failed on. Tracker M85.

**`[derive(PartialOrd)]` is refused at the attribute instead of expanding to nothing.** A derive name nothing declares a macro for — not std, not this file, nothing it imports — was accepted silently, on the recorded reasoning that an unknown derive is a missing macro and the missing impl reports itself at the use site. It does, and the use site is the wrong place to learn it: the program was clean, and forty lines later `a < b` said "type `P` does not implement the `PartialOrd` operator; add `impl P with PartialOrd`" — advice to hand-write the impl the author believed the attribute had just asked for. A program that never compares said nothing at all, and shipped without a derive it declares. The refusal names the derive, says nothing declares a macro for it, and lists what IS derivable, because a "no" with no next step is half a diagnostic. **The list it prints is `STD_DERIVE_MACROS`, and that table is now held to std's own `macro fun`s in both directions** — the item's "one list": a row std does not back offers a name that expands to nothing, which is this very defect one level up, and a derive-shaped `macro fun` std grows without a row is refused as though std had never declared it. The inverse walk covers the whole of `std/src` rather than the modules the table names, because deriving the search set from the table is how an omission hides (measured: the first draft passed with `Hashable` deleted). `[service]` is the one exemption, by name: same shape, dispatched by a different node. The other three states each keep their own sentence — a macro in scope expands, a macro world skips, and a std derive whose module did not register still gets the toolchain or load-order report. Pins: the refusal, its list, a one-character typo on a real derive, all six std derives still expanding on a struct and an enum, and a user's own `macro fun` derive still dispatching. Ledger row `NEW`. Tracker B376.

**The std twin-parity gate says what it means by "surface", and it is the EXPORTED one — which retired fourteen of its twenty-six recorded divergences.** The gate holds `std::ui`'s browser and process halves to the same names, because the same component source compiles through both; nothing said whether a PRIVATE declaration counted, and it did. That made the gate ask a second question it was never built for — do the two files read alike — and that question has a wrong answer: the browser twin routes SVG tags through a `createElementNS` helper where the process twin seeds an `xmlns` attribute inline, and neither is a divergence anybody can observe. It cost real work, most recently a std lane naming the process twin's inlined body `place_when_some` so the two lists would match. The contract is now written at the file's head: the module scope's exported bindings, plus every member of every type declared there — members deliberately unfiltered, because a method reached through a receiver belongs to the type's surface wherever the type does, and `Region.host` is a real divergence only the member half sees. The predicate is the analyzer's own `is_exported_in`, so a twin that curates nothing still offers everything. Fourteen allowlist entries — `mount_target`, `is_svg_tag`, `settled_steps`, the chunk-state helpers, `is_void_element` and the rest — turn out to have been exemptions for implementation choices, each one a standing licence for whatever took the name later; the list's own both-directions check named all fourteen at once, which it now does rather than one per run. The choice is pinned over the real twins (`mount` in, `mount_target` out, `place_when_some` in neither, `View.`'s members still read), red against the filter removed. Tracker N118.

**Two pins that could red for reasons that had nothing to do with the code they guard no longer can — and the rule that would have caught both is written at each suite's head: no assertion reads a clock.** M75's collision-refusal bound asserted milliseconds off `/proc/self/stat`, which is the whole PROCESS's CPU: under `nextest -j 32` every sibling test thread lands in it, and the small leg's delta came back as `-10 ms` — a negative value for the quantity being measured, which is not a regression and not a pass. The millisecond half is gone; the COUNT half (M77's `carried` rows, bounded by the FILES and not by the statement count) was always the same sentence said over a number the pass itself produces, and it keeps its own non-vacuity asserts. The durations are still measured and still printed beside the load average, because they are the right thing to READ when somebody suspects that pass. The native differential's spawn-and-sleep ordering probe slept 1 ms and 12 ms, so a 12 ms scheduling stall left both timers overdue — at which point node fires them in INSERTION order and the native executor in DEADLINE order, and two correct runtimes printed different bytes. 5 ms and 500 ms is the same claim with a stall budget. That probe also now STATES the order it exists for rather than only asking whether the two backends agree: `compare` is a byte equality, so a change that inverted the deadline list on both would have satisfied it. Proven by inverting the two deadlines, which reds on the spelled-out stdout. Tracker N116.

**The completion engine has pins in the crate that implements it.** Every completion test lived in `vilan-lsp`'s integration suite, one protocol layer up, so the engine's own rules were only ever checked through a `Document` — and the playground calls the same `Analysis::completion` with no `Document` anywhere. `vilan-ide` now builds an `Analysis` itself, field for field the one `Document::analysis` builds (a real analysis of a real program against the real `std`, which is the point: a pin needing a different `Analysis` than a front end can build would pin a shape nobody runs), and asks the engine directly. Seeded with E211's three — the span a candidate replaces, the text the client filters it against, and a construct snippet's ranking kind — plus a harness pin so a red says whether the rule moved or the fixture stopped analyzing. Each of the five was shown red against a planted defect: the hyphen dropped from `hyphenated_word_start` (the two hyphenated positions), `filter_text` left unstamped (those two and the every-candidate pin), and the two controls against their own inversions — the hyphen rule applied in expression position, where `a-b` is subtraction, and a construct snippet losing its kind. A future completion behaviour adds its pin here rather than in `vilan-lsp`, which is why the file exists. Tracker N115.

**`()` and `void`: the two spellings the grammar took and the language has no meaning for are refused where they are written.** Three of N113's four holes; all three had the same shape — a form that parsed, could never work, and was reported somewhere other than where it was typed. **`()` in type position** parsed as the EMPTY tuple, and no expression produces one, so a field, parameter or return written at it was uninhabited and the author read `Expected (), but got void instead: this body ends without producing a value` about the body they had just written correctly. It is refused at the spelling now, naming `void`; the production is the ordinary tuple type's, so only the arity-zero case moved, and `g<()>()` moved with it from the parse corpus's accept list to its decliner list. **A binder named `void`** was accepted and could never be read back: the atom production reads every `void` as the unit value unconditionally, so `let void = 3; let x: i32 = void;` was refused about the READ, with the binding three characters away and innocent. One binder production serves `let`, a `for` header, a function parameter and a match capture, so one refusal covers all four — and only binders, because a struct field or a method named `void` is reached through a receiver and reads back perfectly well. The spec's contextual-keyword sentence gains that exception. **And §3's `literal` production** offered `NUMBER | STRING | "true" | "false" | "null"` — five alternatives for a language with six literals, describing one in which the unit value cannot be written. `void` joins it, held by a pin that reads the production by name rather than by the coverage check that only asks whether the word appears somewhere (it appeared, in two prose sentences, which is how this stayed invisible). The fourth hole — `[extern("document.activeElement")]` emitting a CALL to a property — is ui-40's. Tracker N113.

**The language server's analysis fence is pinned, and its internal-error diagnostic now NAMES the file it could not analyze.** B385 took the server down with the analyzer, so N119 asked what an analyzer abort actually costs an editing session. Two of the three answers were already true and nothing held them: `Document::analyze_cancellable` runs the whole pipeline on a dedicated 128 MiB-stack thread, and a panic inside it degrades to the internal-error document rather than unwinding through the `join` and out of whichever handler asked (B40). That containment is now a pin — a planted `unreachable!()` keyed on one entry path, asserting the degraded document, its diagnostic, and that the NEXT analysis runs the normal path and still answers a hover. It is doubly fenced, which the pin's own note records: the thread body's `catch_unwind` and the `join`'s `Err` arm each contain the panic alone, and removing BOTH is what reds it. The diagnostic said "this file", which names nothing in the output channel a bug report is pasted from and nothing at all when a sweep lands several at once; it names the entry path now, and the ledger row is re-keyed (292, the LSP flavor; 293, the compiler's, is unchanged). **The third answer is that a stack overflow is not containable at this seam and never was.** Rust's guard-page handler prints `thread '…' has overflowed its stack` and calls `abort()` from ANY thread, whatever its stack size, so `join()` never returns and there is no `Err` to observe — measured on this host at exit 134, with the line after the join never reached. The guard that ends an unbounded walk therefore has to live in the walk, which is what B385's own fix is; a stack-remaining probe inside the analyzer's recursive descents would generalize it, and is written down at the fence rather than built here. Tracker N119.

**`[internal("reason")]` marks an item that is part of the surface and dangerous to reach for — the editor hides it, dims it and leads its hover with the reason.** Visibility answers whether a module may NAME an item; this answers whether a reader should reach for one that is named. The exhibit is std's own: `std::ui`'s `Region` exports `anchor` and its row methods because `each` and a hand-written `Slot` legitimately need them, and a row moved through them without `hold_rows` corrupts the reconciler's view — public on purpose and dangerous on purpose, with no way to say so. **The reason is required**, `[deprecated("…")]`'s shape, because it is what the editor shows and a label with no reason is how these rot. Completion omits the name unless what is already typed is an exact prefix of three characters or more, and what survives that is sorted after every other candidate with the reason as its detail; a new `internal` semantic-token modifier dims every use AND the declaration (dimmed, never struck through — the item is not going away); hover leads with the reason. **Nothing warns and nothing refuses**: the item stays exported, callable and emitted exactly as before — this is a label, not a lint. It takes two positions in this slice, the two the ruling's first std customers need: a function or method (free, in an `impl`, or an `external` — std's runtime seams are often externals), and a struct FIELD, which is the case declaration visibility cannot serve at all, since vilan has no per-field visibility. std's `Region.anchor` and its five row methods carry it in both ui twins. The retired `[doc(hidden)]`'s refusal now names it as the other thing somebody reaching for that marker may have wanted. Pins: the parse on both positions and the refusal of a bare `[internal]`; the formatter round-trip (an attribute with no printer arm makes `vilan fmt` decline every file that carries one); and six in the language server — absent from a bare list, back on three characters with its reason, absent on two, the field after a dot both ways, hover's lead line at a use and at a field declaration, and the modifier at a declaration, at a use, and NOT on the field beside it. Tracker E213 (RULED 2026-09-21).

**Format-on-save honours your package's `[fmt]` section, and one comment run can be re-filled on demand.** E205 gave `vilan fmt` the `wrap_comments` key and left the editor reading the formatter's defaults, so an opted-in package wrapped its comments from the command line and not from a save — the two formatters in the toolchain disagreeing about the same file. It is offered with the cursor in a comment and only where the wrap changes something — a run already filled, one no line of which is over the width, a trailing comment after code, and each of E205's ten never-reflow classes answer with no action at all, because in every one of those the reprint with the wrap on and the reprint with it off are the same text. That comparison is also why there is no second implementation of the paragraph rule here: the fill, its ten refusals and its width are the printer's own, asked through the entry point format-on-save already takes, so the action and the save cannot answer differently about one comment. The edit it hands back is therefore the whole buffer. **A service can gate its connectionless `POST {mount}rpc` leg per request: `Service::authorize_request(|request| ..)`, a second hook beside `authorize`, whose `Session` rides on the request.** A service with `authorize` refused its POST leg outright — 401, deliberately, because the leg has no handshake for `authorize` to read and leaving it open would be the back door around the gate — so a service reached over plain HTTP (`over_http`) could not be gated at all. A POST has no subprotocol list, but it has headers: `authorize_request` runs on each POST after the leg's own method and content-type checks and before the frame is read; `Ok(session)` is stamped on that request's new `RpcRequest.session` (a hand-written `Dispatcher` route reads it), and `Err(reject)` answers the reject's own status — 401/403 as a `Failure(Unauthorized)` envelope and 503 as `Failure(Unavailable)`, the arms a refused socket already gives a vilan client, and 429 as a bare status a client reads as `Transport(..)`. A second hook rather than `authorize` reading a request, because the credential lives elsewhere (`Handshake::token()` answering `None` for a request with a perfectly good `Authorization` header would be a trap). The two compose and neither opens the other's leg: `authorize` alone still answers the POST 401, a good bearer included; `authorize_request` alone leaves the socket open; both gate both. A `Service::factory` service stays 501 on the POST leg whatever the hook says. `Session` moves to `std::rpc` (it is re-exported from `std::rpc_server`, so every existing import still names it), and a socket's session is stamped on its requests too. Pins: `service_layer`'s `the_two_hooks_compose_per_the_table_and_neither_opens_the_others_leg` (the four rows on both legs, the three reject arms, the session reaching a hand route, the factory's 501) and `a_vilan_client_refused_per_request_reads_the_arm_a_refused_socket_reads`. (A120 S4, `transport-rpc.md` §9.7.6)

<!-- family: feature -->
**The `POST {mount}rpc` leg answers the STATUS its envelope earns — 400 for a decode failure, 404 for an unknown method, 405 for a non-POST, 501 as an envelope — and requires a content type, which is the whole CSRF posture.** The leg answered **200** for everything the protocol itself decided, and the reason that survived is that `HttpTransport::call` never read `response.status()`: it read the body and handed it to the codec. So a vilan client cannot notice this change, which is what makes it non-breaking and what makes it worth doing — the status is the contract for everything that is *not* a vilan client: curl, a `fetch` in a page, a proxy, a load balancer, a monitoring probe. **The rule: the envelope is the vilan client's contract, the status is everyone else's, and the two never disagree.** An application error stays a **200** (Q5, ruled NEVER): `Result<Token, str>`'s `Err` arm is a value that crossed successfully, and a server answering 401 for "wrong password" would be claiming the CALL was unauthorized — a different fact, and the one `authorize` reports. The cost is stated in the guide rather than hidden: a dashboard reading statuses alone cannot see application errors, because they are not errors of the transport. Two things that were not statuses at all: a **GET** on the rpc route was answered as though it were a POST with an empty body (nothing read `request.method()`) and is now 405 with an `Allow`; and a `Service::factory` service's 501 was a plain-text sentence, so a vilan client meeting it read `Decode("unrecognized reply envelope")` about it — it is an envelope now, and reads as a typed `Remote(..)`. **The content-type gate is the security half**, and it costs one comparison: the leg requires `application/json` or `application/octet-stream` and answers 400 otherwise, which makes a cross-site HTML form structurally unable to reach ANY `[service]` — a form can produce only the three CORS-safelisted types, and `text/plain;charset=UTF-8` is exactly what the host sends for a string body, so a cross-origin form submission used to be indistinguishable on the wire from the shipped client. Not exploitable today, because no vilan service is gated on an ambient credential; the hazard arrives the day one reads a cookie, and the author who never thought about CSRF is the one this protects. `HttpTransport` sets the header on the way out. **And the client reads the answer back**: every envelope carries one of those two media types whatever its status, and an answer that does not is `Err(RpcError::Transport(..))` naming the status rather than a `Decode` blaming the codec — a proxy's HTML error page stops being the codec's fault. The discriminator is the media type and not the status, deliberately: the leg's own 404 for an unknown method and an app's 404 for an unclaimed path are the same number. `std::fetch` grows `Response::header(name)` and `post_bytes_typed(url, body, media_type)` for it. std still does **no CORS** (Q3, ruled): the mechanism is already on the builder and an allowed-origin list is a decision std has no information for — the services guide carries the three-line recipe and the two sentences about where a credential belongs. Pins: one row per status with BOTH halves asserted (a status alone would pass for a server that stopped answering), the 405 with its `Allow`, three refused content types against the `application/json` control, and the non-envelope answer end to end — each red with its half removed. Four recorded-byte assertions move from 200 to 400 (their bodies are decode failures), which is the designed consequence. Tracker A120 S3, `transport-rpc.md` §9.7.7/§9.7.9.

<!-- family: feature -->
**A `[service]` can be reached as a plain HTTP API: `FooClient::over_http("/auth/", json_codec())` speaks the connectionless `POST {mount}rpc` leg with no socket, no handshake and no mirrors.** kolt cannot use a `[service]` for its login door, because login must succeed *before* a socket can be authorized — the token the handshake carries is what login returns — so it hand-writes the whole path three times over. The surprise, and the correction the paper turned on, is that **the client already spoke this leg**: the generated client is `struct <Name>Client<T: Transport>`, the transport is a type PARAMETER, and every plain stub plus `verify()` and `contract_hash()` lives on the unconstrained impl, so a hand-built `AuthClient<HttpTransport> { .. }` has worked on the shipped toolchain since the day the leg existed. What was missing is the constructor and the rule about which services get one. It takes the MOUNT and not the endpoint URL, so `connect("/auth/", codec)` and `over_http("/auth/", codec)` read the same and a service that moves mount moves one string on each side; `HttpTransport { url }` stays the raw door for another origin. It is SYNC and it makes **no call**, where `connect` verifies the contract in one round trip: over HTTP there is no connection, so "once per client value" is an arbitrary unit — a login form constructs one per mount and may make exactly one call through it — and the check has a better home, since `verify()` is reachable for a caller who wants it. An HTTP client is unversioned unless you call `verify()`. **The rule it is generated under is the client struct's own field list**, which is already a total refusal: an `[expose]`d field puts a mirror on the client that only `connect`'s `__attach` can fill, and a handle-returning method puts a `reactive` field there that only `connect` mints. The one shape the field list does not catch is `client = H`, whose reverse direction is dead over HTTP — `with_handlers` is `SocketTransport`-only and the server's `notify` on this leg finds no client channel — so those three get no `over_http` and the call is refused by name. Pinned end to end over a real server: a `Result`-returning method round-tripping BOTH arms (the outer arm is "did the call happen", the inner is "what did the server decide"), a plain method, an awaited `void` whose ack is asserted to come after its handler ran, and `verify()`; plus one refusal per excluded shape. No contract hash moves — nothing here touches a surface string, and the frozen `78bdada7` control still reads. Tracker A120 S2, `transport-rpc.md` §9.7.4/§9.7.5.

**The binary codec's reader gets the JSON reader's audit: an `Option` marker that is neither `0` nor `1`, a `bool` byte that is neither, and a frame with bytes left over are decode failures.** The class 2321790e closed on `std::json` — a typed read that never poisoned on input the schema does not describe — is a question about `std::binary` too, and most of it was already answered: the format is schema-ORDERED, so there is no kind on the wire to mismatch; `expect(count)` refuses a read past the buffer; `read_length` refuses a prefix longer than the frame, which is also what bounds a hostile list COUNT, since the count is what the generated rebuild loops on; and an unknown variant tag is poisoned by the derive's own fallback arm, shared with JSON. Three shapes were not answered, and each is a byte the writer never emits being read as the thing the schema says is at that offset. An `Option` marker: every non-zero byte was read as "present", so a `0x07` took the value one byte on — a shifted read of whatever followed, silently. A `bool`: every non-zero byte was `true`. And a frame LONGER than the value it declares was read as a prefix, so a caller got a value that was never sent — the binary twin of the JSON reader's unread-element check, and the reason `decode_binary` now asks where the cursor stopped. Six pins, three red with the gates removed, and the two already-held shapes pinned as well so the audit's own claim is checked rather than asserted. Tracker N117.

<!-- family: fix -->
**An rpc call carrying MORE arguments than its method takes is a decode failure, not a silent success — and a no-argument method finally has a decode gate at all.** `open_request` opens the envelope's `args` list, records the arity it declares, and hands the deserializer to the route to pull from; nothing ever read that arity and nothing ever closed that list. So `{"method":"add","args":[1,2,3]}` on a one-argument method decoded cleanly, the extras were dropped in silence, and the handler ran — and a no-argument method's route had no `decode_failed` check whatsoever, because with nothing to decode there had seemed to be nothing to check. Every generated route now goes through `rpc::decode_args_failed`, which does three things in order, each closing a different door: **arity first**, because it is the only one that can name what is wrong in the caller's vocabulary (`expects 1 argument(s), got 3`, where a short list previously produced the reader's `expected a number, found an object` — the read running off the end of the arguments and into the enclosing envelope); **then `end_list`**, which is what makes a long list a failure rather than a tail nobody reads, and which `open_request` cannot call itself because it deliberately leaves the list open for the route; **then the reader's sticky error**, untouched, still catching everything about the argument values. vilan-to-vilan none of this can fire — one surface generates both sides and the contract hash refuses a client that disagrees — which is exactly why it went unnoticed and exactly why it matters: for a plain-HTTP caller the arguments are whatever a stranger sent. Seven rows pinned over the real POST leg, the controls last, red with the gate removed. Tracker B383 (A120 S1's remaining half).

**`i32::from_json("1.5")` is an error, not `Ok(1.5)`: the scalar decoders take the integer lanes' value check the codec reader already had.** The typed reader learned two rules last release — an integer lane wants a whole number, an unsigned one a non-negative one, because `1.5` typed `i32` is a value outside its own type — and the scalar `from_json`/`from_json_value` entry points did not go through it: they checked the JSON KIND and handed the number to `Number(x)`. So `i32::from_json("1.5")` answered `Ok(1.5)` and `u32::from_json("-1")` answered `Ok(-1)`, each one an `i32`/`u32`-typed value that no `i32`/`u32` can hold. One lane read two ways is the shape of every hole this file has had, so the fix is a shared predicate rather than a second copy of the rule: `integer_lane_failure` is what the reader reports through and what the scalars answer `Err` from. **This reaches the derives**, which is why it matters more than a scalar entry point suggests — a `[derive(Json)]` type decodes each field through that field's `from_json_value`, so a struct field of type `i32` is gated by it too, and that is the pin that says so. The MAGNITUDE stays unchecked, deliberately and as recorded: `i32`/`u32` are the runtime's numeric lanes rather than hardware widths, and refusing a large value is its own question with its own estate sweep. Five pins, each red with the lane check removed, and the controls last so a green proves the lanes still read. Tracker B373.

**An unreachable host no longer takes the process down: `HttpTransport` answers `Err(RpcError::Transport(..))`, which is what `Transport`'s own contract always said.** `Transport`'s doc says "a transport can FAIL (a dropped socket, an unreachable host) — `Err(reason)` is the infrastructure path", and `HttpTransport::call` did not honour it: the host `fetch` REJECTS on a closed port, a rejection is not a throw on the calling stack, and the rejection left as an unhandled one. Node printed `TypeError: fetch failed` and exited 1; the caller's `match` never ran. That was tolerable while nobody reached for `HttpTransport` in production, and it stops being tolerable the moment a login form is the thing holding it — a form on a dropped network must say "offline", not take the page down. The `fetch` is now guarded, on the POST **and** on the body read (a connection dropped mid-body rejects at `text()`/`bytes()`, not at `send()`), by `__guarded_async` — the suspending twin of `std::reactive`'s `guarded`, in the `try`/`catch`-as-glue shape `std::db`'s `exec_guarded` already uses at this boundary, since vilan has no exception syntax. The reason carries the host's `cause` as well as its message, because undici's own message is the bare `fetch failed` and everything an operator needs (`connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:59999`) is on the cause. Pinned end to end against a port the OS itself named free, asserting both halves — the typed `Transport(..)` arm is reached AND the line after it prints — and proven red with the guard removed. Tracker B374.

**A trait whose supertrait is the bound of its own blanket impl no longer crashes the compiler, and is accepted.** `trait Feed<T> with Source<List<T>>` beside `impl type S: Source<List<type T>> with Feed<T>` — the direct way to write "a capability every source has", and A112 S3's `DeltaFeed` — overflowed the compiler's stack; with the pair in std, every program importing `std::reactive` aborted, a five-line one included. Whether a type provides `Source` asked every impl that provides it, the blanket provides `Source` (a supertrait comes with the trait), and whether the blanket applies is whether the type provides `Source` — the same question, asked until the stack ran out. A question already open further up the proof is no evidence for itself now, so the type's other impls decide it: a cell with its own `Source` impl still provides it, and a type with none still does not reach the blanket. With a trait of your own the recursion never started and the impl was refused instead — "'S' does not implement trait 'Feed<T>': missing 'read'" — because conformance looked for the supertrait's members in the impl or in a separate impl on the same subject, and a blanket's subject is a binder bounded by that very supertrait. The bound provides them, at its own arguments: a subject bounded on `Base<i32>` still does not satisfy a `Feed<str>` that needs `Base<str>`. `spec/types.md` §5.5 says so. Found by Order 40's collections lane.

**A reordered list is reconciled in one pass: `each`, `each_values`, `each_by` and `reconcile` now ask their KEY for a hash as well as an equality (`K: PartialEq + Hashable`), and a 1,000-row reversal costs 1,000 key comparisons instead of 500,500.** M82 gave `reconcile` a position index and made every change that did not reorder linear; a reorder stayed quadratic, and the reason was that nothing bound the key's hash to the key's equality. The index is keyed on a hash, so an earlier equal key could sit outside the chain the index named, and the stretch from the smallest unclaimed index up to the candidate had to be scanned with `==` as well. That stretch is empty when nothing moved — which is what made the append case linear — and it is the WHOLE prefix when a list is reversed, so sorting a list in place in front of an `each` was N(N+1)/2 comparisons per change at every size. A COLLISION is still ordinary and still correct: two keys that are not `==` may share a hash (an impl hashing a subset of the fields its `eq` reads), and the chain walk steps past them. What the bound refuses to compile is the other direction, an `==` coarser than the hash, which is exactly the case that used to hide a moved row behind a quadratic scan. **Breaking:** a key type that is a struct or enum needs `[derive(Hashable)]` when it is equal by all of its fields, and a hand-written `impl Key with Hashable` hashing exactly the fields its `eq` reads when it is not — every key in std, the corpus, the book and the examples is an id or a string and needs nothing. Tracker A125 (RULED 2026-09-22).

So `vilan-rt::http` is the native twin of what `vilan/std/src/process/http.vl` binds in `node:http`, item for item, and every one of them names the binding it exists for: `createServer`, the request's `url`/`method`/`headers`, the response's `statusCode`/`setHeader`/`write`/`end`, the server's `listen`/`address`/`close`, and the raw socket a protocol upgrade hands over. Parsing is a request line, fields whose names are lowercased on the way in (because node lowercases them and `Request::header` is documented against that), a repeat joined with `", "` — a bare comma for `set-cookie`, exactly as `std::http` says it arrives — and a `Content-Length` body. Four things a stranger on a socket can send are refused with the status they earn rather than half-handled: a head over 64 KiB is `431`, a request line or field line that is not one is `400` (including whitespace before a colon, which RFC 9112 §5.1 makes a must-reject), a `Transfer-Encoding` is `411` because this v1 does not decode chunked and reading one as length-delimited would hand the handler framing bytes as content, and a body over 16 MiB is `413`. **The event-loop half is the part that had to be designed rather than written.** `std::net` offers `set_nonblocking` and nothing else — an `epoll`/`kqueue` registration needs libc, which needs a dependency and `unsafe` — so the executor gains an `IoSource` trait: a source is POLLED once per turn, a `true` answer sends the loop back to the microtask queue exactly as a fired timer does, and a source that answers `is_live() == false` is dropped so the program can still exit. With nothing registered the turn model is EXACTLY J6's, unchanged, which is what keeps every ordering rule it pinned true for every program that does no I/O; with a live source the same one-macrotask-per-turn rule gains one kind of macrotask, and the wait before looking again is bounded by the poll interval (1 ms) and by the next deadline, so a bound server neither starves the deadline list nor spins. The request handler is SPAWNED and floating, because node ignores the promise its callback returns: a handler that panics reports through the unobserved-failure path and the server goes on serving. A write is queued and flushed by the poll, which is why `destroy()` flips `destroyed` at the call (node's does) and closes one poll LATER — closing at the call would discard a handshake a handler had just written. Fifteen `vilan-rt` pins: eight on the parser, one per rule, and seven over a real socket on a port the OS chose — a GET answered with the status, headers and body the handler set; a POST whose body arrives in a second write; a chunked request refused on the wire; a streaming response that declares no length and sends both chunks; timers still firing while a server is bound; a closed server letting `block_on` return (the test terminating IS the assertion); and an upgrade reaching its handler with the socket and the head bytes. What is deliberately not in v1, by name: keep-alive (every response says `Connection: close`), chunked requests, HTTP/2, TLS, and the RFC 6455 accept key — the upgrade HANDOVER is here so a `std::ws` written in vilan has a socket to write its handshake to. Tracker F18.

<!-- family: performance -->
**The native executor reuses a settled task's slab slot, so a program that spawns per unit of work no longer grows the slab for its lifetime.** J6's slab was `Vec<Option<Rc<TaskNode>>>` and a reaped task's slot became `None` and stayed `None` — deliberately, because that is what made a stale wake harmless: a wake list holding the id of a task that has since been reaped woke nothing rather than waking a stranger, since nothing could ever take the slot. It is also unbounded, one word per spawn forever, which is fine for a CLI program and wrong for the server F18 makes this runtime run: a per-request spawn means the slab is a leak with a rate. The slot now goes back on a free list and the handle carries a GENERATION, which is how the guarantee survives the reuse — `reap_settled` bumps the generation as it frees the slot, so every handle minted for the task that just left stops naming that slot AT the reap, whether or not anything takes it afterwards, and `task_at` answers `None` for it. `TaskId` is that pair rather than a bare index; nothing outside the slab's three functions changed, and the emitted source never mentions either. Three `vilan-rt` pins, each proven red against the mechanism removed: 200 spawn/settle rounds keep the slab at a handful of slots (201 with the free list disabled), a reaped handle does not name the task that takes its slot — checked before AND after the reuse, and the reuse itself asserted, so an implementation that merely left the slot empty would not pass — and a wake THROUGH a stale handle polls nothing while the same wake through the live handle still runs its task. Tracker F24.
