**A context-threaded hidden parameter's TYPE is recorded where the pass mints it, so the native backend looks it up instead of inferring it back from the call sites.** `context.rs` gives every needs-context function a deliberately record-less parameter — no `parameters` entry, no span, no type, because a fabricated entry would dress compiler plumbing as source in completion and every other consumer keyed on that table (editing-dx.md §19.3). The Rust backend is the one consumer that must write a type down, and J6 gave it a worklist to recover the flavour reactive-turns.md §5.1 names (the context's value, or an `Option` of it for a `get_safe`-reachable region) from what the callers PASS: a literal `None` or a `Some(..)` wrap settles a callee outright, a read of the caller's own hidden parameter propagates, and a clause-typed parameter had first to be connected to every closure literal any call site can hand it — a second graph walk, over the arguments, to answer a question the pass had already answered. Where nothing settled it the strict reading stood, which is a GUESS: right in the direction that becomes a rustc type error rather than a wrong answer, but a guess. The flavour is now `Program::context_optional_hidden_parameters`, a marker set beside `context_hidden_parameters` and minted in the same loop: `holds_bare` — the node's provider is a strict node or a `run` closure — is what the coverage analysis just computed, so it is one bool carried on the plan and one insert where the parameter is created. `context_parameter_type` and `context_clause_type` become lookups; `compute_context_flavours`, `flavour_of_argument` and `receiving_parameters` are deleted (98 lines), and the emitter no longer has a pass that can disagree with the pass it is reading. Nothing moves: the corpus is byte-identical and `nursery.vl` still prints identically as a native binary. Pinned as an emitted-signature probe that carries BOTH readings in one program — a safe reader whose parameter must be `Option<i32>` and a strict one whose parameter must be the bare value — proven non-vacuous by flipping the recorded bool, which swaps the two signatures. Tracker F23.

**A diagnostic still carries ONE note, and the first real candidate for a second one is why.** The house rule is C3's: a note is a secondary LOCATION with a label — "first call here", "the trait declares it here" — one, not a list, because diagnostics stay terse. E189's broad gate is the first place that pinched. When a program already carries an error the context family stands down whole, and the count of checks that did not run has to reach the reader; attached to the primary error it would be a footnote about a different subject (one wrong expression against a statement about a pass), hung on whichever diagnostic happened to be last, which is not a relation a reader can read. It ships as its own warning, and that generalizes: **a second fact that is not a second location for THIS error is its own diagnostic, not another line under this one.** Growing the field to a list is one line here and a cost at every consumer — the terminal renderer, the HMR overlay, the language server's related information and the playground each gain a list to order and truncate, and the terseness rule stops being enforced by the type. The one shape that genuinely is a chain already has its own field (E78's requirement trace) and deliberately is not this one. Written down where the next person will ask: at the type, and at the gate that asked. No behaviour changes. Tracker N112.

**A nominal declaration's generic parameter has ONE spelling in its own body, and it is now written down and gated instead of defended against.** The item behind this reported two: that a generic ENUM's variant payload records the constraint id itself, typed `Any`, where a generic STRUCT's fields record `Generic(..)` nodes — and the emit-Rust backend carries a second copy of the parameter-binding walk whose first branch exists to accept the first spelling. **The second spelling does not exist.** A census over the whole loaded world — std's `external` declarations included, against a fixture declaring an unbounded parameter, a bounded one, two parameters, payloads that are nested nominals, tuples and `Option`s, a RECURSIVE enum carrying itself, and a `[derive]`-generated struct and enum the macro engine writes rather than the author — reads **44 declared parameters, 131 `Generic(..)` nodes in declaration bodies, and zero bare constraint ids**, in struct fields, enum payloads, nested arguments and impl subject arguments alike. The emitter's branch is dead over the whole corpus too: instrumented, `bind_parameters` is entered twice in a build of all 131 corpus programs through the Rust backend, and both take the `Generic(..)` arm. It is stronger than "unused". Planting the second spelling to prove the new gate non-vacuous does not work, because a body type that is a bare constraint id is not a key of the type map at all — the analysis panics on the first lookup, long before any gate runs. So the deliverable is the invariant itself: stated at `Type::Generic`, where a reader of the type meets it; restated at `impl_select::bind_subject`, the shared walk that matches that node and nothing else, so the next reader knows the single arm is COMPLETE rather than a happy path; and gated by a new `nominal_generic_spelling.rs`, whose failure names the declaration body that broke it and says to mint the node rather than teach the walks a second shape. The detector is pinned on synthetic inputs, since the analyzer cannot produce the one it looks for. Nothing in codegen moves — no golden, no emitted byte. The forty lines the emitter can now delete are the native backend's to take. Tracker B366.

**A generated name inside a `// witness:` is a hole, so the claim gate can no longer be reddened by the counter it says nothing about.** A corpus program's `// witness:` line names the emitted bytes a prose claim rests on, and twenty-three of the thirty-seven in the tree (ten annotated programs) quote a generated name — `$b(file); file = null;`, `$a = 7; process.exit($a);`, `function $j($k) { $b($k[0]); }`. The byte gate is judged against exactly that (the integrator's regeneration diff is gensym-normalized); the witness gate was literal substring containment, so a pure shift failed it — and failed it with a message that tells the reader THE CLAIM IS UNWITNESSED and forbids relaxing the witness, which is the worst possible thing for a gate to say about a change that is not one. `reactive-on-change.vl:60` was re-keyed once in Order 38 and survived the merged-tree regeneration by luck. A `$`-prefixed identifier in a witness is now matched as a hole against a `$`-prefixed identifier in the golden, and the binding is one-to-one in both directions — so `$a = 7; process.exit($a);` still says "the same generated name is assigned and then read", and `function $j($k) { $b($k[0]); }` still says three DISTINCT names stand in those three positions. Nothing else widens: a hole is one identifier, never a wildcard over bytes, it does not match a source name, and a witness naming no generated name is compared byte for byte exactly as before. No witness in the tree had to be rewritten — the spellings already there are read as holes — and all thirty-seven still match their goldens. Pinned in both directions, because the failure mode of this fix is a gate that has quietly stopped saying anything: the shift passes, while a dropped argument, one spelling bound to two names, two spellings bound to one, a hole asked to match a source name, and a hole asked to swallow the bytes after it all still fail. Proven red with the old literal matcher restored. Tracker N110.

**`List::new` and `List::push` are `Intrinsic` rows like every other built-in lowering, and the class of defect B359 was one instance of is closed at the table instead of patched at each reader.** The compiler lowers about fifty `external` std functions to native JavaScript or a runtime helper, and every one of them is a row in `Program::intrinsics` keyed by function id — except two. `List`'s constructor and its `push` were carried in two `Program` fields of their own, found by a second walk of `List`'s impls, threaded through the analysis `World` as three more fields that were `None` in every stored world and filled after the unpack, and recognized in the emitter by a bare `if Some(target_id) == self.list_new_fn_id`. **That is why B359 existed**, and the shape is worth stating: the JS emitter reaches a member two ways — by named callee, and by DISPATCH once a trait call resolves to a concrete type's member — and the dispatch side reads the intrinsic table. A pair keyed outside the table therefore had no dispatch arm at all, fell through to the emitted-function name, and minted a mangled name for a function nothing ever emits, so `impl List<type T> with Pusher<T>` plus a `self.push(v)` in a trait default compiled clean and threw `ReferenceError: $b is not defined` at runtime. Zero output change, and that is the gate: every corpus golden byte-identical, and the native differential byte-identical in both its modes over the whole platform-free set. Pinned in `intrinsic_binding.rs` beside B265's: the two rows exist, are unique, and the two surviving fields name exactly the ids those rows are filed under — proven red with the rows removed. Tracker N109.

**Four smalls Order 38's lanes left behind: the stack-frame record says what was measured, the depth line survives a refused parse, the temp scripts cannot be written through a symlink, and the JSON census says it is a census.** Each was found by a lane reaching for something and finding it wrong, and none of them is worth its own release note — together they are the shape of rot this kind of pass exists for. **The walk frame.** N97 re-measured the phase-1 expression walk two ways that agree to the byte — 42,464 B (41.5 KiB) per level of nesting unoptimized, ~4,650 B optimized — and re-keyed the record everywhere it was held except three comments, which went on quoting the old ~36 KiB and the ~18 MiB-at-the-bound that follows from it: `WALK_DEPTH_LIMIT`'s own doc, the wasm suite's big-stack helper, and `deep_nesting.rs`'s own header, which is where the measurement LIVES. All three now carry the measured numbers (20.3 MiB at the 500-level bound) and name N97 as their source, so the next reader finds the harness rather than a folklore figure. **The depth line.** `VILAN_DEPTH_STATS` prints its per-family peaks at the end of the analysis, and `vilan build` drops the tree of a file that did not parse cleanly — so the instrument said nothing for exactly the analyses the PARSER's own bound (B142, 500 levels) exists for: the refusal printed, the numbers did not. The no-tree path releases the instrument itself now, and the line carries the anchored parse's real peak. Pinned both ways, because the fix's failure mode is a doubled line: a refused 600-level program prints one line whose `parse` depth is past the bound, and an analysed build still prints exactly one. **The temp scripts.** `vilan run`, `vilan run --watch` and `vilan test` each write a `<name>-<pid>.mjs` into the system temp directory and delete it again. That is the right home for a file its writer removes — it is not the package tree, which is N103's concern — but it is SHARED, every one of those names is predictable, and `fs::write` follows a symlink: a path planted there by anyone else on the machine had the run truncate whatever it pointed at and then hand it to `node`. One helper now serves all three: the path is unlinked first (which takes the LINK, never its target) and then created with `create_new`, so the file executed is a file the process made, and the remaining race can only make the create fail. The unlink is also what stops a script leaked by an abnormal exit from wedging a later run whose pid happens to match. Three unit pins, the symlink one proven red against `fs::write`. **The census.** `json_boundary.rs` greps `.vl` source for `to_json`/`from_json` and counts lines; it compiles nothing and runs nothing, and two lanes have reached for it as the place a `std::json` behaviour pin goes. Its header says so now, and names the three files where codec behaviour is actually pinned. The fifth small — `Map`/`Set` have no `impl Js` in `vilan-rt` — rides the native backend's own work. Tracker N111.

**Every completion candidate now states the prefix it replaces and the text to filter it by, so a hyphenated name survives in a client that is not VS Code.** E194 closed the visible half of this from the CLIENT's side: `editors/vscode/language-configuration.json` declares a `wordPattern` that reads `stroke-width`, `font-family` and `--card-gap` as one word each, because VS Code's default excludes `-` and so filtered the one candidate the author was typing towards out of its own list. Every other LSP client has its own word rules and no such file, and nothing server-side could override them — `Completion` carried no `filter_text` and the server sent no edit range. It does now. A candidate carries the span it REPLACES, in live coordinates, and the language server sends it as a `textEdit`: a client handed an explicit range filters against the text in THAT range rather than against its own notion of a word, and accepting replaces the prefix instead of doubling it. The edit's text is whatever insertion the other passes settled on — a call shape, a snippet body, E160's `name = ` — because `textEdit` wins over `insertText` per the spec, and letting the two disagree would silently drop one of them; `insertText` stays set beside it for a client that reads that instead. **The span is a property of the REQUEST, not of the candidate**, so it is stamped once over every context's list rather than invented per candidate, and the hyphen is admitted in exactly the two places a hyphen can be part of a NAME: inside a css block and inside an element head. In code a `-` is subtraction and no vilan identifier carries one, so `1-al` still completes `alpha` from `al` — the widening E194's `wordPattern` had to accept for double-click and word-wise motion does not have to be repeated here. The playground's `CompletionItem` carries both as well, so the two front-ends filter and insert alike. Six pins: E194's own `<svg stroke-w` position, a css property prefix, an expression prefix that stops at the word, every candidate of three contexts carrying both fields, and the server's two — the `textEdit` carrying the call shape, and a candidate without a span still sending none (which is what the keystroke path's candidates are). E194's client-side pin stays: the word pattern is double-click and `Ctrl+D` too, not only completion. Tracker E211.

**A generic `<` closes itself, and a backtick pairs in prose — the two the editor made you type by hand.** `List<`, `Map<`, `fun pair<`, a generic call's own argument list: each got its `>` typed by the author, because `editors/vscode/language-configuration.json` declared auto-closing pairs for `{}`, `[]`, `()` and `""` and nothing else. The obvious fix is the wrong one. **`<` is also the comparison operator, and a static pair cannot tell `List<` from `a < b`** — its only filter is `notIn: [string, comment]` — so a `<` entry there would grow a `>` in every comparison anybody typed, which is worse than the gap: a character the author has to delete, in the middle of an expression, every time. The decision is the SERVER's, where the names have meanings. `vilan-lsp` gains its first `textDocument/onTypeFormatting` provider, registered for `<` alone, and it says yes on a deliberately narrow reading: the `<` sits immediately after an identifier (no space — `vilan fmt` writes a comparison spaced, and it is not optional here) which either names a struct, an enum, a trait or a generic function the analysis knows, or is a declaration's own name right after `fun`, `struct`, `enum`, `trait`, `impl` or `type` — that second arm because the declaration being written is by definition not in the analyzed program yet. A binding, a literal, a name mid-rename and a `<` inside a string or after a `//` get nothing. It reads the RETAINED program, so it keeps working while the buffer is ahead of the analysis, which is the whole reason to ask a server rather than a regex. `<`/`>` also joins `surroundingPairs`, where there is no ambiguity at all: wrapping a selection in `<>` has only one reading. **The backtick is the other half**, and it needs no cleverness: it means nothing to the lexer, so it pairs GLOBALLY with one exclusion, `notIn: ["string"]` — a string body is text the author is writing literally, while doc prose is a comment, and every `///` in std is full of backticks. A grep pin holds the premise the global pair rests on, counting rather than containing: the day a backtick becomes a token, the pin reds and the pair's scope is decided again with the real case in hand. The extension defaults `editor.formatOnType` on for `[vilan]` files, since VS Code sends the request only when it is, and it now declares its own `autoCloseBefore` — the conservative set a pair fires before — so the rule a backtick depends on (typing one before a word character must not pair) reads off this file rather than off a default that could move under it. One thing door 2 does NOT buy is written down beside the pin that keeps `<` out of `autoClosingPairs`: VS Code types over a closing character only when it inserted that character itself, so the `>` of `List<i32>` typed by hand still doubles, and no text edit can fix it — a caret cannot be moved past a character an edit leaves in place. The only configuration that buys overtype is the `<` entry this whole item exists to avoid. The book's editor appendix says what closes and what does not, and the capability gate that used to pin on-type formatting ABSENT now pins that sentence against the provider. Tracker E202, E203 (R9 at Order 39's GO).

**Hovering a generic call shows two signatures: the declaration as written, and the exact function that call reached.** The owner's ask, in the owner's own spelling — `fun get_or(self, key: K, make: || V): V`, a blank line, `fun get_or(self, key: UserId, make: || SignalCell<Option<User>>): SignalCell<Option<User>>` — one fenced `vilan` block holding both, the declared reading first because it is the thing that exists in the file and the computed one second because it answers "and which function did THIS call reach". **`scoped_effect` — an effect whose every run gets its own `Owner` — and the free `on_cleanup` beside it.** A113 row 4 recorded that vilan has no per-run cleanup: `Owner::defer` runs at DISPOSAL only, so an effect body that subscribes, arms a timer, or opens a channel accumulates one of those per change for as long as the boundary lives, and the only way to get the run-scoped lifetime was to route the work through a FORM — `swap` mints a fresh `Owner` per instantiation and disposes the last — which costs a DOM boundary for a lifetime question. `Source::scoped_effect(body)` and `scoped_effect_on_change(body)` are that mechanism with no view in it, as trait defaults beside `effect`, so every `Source` has them: a mirror, a derived cell, a `Source` of your own. `on_cleanup(|| ..)` is `get_owner().defer(..)` under a name, and it is ONE NAME whose meaning the ambient owner decides — inside a scoped effect the ambient owner is that RUN's, so the cleanup runs before the next run and once more when the boundary goes; inside any other boundary it is the boundary's, so it runs once, at teardown. It reads the owner strictly, like `effect`: a cleanup with nothing in scope to run it is a compile error rather than a silent no-op. Three things are deliberate. The order inside a run is release-previous, install-fresh, call-body, so a body that THROWS has already had its owner installed and what it registered before throwing is released by the next run — pinned, because the other order leaks everything the failed run opened. The last run is released through `on_cleanup` against the enclosing boundary, read where the machinery is built rather than where a run happens, which is what closes the leak a form-less per-run owner otherwise has no way to close. And `body` is INJECTED (`context owner_scope`) rather than captured, because it is a literal at the user's call site, born before the run's owner exists — capture-at-creation would hand it the boundary's owner and the whole point would be lost. The item's own proven user-code probe now runs through the std form and prints byte-identically. Four pins: the probe's sequence inline and in a turn with disposal count equal to creation count, `on_cleanup`'s other meaning under a plain boundary, the lazy twin's missing first run, a throwing body, and — on the wire, in `reactive_channels` — a `RemoteSource` LEASE taken inside a run, where the link counts `Subscribe`/`Unsubscribe` frames and reads three up and three down against a plain `effect`'s one and one, with one live observer after three runs instead of three. **Effect order within one settle is now a CONTRACT: derivations run to a fixpoint, then effects run in ascending subscriber id — so a parent form's effect runs before anything its render created.** A110 door 2, ruled after two independent measurements (`reactive-turns.md` §7). `drain` used to take a wave out of `pending` and run it in SUBSCRIPTION order, which is the order observers were attached to whichever cell fired, and two nested forms standing on one source are never in that order: the idiom the guide teaches — project the outer key so the outer form does not rebuild on every navigation — puts the outer observer on a DERIVED cell, so it is not on the source's subscriber list at all and no order read off that list can ever put it first. The inner form therefore rendered a subtree for a value the outer was about to exclude (a wasted build, and a panic if that arm is `unreachable`), and an effect in the same wave as the first link of a derivation chain read the chain's stale tail. The dedup set is TWO keyed maps, one per bucket, so each is still cleared wholesale when its own wave is taken out and door 2 is not charged for the per-id bookkeeping that a single shared map would have forced (tracker M83, measured separately). Phase 2 walks a snapshot and leans on door 1's liveness flag rather than a live queue, which is what §7.4's "finding one" asks for now that the flag exists. And the ordered insert reads the queue through a `&mut` view and not through `read()`, because `read()` yields a value: binding the queue to a local copies the whole list, and a wave of n observers on one cell then costs n² element copies — 7.6 s against 80 ms on A44's 2,000-observer pin, which is the trap §7.5 warned whoever built this about, caught here by the pin that already existed. **Nothing in the estate changes its observable order**: all nine moved corpus goldens are runtime-identical, and the one shape in the tree where door 2 is visible is the one apps are told to write — `ui_rows`'s nested-`swap` pin goes from three builds and three teardowns to two and two. For a list that did not reorder — which is nearly every list — item *i* matched at index *i* after walking *i + 1* entries, so a pass cost N(N+1)/2 iterations **whatever the change was**: 500,500 comparisons at 1,000 rows to place one appended row. A98 (Order 36) fixed the DOM half of `each`'s per-change cost — 1,000 row cuts to 0, ~4,000 host insertions to one — and left this half untouched, and nothing in the tracker recorded it until A112's paper measured `each`'s scan half at 358 M Ir per change and 3.8× per doubling. The fix is the index `KeyedCell` has kept since A54, built once per pass: for each canonical key, the chain of old positions holding it, as one native map of at most N entries plus one N-element list of next-in-chain links. Heads are advanced past claimed entries permanently, so the total cost of skipping claims across a pass is bounded by the number of claims. **Measured, callgrind Ir per change under `node --jitless` over the paper's own template** (loadavg 52.7 at the start of the before leg, 23.6 at the end of the after leg — Ir is an instruction count and does not move with load): 95.1 M → 14.8 M at 500 rows, 355.1 M → 29.1 M at 1,000, 1,369.9 M → 58.5 M at 2,000. Per doubling that is 1.97× and 2.01× where it was 3.73× and 3.86× — linear, confirmed empirically as well as by reading the loop. **The plan is identical for every key type, and a DIFFERENTIAL says so rather than a golden.** The answer the scan gives is the smallest unclaimed index whose key `==` the item's, and an index over canonical value identity answers that directly only when the key's `==` IS value identity. A `K` whose equality is coarser — a case-insensitive string, a struct comparing a subset of its fields — can have an earlier match that hashes differently, so the stretch from the smallest unclaimed index up to the index's candidate is still scanned; where the two agree, which is every key in std, the corpus, the book, the examples and kolt, that stretch is empty and the pass is one walk. One golden moves (`reactive-keyed.mjs`), runtime-identical. Tracker M82, found by A112's paper.

**The native backend has an event loop: `vilan-rt` gains a hand-written single-threaded executor, and it is the JS turn model rather than a second one.** `Task<T>` is an `external struct` over the host promise, so before any `async` vilan program could compile natively something had to supply the promise, the microtask queue and the turn model. That is `vilan-rt::executor`, ~1,600 lines with its pins, and it takes **no dependencies** — no tokio, no futures crate, which is the rule this runtime was created under. `transformer.rs::helper_source` is the contract, not an inspiration: `__task`, `__nursery_new`, `__nursery_new_detached`, `__nursery_run`, `__sleep`, `__timer` and `__with_finally_async` already define what an `async` vilan program MEANS, and each rule in the executor names the helper it was read off. Seven primitives. `Task<T>` is a slab handle whose copies are the same task: eager, so the body runs to its first suspension inside the spawn expression; a failure latches at settle time; an unowned, unobserved failure is reported once with its spawn origin, to stderr as `console.error` does, so it cannot move a differential. The loop drains a **microtask queue to exhaustion** and only then fires the SINGLE earliest entry of a deadline-ordered timer list — one macrotask per turn, because two `setTimeout(_, 0)` callbacks are two macrotasks with a full microtask drain between them, and firing both in one pass is a different program. `Nursery` is an `Rc` body with a `Weak` parent, and `CancelSignal` is that `Weak`; cancellation walks the descendant chain downward to wake a nested extent's parked `sleep`, which is what the JS abort listener does. The join is reproduced as written — the child list may GROW mid-drain, every child is raced against the fail-wake, a failure cancels and absorbs the rest, the body's own error wins over a latched child's, and a latched winner carries `" (in task spawned in …)"` into its message. A detached nursery overrides the failure path instead of latching, so one owned child's failure neither cancels its siblings nor is lost. `sleep` is an abortable registration that clears its timer on the abort, and `Timer` is a memoized verdict plus a waiter list, where an abort rejects THAT waiter and leaves the verdict unsettled and the host timer running — the difference that is the point of the type. **Two mechanisms are worth naming because they are what keep this crate dependency-free and `unsafe`-free.** There is no `RawWaker`: every leaf future parks by writing the current task's id into the wake list of the thing it waits on, and that thing enqueues the id when it settles, so `Waker::noop()` is handed to every poll and nothing consults it. And a panic is caught at the poll boundary — `catch_unwind` around `Future::poll` — which is what latches a task's failure and, wrapped as one small combinator over a `Pin<Box<..>>`, gives the nursery join and `with_finally_async` the `catch_unwind`-across-an-await that std has no combinator for. A cancellation is its own payload TYPE rather than a magic name, so a vilan `panic("AbortError")` cannot be mistaken for one. Eighteen unit tests, each naming the ordering rule it pins, and the four rules the design turns on are proven red against the rule removed: the microtask queue's drain to exhaustion, one macrotask per turn, the eager spawn, and the detached nursery's override. Nothing in the emitted source mentions `Pin` or `Send`. Tracker J6.

**The native backend compiles GENERICS: a generic function, a generic struct, a generic enum and a trait default each emit one Rust item per instantiation, and 51 of S1a's 98 refusals are gone.** This is `native-apps.md` §5-S1's second half, and the sizing was right - monomorphisation was more than half of what the first cut could not reach. The mechanism is the JS emitter's, reproduced rather than shared: a substitution threaded through the walk, a `resolve_type_id` that follows a generic parameter to its binding, a structural instance key, and one memo per instance. **The instance set could not be consumed**, which was the slice's first open question: `Transformer::instances` is minted DURING the JS walk and its values are JS function nodes, so there is no pre-computed set on `Program` to read. What IS shared is the backend-independent half, and it is what this emitter reads - `impl_select`'s `select_member`, `bind_subject` and `applying_trait_ids`, plus the analyzer's `method_call_substitution`, `generic_dispatch`, `own_generic_call_bindings` and `bound_dispatch_traits`. **One thing is genuinely different**, and it is why the reproduction is not a copy: JavaScript needs no concrete types and Rust needs nothing else. The JS emitter resolves a bare generic and stops, because `List<T>` and `List<i32>` are the same array; here `List<T>` must come out `Vec<i32>`, and `struct Pair<T>` must come out as one Rust `struct` per instantiation with its own `impl Js`. Three corollaries fell out of that: a generic ENUM's parameter arrives as the constraint id itself where a struct's fields arrive as `Generic(..)` nodes, so the substitution is consulted by type id before a type's shape is; a variant constructor's own site can record an OPEN type (`Tree::Leaf(7)` is `Tree<any>` until the annotation beside it closes the hole), so its arguments are recovered from the constructor's own arguments or from the position it fills; and a function that writes no return type - which is every trait-impl member whose trait declared `Self` - needed its body's type inferred, because `-> ()` for a body handing back an `Id` is a rustc error JavaScript never had to think about. Beside the generics: module-level bindings become `thread_local!` cells (read and written), `Weak<T>` and six more intrinsics reach `vilan-rt`, a struct holding a closure gets the reference equality JavaScript's `===` already gives it, and a hidden context parameter resolves its type through the context binding it threads. The whole-corpus differential moves from 29 identical / 84 refused / 4 broken to 45 identical / 72 refused / **0 broken**; `board.vl`, the paper's own probe, gets past every wall S1a named and stops at one - an `is`-test capture outside an `if` condition - which its pin now holds by name. Tracker F1 (slice S1b), C15 measured (the boxed-binding count is pinned rather than reported).

**`--backend rust` works from an INSTALLED toolchain: the runtime crate the emitted program links is embedded in the binary and materialized under `~/.vilan/rt-cache/`, beside the standard library's own cache.** S1a resolved `vilan-rt` through `$VILAN_RT` or a compile-time source sibling, so the second backend compiled a program only inside a vilan checkout - a released binary had neither path, and the failure was a refusal at the end of a successful compile. The runtime now rides in the binary the way `std` and `macro_std` do: its own table (`RT_FILES`), its own content hash and its own cache root, so a std edit never re-materializes the runtime and a runtime edit never invalidates a machine's std trees. Its `Cargo.toml` is GENERATED rather than embedded, and that is the one way the two tables differ: the real `crates/vilan-rt/Cargo.toml` is a workspace member whose `[lints] workspace = true` resolves only inside this repository, so the cache carries the crate's `[package]` block copied through, an empty `[dependencies]` (the crate has none, by rule) and a `[workspace]` of its own so cargo stops walking up out of the cache. **Three roots, in a fixed order, and the order is B346's one-root rule applied to a second toolchain asset**: `$VILAN_RT` wins and never falls through - a variable naming a directory with no `Cargo.toml` is reported, not quietly replaced, because linking a different runtime than the one a developer pointed at is the outcome worse than refusing. With nothing named it is the `crates/vilan-rt` of the checkout the entry sits in, found by `std_dir`'s own ancestor walk and required to carry `vilan/std/vilan.toml` beside it, so the runtime and the standard library can never come from two different trees; else the embedded copy. `vilan cache prune` sweeps the new root with the other two, on the same age guard and with the running binary's own tree exempt. Pinned in `install.rs` (a copied binary with no checkout in any ancestor and no `$VILAN_RT` builds and runs a native program, the cache entry is there, the manifest stands alone, and a misnamed `$VILAN_RT` refuses by name) and in `embedded_std.rs` (the table matches the crate in both directions; materialization is complete and idempotent). **An `[rpc]` method may return NOTHING and still be awaited: `void` is admitted as an rpc return, the reply is the ack, and the stub waits for it.** Two shapes existed and neither was this one. A method with something to say declares a Wire return and the caller awaits the value; a notification (`[client_service]`, or the server's `connection.client().…`) has no reply lane at all and returns the moment the request is sent. A method with **nothing to report and something to wait for** had to lie about one or the other — kolt's `store.vl` wrote `bool` for `remove_message` and put a FIXME over it naming this item. Write no return type, or write `: void` (they mean the same thing here, as they do on any other function), and the call is a round trip whose answer is `Result<void, RpcError>`: `Ok(void)` is the ack, `Err(error)` is a call that did not land. **The ordering is the whole content of the feature** — the handler runs to completion on the server before the stub returns, so the next call sees its effect, which is exactly what a notification cannot promise and why A75's `notify` does not cover this. The end-to-end pin asserts the ORDER and not just the values: the handler's print lands before the client's ack, which a notification could produce either way round. **The answer is `Result<void, RpcError>`, every other stub's shape with the unit value in its `Ok`.** (This entry first said `Option<RpcError>`, "because vilan has no unit literal" — that was false: `void` is the unit value and `Ok(void)` builds and runs; only the `()` spelling is refused. Corrected before any release carried it; tracker B363.) **The wire does not move.** The reply is the same ack envelope `notified` already wrote for every `[client_service]` notification (a one-byte body the caller reads the ENVELOPE of, not the value), so nothing enters `Serialize`'s vocabulary and no existing frame changes; the contract entry is `remove(i53)->void;`, and no service that compiled before this had a void method to hash. `[client_service]` is deliberately untouched: a declared return there is still refused, `: void` included, because that direction has no ack for a caller to await and omission is its only legal spelling — so the awaited void is a server-side shape and the guide says so. The analyzer's admission is one test on the RENDERED spelling, which is the same string the `[service]` generator branches on, so what is admitted and what is generated cannot disagree about which methods are void. Six pins: the admission in both spellings, three controls (a non-Wire return still refused, the `[client_service]` refusal intact, and ledger row 5 — `must declare a Wire type` — still reaching an unannotated PARAMETER now that the return type has left it), the awaited round trip with its ordering over a real socket (`service_layer`), and the same call over the connectionless `{mount}rpc` POST leg (`rpc_http`), which needs no connection at all. No new diagnostics. **One existing pin turns over rather than being deleted**: `generics::rpc_rejects_a_missing_return` is now `generics::rpc_admits_a_missing_return`, and its comment says which of the two void calls answered the parenthesis it used to carry ("fire-and-forget needs its own design") — `notify` did, one order ago, and this is the other one. **`Result<i53, str>` — the item's other half — needs nothing**: A82 built it, `an_rpc_answering_a_result_over_a_u53_id_round_trips_both_arms` has pinned it since, and the kolt FIXME the item quotes is already gone from that file. Tracker A107, `proposal/transport-rpc.md` §9.3.

**An awaited `void` rpc stub answers `Result<void, RpcError>`, not `Option<RpcError>`.** A107 (unreleased) shipped the stub as `Option<RpcError>` on the strength of a probe that tried `Ok(())`, found it does not parse, and concluded the language has no unit value. It has one: `void`. `Ok(void)` is an ordinary expression, `Result<void, E>` an ordinary type, and std's own `!` on an `Option` builds `Verdict::Bad(void)`. No wire byte and no contract hash moves: the reply is the same ack envelope and the contract entry is still `name(args)->void;`. The guide's services page, `call_ack`'s documentation and both pins (`an_awaited_void_rpc_acks_after_its_handler_ran`, `an_awaited_void_rpc_is_served_over_the_connectionless_post_leg`) say the true thing now. Tracker B363 (S3).

The records are built in `json_codec`/`binary_codec` instead, over the `mut` local of the frame that mints them, because a closure captures the BINDING (spec §6.9) — which is the same relation the cells were buying, spelled by the language rather than around it. **Migration:** a hand-written `impl .. with Wire` moves its two signatures to `serializer: &mut S` / `deserializer: &mut D` and changes nothing else — nested forwarding was already bare. A describer closure handed to `call`/`notify`/`encode_patch` re-binds and takes the view: `|s: Serializer| id.describe(s)` becomes `|mut s: Serializer| id.describe(&mut s)`. A hand-written `impl .. with Serialize`/`Deserialize` — a custom codec — moves every method to `&mut self` and may then hold its state in plain fields. `[derive(Wire)]` types need NO source change: they re-expand. The estate census: seventeen std `impl .. with Wire`, both derive emitters, six describer literals across `examples/rpc` and three benchmarks, eleven inference pins over two shared program consts, and five describer literals in the cli suites' own fixtures; kolt writes ZERO hand-written `Wire`/`Serialize`/`Deserialize` impls and two `[derive(Wire)]` structs, so kolt migrates by rebuilding. The resolve adds about a megabyte to a four-megabyte world; the bulk is what the LOAD WALK built — the scopes, the entity and expression maps, the registry clone — and both shapes build all of it. 21.7 against a shipped 24 is a 13% over-charge on the entry-shaped worlds alone, which on kolt is six of eighteen and 2.6 MiB of a 192 MiB budget; it is in the conservative direction (the cache evicts slightly early, never late), it is inside the 3x band M50's pin already asserts, and a second currency to recover it would cost more than it buys. **No second factor ships. One shape per test, one process per test, which is what nextest gives for free. Tracker M74.

**Vilan has a second backend: `--backend rust` emits your program as Rust, builds it with the `cargo` already on your machine, and the binary prints byte-identical output to the JavaScript one.** Two new crates: `vilan-rust`, the emitter, which sits beside the JS transformer and reads the same finished `Program`; and `vilan-rt`, the runtime it links, which takes **no dependencies at all** — its whole footprint is Rust's `std`, so a native build's cost is the emitted program and nothing else. `vilan build --backend rust` writes a cargo project under `dist/native/<entry>/` and builds it, `--stdout` prints the emitted Rust instead, and `vilan run --backend rust` runs the binary. **Debug by default**, and the CLI help says so: rustc is the inner loop from here, the design probe's release build was over a second of CPU for seven hundred lines, and someone asking to run their program is not asking to optimise it. What the emitter reaches is what the paper's probe translated — structs (a real `struct`, not the JS backend's positional array), enums (`Option` and `Result` become Rust's own), `str` as `Rc<str>` so a value copy is a refcount bump rather than a `String` clone, `List` as `Vec`, insertion-ordered `Map`/`Set`, closures, `impl` blocks, `match`, loops, recursion, `print` and `panic` — and its limits are REFUSED BY NAME rather than mis-compiled: a generic function, a module-level binding, `async`, a `resource` type, any host binding, each says which construct stopped it and to build with `--backend js`. That refusal is the design, not an apology. A backend that quietly emitted something else for a construct it did not understand would fail its own differential in a way nobody could read; one that names the construct turns its gaps into the next slice's work list, and the gate prints that list. The gate is `native_differential`: every program the emitter accepts is compiled by BOTH backends and their stdout compared byte for byte, over the platform-free half of the test corpus — the `ssr_differential` shape applied to a backend instead of a platform, which is the right one because it needs no new oracle. Three rulings are built into it. Interior mutability is `RefCell`, so a rule-4 violation is a panic with a message rather than a compile error — honest, and the count of boxed bindings is now measurable, which is what pays for the by-value capture optimisation later. A closure value is a counted `Rc<dyn Fn>` wherever it can be stored, because the probe's translation hit a use-after-move the moment a callback was both kept and called. And `i53`/`u53` are `i64`/`u64` natively, with the range guarantee still JavaScript's, so a program that round-trips both backends behaves the same. Two rows `NEW`. No async, no UI, no rpc, no filesystem, no platform surface — those are later slices, and `guide/native.md` says so out loud. Tracker F1 (slice S1a), with F16 and C15's rules decided in it.

**A closure that captures a view and is handed to a callee that KEEPS it is now refused, which closes the escape rule's last hole before a non-GC backend.** `fun make(v: &mut i32): Holder { keep(|| *v) }` compiled and printed 3: the closure captures `make`'s `&mut` parameter, `keep` stores it in the `Holder` it returns, and the caller gets back a closure reading a view of its own dead local. Every other position was already refused — returned, stored in a field, placed in a collection, carried in an enum payload — and argument positions were skipped on purpose, with a reason that is true of most callees: an ordinary callee only borrows the closure for the call. The reason stops being true the moment the callee keeps what it is handed, and there was no way to ask which it was. There is now: a per-parameter summary of the positions a callee keeps past the call (stored, collected, assigned, returned, or passed on to a callee that keeps it), computed as a monotone fixpoint and asked ONLY of arguments that are view-capturing closures — so `twice(|| *v)`, whose callee just calls what it is handed, still compiles, and that control is pinned beside the refusal. A callee with no readable body keeps everything, which is the safe direction: the choice is between refusing a program and miscompiling one. The refusal gets its own sentence because the old one enumerates four positions and an argument is none of them, and because the whole diagnosis is WHICH callee keeps it — it names the callee. Nothing in std, the corpus, the docs, `examples/` or kolt fires, and the summary is not even computed for a program in which no closure captures a view, so this costs nothing anywhere it has nothing to say. This was memory-safe only because JavaScript boxes the place and traces it; under the emit-Rust backend it is a freed slot, which is why it is that backend's precondition rather than a later tidy-up. One row `NEW`. Tracker C16, closing C13's pinned-and-ignored case as its first exhibit.

**std's two back edges are weak: `observe`'s captured value cell and `Subscription`'s alias of the subscriber list.** `lifetimes.md` §5's V1 shortened the subscription cycle — the notify closure captures the VALUE CELL, never the signal — and what it left is four nodes: `cell → subscribers → Subscriber → notify → (captured) cell`, a loop in which every edge is a holder and which therefore no refcount can ever collect. The second edge is the same shape read from the other end: a `Subscription` is an alias of the signal's subscriber list, held by an owner's cleanup list or by an app's own binding, and none of those holders owns that list. Both are edges that must be FOLLOWED and must not decide a lifetime, which is exactly what `Weak` says: `observe` captures `signal.value.downgrade()` and upgrades on each notification, and `Subscription.subscribers` is a `Weak<List<Subscriber>>` that `dispose` upgrades before it detaches. **`upgrade` rather than `get` at the notify**, deliberately — the observer takes a value and `read()` is the spelling that copies one out of the cell, and a notification genuinely holds the cell for the length of the call rather than merely touching it. The signal-less `Subscription::teardown` shape (`std::dom`'s `listen`) has no list to alias at all: its cell dies with the call and its weak answers `None` once anything counts, which is the right answer, because the whole of that shape's teardown is the `release` one-shot and that is a cell of its own — `dispose`'s `None` arm runs it. **A correction to the slice's exit test, and it is the load-bearing sentence here: the mounted SCC count does not drop, and cannot.** `a_disposed_exemplar_holds_no_reactive_cycle` reads a real V8 heap snapshot, and on this backend `downgrade` is the IDENTITY — a weak handle *is* the cell object — so the emitted graph is unchanged by construction and the walk measures what it measured before: **mounted reachable=243 cycles=2, unmounted reachable=122 cycles=0, before and after, identical**. The planted-red form the slice was written with ("restore the strong capture, watch the mounted count rise") is unrunnable for the same reason, and the experiment was run in both directions to say so rather than inferred. What the slice buys is that the edge is now WRITTEN where the graph can be checked against it, so the counted lowering has nothing left to change in std; the count itself is what makes the cycle collectable, and the SCC walk cannot see a cycle the host collector already took. `derivations_detach_from_their_source_with_their_boundary` still 25→0 and the three `b291`/`b292` pins are unchanged. **Cost, measured** (`node --jitless` under callgrind, 2,000,000 notifications): 10,279,996,775 Ir before against 11,461,199,073 after over a 150,827,228 Ir interpreter baseline — **+591 Ir per notification, +11.7 %**, the `[ 0, cell ]` array and its branch. Under the JIT the two are indistinguishable at loadavg 130 (0.06–0.10 s user, overlapping), because V8's escape analysis removes an array that never leaves the frame. Nine corpus goldens move for the new reactive body (`blanket-impl`, `reactive`, `reactive-flatten`, `reactive-on-change`, `reactive-owner`, `reactive-selector`, `reactive-turns`, `signal-update`, `spread-parameters`); `reactive-on-change.vl`'s witness directive is re-keyed to the two gensyms its claim names, the claim itself unchanged. Tracker C14 S3.

**`Weak<T>` lands: `Shared::downgrade`, `Weak::upgrade`, `Weak::get` — the handle that names a cell without keeping it alive.** C1 was filed in July and blocked ever since on "Tier 2 refcounting, the native arc", because a *deterministic* `upgrade() → None` needs a release event and nothing in the language releases anything (the GC-timing `WeakRef` spelling was rejected 2026-07-07 for exactly that). The C14 paper split the blocker in two: the SHAPE — the type, the `Option` on the way back, the graph edge that says "follow me, do not keep me alive" — is decidable today, and only the `None` waits. So the surface ships now, JS-lowered, with the guarantee documented at the type: `Shared::downgrade(&self): Weak<T>`, `Weak::upgrade(self): Option<Shared<T>>`, and `Weak::get(&self): Option<&T> borrows self`, exactly as `destruction.md` §10 and `claims-and-epochs.md` §5a specify them. **`upgrade` is for keeping the cell alive; `get` is for touching it** — the first hands back a holder, the second a second-class view good where it stands and storable nowhere, and it is the same verb and the same `Option<&T>` shape as `Arena::get`, which is what makes every dynamic alias in the language answer one question one way. **The lowering costs nothing**: `downgrade` is the receiver unchanged (`SharedClone`'s twin — a weak handle has nothing to be weaker *than* until something counts), `upgrade` is `[ 0, cell ]` and `get` is `[ 0, cell.v ]`, so no wrapper is allocated and the native representation stays free to be a second word on the cell rather than a box around it. **`Weak` is a primitive beside `Shared`** — registered in `primitive_struct_ids` off `shared.vl`'s own scope (so a user's `Weak`-named type is untouched), fenced against holding a resource with the same sentence `Shared`/`List`/`Map`/`Set`/`Context` carry, and excluded from the HMR transfer by the rule that already excludes every bodyless `external struct` — a transferred weak handle would carry the *old* module's cell object across, which is the one thing a handle that does not decide a lifetime must not do. **One analyzer seam was genuinely missing, and it is worth naming.** A view is a property of an EXPRESSION, not of a `Type` — there is no view variant in `Type` — so `function_returns_wrapped_view` reads a body's tail leaves, and a BODYLESS declaration cannot say `Option<&T>` in a way any checker can see. Without a seam, `Some(let view)` over `weak.get()` bound a value wearing an ampersand: `*view` was rejected as a non-view and storing `view` in a `List<&i32>` was allowed, where the identical `Arena::get` program is refused. `Weak::get` is the one extern in the language with that return, so it gets the one exception — found by the primitive's identity, the way the `Shared` intrinsics are — and the capture is a view binding again: `*view` is the only way across, and handing it anywhere that wants a value is refused with the same sentence `Arena::get` earns. Thirteen pins in a new `crates/vilan-core/tests/inference/weak.rs`: the three signatures, the aliasing (a write through the strong handle read back through the weak one, and through an upgraded one), the live view, the second-class refusals, the readonly refusal, the resource fence, the HMR exclusion, and the two emissions. The view seam and the resource fence were each planted red. **The const channel needed no arm either**, and the pin says so in both directions: the intrinsics lower to shapes the const-eval interpreter already evaluates — an array literal and a property read — where `Shared::new` and `Shared::identity` each needed a runtime helper and an interpreter arm of their own. Docs: a `Weak<T>` section in the cells reference saying which of the two verbs to reach for and why both answers are `Some` today — **write the `None` arm anyway**, because a program that handles it is a program that keeps working when the count is real. Tracker C1 (C14 S2).

A slot NOTHING ever fills is already B131's starved-parameter refusal, which names the parameter and asks for an annotation, so the deferral cannot go silent. **A `lazy let` carries its value across a hot swap once something has forced it; one still pending is re-minted.** v1 excluded every lazy binding from HMR transfer for a reason that only covered half the question: what a swap carries is a VALUE, a lazy binding may not have one yet, and adopting the CELL would hand the new bundle the old bundle's thunk, closed over the old bundle's functions. Pinned three ways in `inference/hmr.rs` and, where it can only be proved by a ROUND, in the swap e2e: a `lazy let` forced before the swap reads the OLD bundle's value afterwards while the new bundle's initializer never runs, and one left pending runs the new bundle's initializer for the first time on the other side. A thread clock is load-proof in the MEAN (M15), which is what every absolute budget in that file rests on, but a RATIO of two 8 µs readings is a different instrument: that is a handful of scheduler slices, the caches between them belong to whatever else is on the box, and at loadavg 90 on sixteen cores the two ends are not drawn from the same distribution. So the bound gains an ALLOWANCE denominated in the reading itself — 0.02 ms on a quiet box, 0.08 ms at four times the core count and above, scaled by the load average's share of the cores — and the vacuity guard beside it (`scan > fetch × 5`) takes the same allowance on the side that can hurt it. Both keep enormous headroom: the whole-program scan this gate measures on the same run costs 5.6–11.6 ms, 700–900× the fetch, so the regression the bound guards against — a table that follows the codebase, which means reverting to that scan — cannot hide inside 0.08 ms. The allowance is the noise floor alone where there is no `/proc/loadavg` to read, on the principle the cost claims already decline on Windows. **The rpc handle-over-POST pin waits for its lease to settle instead of assuming one round-trip is enough.** Since A92 the stub is sync and makes no call, so the failure is recorded when the first LEASE issues one — on the transport's turn, not the caller's — and the single settling `touch()` after the subscription was enough on a quiet box and not under nine-lane load, where the pin printed `note err Waiting` and nothing in it could tell that from a real regression. It round-trips until the status leaves `Waiting`, bounded at a hundred rounds, so a genuine hang still fails the existing assertions with the state it is stuck in printed rather than with a timeout nobody can read. Tracker N84.

**A `[derive(..)]` reached inside a macro WORLD is skipped instead of being refused as a compiler bug.** A world is a nested analysis of one macro-defining file, blanked to its definitions and compiled against `macro_std`, and its own analysis registers NO macros by design — std's prelude modules declare `macro fun`s, and registering them would recursively compile their worlds without bound, so the expander's scope inside a world is empty on purpose. N79 then deleted the Rust generators that stood behind std's derive macros, and the arm that lost its fallback answers an unresolved `[derive(X)]` with one of two sentences: a load-ordering bug (B21's class) to be reported, or a std that does not carry the derive. **Inside a world both are false** — the scope is empty deliberately, and the std is fine — so a derive written into one of the eleven modules a world force-loads (`boolean`, `list`, `null`, `promise`, `compare`, `default`, `debug`, `json`, `hash`, `number`, `string`) would be answered with "please report how this module is reached" about a perfectly good std, by an ordinary std change. The reach is EMPTY today, which is why this is a guard rather than a fix: the entry a world sees is blanked, `macro_std` declares none, and none of the eleven derives anything. So the pin PLANTS the shape rather than waiting for it — a staged std whose `boolean.vl` carries a `[derive(Debug)]`, an entry whose own derive compiles a world over it, and the assertion that no load-ordering refusal is reported and the analysis is clean; with the guard commented out it reds with the false message verbatim. Its own test binary, beside `macro_world_census.rs` and for that file's reason: the world cache is process-global, so a test analyzing against a DIFFERENT std stays out of any process asserting on it (and it stages under `CARGO_TARGET_TMPDIR`, not the shared `/tmp`). Tracker B339.

**A quickfix can edit another file, and B318's "Export `S`" / "Export `hidden`" become actions instead of sentences.** `Document::QuickFix` carried a title, a span in THIS document's live text, and a replacement — so the visibility paper's third fix, which inserts one word in front of a declaration WHEREVER it lives, was not expressible at all and shipped as a sentence in a message while its two one-character siblings (`Import as #leaf`, `Delete the #`) shipped as actions. **A head item with no parentheses of its own paints as an attribute name too: `disabled` and the `hidden` of `hidden.show(flag)`.** E170 gave the element head its attribute vocabulary and reached exactly the names a `(` follows, so the two head items that carry no parens painted as NOTHING at all — a bare boolean attribute (`<input type("checkbox") disabled />`) and the attribute half of an attribute-then-chain item, whose `show` is a chain link and is correctly coloured as the call it is. Both are attribute names by the grammar's own one-token disambiguation — a leading `.` is chain form, `on` plus `:` is the event form, an ident plus `(` is an attribute with a value, and a bare ident is a boolean attribute — so the vocabulary was owed to them and E170's rule simply could not ask for it. One more rule inside E164's head region, after E170's and before `$self`, with the same lookbehind (a `.` leaves a chain link alone, a `-` leaves a hyphenated name to the rule that paints the whole of it, a `:` leaves `on:click` to the event rule) plus a `<` that keeps it off a tag name in any shape where the head's own `begin` did not consume one. **What is new is the LOOKAHEAD, and it is what the rule is**: not a `(`, which is E170's; not a `:`, which would otherwise take the `on` out of `on:click` and leave the event name uncoloured, since this rule sits ahead of `$self` and wins the tie at the same character; and not a `-`, the first segment of a hyphenated name. A `.` is deliberately allowed, because that is the `hidden` case. A `{hole}` never reaches the rule at all: the head region ends at a `{`, so a child hole is outside it, and a value's parentheses are `#element-head-value`'s own region. **Blast radius, measured by tokenising both grammars over the tree and diffing per character**: of all 257 tracked `.vl` files and all 464 `vilan` fences under `vilan/docs`, 10 characters move and they are one token — `disabled` in `vilan/test/element-syntax.vl`, the estate's only parenless head item. kolt's 26 `.vl` move nothing: every head item it writes is the dotted chain form. Two scope pins over one exhibit carrying all of it — both parenless shapes painted, the `on:` form and the valued and hyphenated names still painted, and the controls: both tag names still `entity.name.tag.vilan`, a `{hole}` child neither an attribute nor inside the head, a chain link still a call, a call outside the markup untouched. TextMate only — the book's highlight.js theme has no head region and never carried E170's vocabulary either, so there is nothing to mirror. Tracker E176.

**`vilan fmt` gives the module-level `export *;` marker a canonical place: the slot just below the file's imports, with a paragraph gap on both sides.** B318 S1 introduced the marker and the printer left it wherever it was written — probed on 9b22ec36, all four placements (above the imports, mid-file, glued to the next item, at the end) survived a reprint unchanged — because top-level statements print in source order and only imports sort WITHIN their run. S6's estate sweep is about to write hundreds of markers, so the rule lands before it and the sweep's output is already canonical: module comment, the imports, the marker, then the items. **The slot is the leading import BLOCK, not the sort RUN**: `import_run_end` stops at a standalone comment, because imports may not reorder across one, and inheriting that break moved a correctly-placed marker UP into the middle of the import list — kolt's `views.vl` has a `// FIXME:` line above its second import and its marker correctly below all thirty, and `vilan fmt --check` over a copy of kolt flagged exactly that one file until the slot was measured over every leading import, comments and blank lines and all. It is measured with the marker lifted out, which is what makes a marker written above the imports find the same place as one written below them — the imports are the file's leading run either way, and the marker was never part of it. A file with no leading import run puts the marker before its first item, after the MODULE comment: the split between a module comment and a doc comment written against that first item is the blank line between them, which is the distinction the language's own files already draw, so `/// what main does` is never separated from its `fun`. A comment written directly above the marker travels WITH it — it is about the marker, not about whatever the marker left behind. **Only the bare marker moves.** `export import …` is a re-export and sorts inside the import run like any other statement; `export item` and `export(in PATH) item` are declarations and hold their place; a SECOND `export *;` is left exactly where it was written, because the formatter must never hide a diagnosis by tidying the evidence away. `blank_line` is idempotent now, since the forced gap below the marker is asked for before the next item's comments are flushed and the source may have written a gap there too. **The token-level safety net gains its sixth order-insensitivity**, and it is a RELOCATION rather than a deletion: `hoist_export_all_markers` moves every `export * ;` triple to the front of both streams, so the net forgives the printer's move while still refusing a marker that the reprint LOST or gained — dropping the tokens would have accepted exactly the failure the net exists to catch. `export *;` is the only production that lexes to that triple (the parser takes the `;` in its lookahead for that reason — `export * helper;` is a deref), so the scan cannot mistake anything else for it. **Insertion points respect the slot**: the add-import quickfix and auto-import completion put a NEW leading import ABOVE the marker — into the existing run when there is one, and on the file's first line when there is not — never below it, where the next format would have to step over it. The organizer's `import <module>;` rescue lands inside the run as before. **The estate**: the six benchmark modules that carry a marker all wrote it on line 1, above their own module comment, and are reformatted here; `vilan fmt --check` over the tree is green, which is the gate sweep-36's hand-placed markers merge into. Eleven pins — the four placements, the already-canonical file, the marker-only file, the duplicate, the three export declarations holding their place, the net forgiving the move but not a lost or doubled marker, and the add-import insertion above the marker — each asserting idempotence and that the reprint did not silently bail. Tracker E181.

**`lazy let database: Database = Database::open("kolt.db");` — a module binding whose initializer runs at its FIRST USE and then memoizes.** This is the whole of the lazy-database answer the paper was filed from: one line, no accessor, no `mut Option<Database>`, no view returns. *Everything else about the binding is unchanged* — the module owns the value, it has process lifetime and never drops, a resource stays loan-only and write-frozen, a closure may reference it under R9's module-level exemption, and the platform coloring of the initializer colors the entry exactly as an eager binding's does (the reachability path still reads `main → database → open`). `lazy` moves one event's TIME and nothing else, which is why it needed no new alias kind, no new epoch event and no change to the law. **The same memo cell S1 built serves it**: the declaration emits `__lazy("database", () => …)` — the initializer walked into the THUNK's own block, so nothing its lowering needs runs at load — and every read emits `__force`, which is the same arm a lazy parameter's reads take. A binding nothing reads emits nothing and runs nothing, which is the point; it is also why the unused-binding path may not fall back to emitting the initializer for its effects. **The two runtime laws are §2's, verbatim.** An initializer that (transitively) reads its own binding meets the cell's `running` flag and panics `` lazy initialization cycle: `database` `` rather than hanging — and it is deliberately NOT a compile error, so `init_order`'s load-time relation gives a lazy binding no out-edges at all (its declaration builds a closure, and creating a closure is inert — the rule that already keeps the mutually-recursive module-closure idiom legal). A failed initializer POISONS: the first touch propagates the author's own panic, and every later touch re-panics with `` lazy `database` is poisoned: its initializer panicked: … ``, because retrying would turn "at most once" into "at least once per attempt". **Sync and context-free, with one diagnostic each.** The sync half is already the rule every module initializer obeys, lazy or not, so `lazy` adds no second sentence about the same mistake (B5); the context half is new and steers to doing the work inside a turn that threads one. **§3's exclusions are refused where they are written**: a lazy LOCAL (an end-of-scope drop would need the was-it-initialized flag drop flags were ratified out to avoid), a `lazy mut`, a lazy destructure, a lazy binding with no initializer, and a bare `lazy name = …` — that last one consumed and reported rather than declined, because `Parser::attempt` truncates a declining branch's errors and the author would have got "found 'lazy' expected an item" about a keyword they spelled correctly. **HMR excludes lazy bindings** (`TransferForm::Excluded`): what a swap carries is a VALUE, and a lazy binding may not have one — adopting the cell would hand the new bundle the old bundle's thunk, closed over the old bundle's functions. **Eighteen more pins, and two of them drive the real thing.** In `inference/lazy.rs`: first-use order and the memo in one print sequence, an eager binding beside it saying what the difference is, an unused binding initializing nothing, the cycle trap by name, the poison with both touches visible in one run, the emission shape, a module binding FORWARDING into a lazy parameter (the two positions share one cell), the context refusal, the async one staying single, the platform fence, and each of §3's five refusals; the formatter's round trip on `lazy let` beside S1's. In `vilan-cli/tests/database.rs`, against the host `node:sqlite`: a `lazy let database: Database` that opens at the first read and stays ONE handle across three reads through two functions, and the loan-only refusal firing on it exactly as it fires on the eager form. Two ledger rows `NEW`; four new parser rule statements. Docs: spec §6.10 and §3.4's production, the appendix's reserved words (which gains `css` too — it had been missing since the `css` block shipped), the tour's "Lazy resources" section beside the module-level idiom it does not replace, and the `Option`/`Result` page's note that `unwrap_or`'s fallback and `expect`'s message are still EAGER and that the retrofit is a deliberate sweep, not this commit. A100 S2, `proposal/lazy.md` §2/§3/§6.

**`lazy` is a keyword, and a `lazy` parameter defers its argument to the callee's first read of it — evaluated at most once, late, and not at all if the callee never reads.** `fun expect(self, lazy message: str)` is the shape the ratified paper opens with: the call site does not evaluate `i"no row for {key} in {table.describe()}"`, it packages it, and `expect`'s happy path — which never touches `message` — never runs it. The callee side is fully transparent: the parameter reads as a plain `str`, the FIRST read forces the package and memoizes the result, and every later read reuses it, so a side effect in a lazy argument happens at most once rather than at most once per read. Forwarding a lazy parameter into another lazy position passes the same package along, so a chain three calls deep still has ONE memo; handing it to an eager position forces it there, because that is a read like any other. **`lazy` is part of the SIGNATURE, not a private decision of the body** — it changes what the caller builds — so hover renders it beside the type and an `impl` of a lazy-parameter trait signature must agree in both directions, which `check_one_conformance` now holds position by position beside the conventions it already held. (The paper asked for a targeted check because B29 had not landed when it was written; B29 has, so laziness is one more comparison rather than a check of its own.) **Three v1 restrictions, each the conservative direction, each with its steer.** A resource stays eager, refused at the declaration (`lazy handle: Res`) and at the argument, because the package that carries a lazy argument would own the resource and a closure may not; a resource LOCAL named inside a lazy argument is refused by R9 itself, in R9's own words, and a view binding by rule 3 in rule 3's — the package IS a closure, so every existing capture rule applies to it unchanged and neither needed a new refusal. An argument that suspends is refused with the `async <expr>` → pass the `Task` steer, counting both spellings of the suspension exactly as E3 counts them (the `await` the author wrote, and the implicit one a call to an async callee performs). An argument that requires an ambient context is refused with the pass-a-closure steer, for the reason a `drop` body is context-free: the forcing point is inside the callee, where the call site's contexts may be gone. **BREAKING: `lazy` is a hard keyword, so it can no longer be a binding, parameter, field or type name.** One program in the tree used it — `vilan/test/reactive-on-change.vl`'s `let lazy = count.on_change(..)`, renamed to `quiet`, which moves two lines of its golden and nothing else; std, `examples/`, the templates, the benchmarks, the docs' fences and kolt spell it nowhere. It lands in all three homes in this commit (the lexer's `KEYWORDS`, the TextMate grammar and the book's highlight.js theme, both generated from `grammar_sync.rs`'s `KEYWORD_ROLES`), and joins the tour's reserved-word list. **One shape lowers it**, the one §2's module bindings will reuse: a memo cell `{ state, value, thunk }` — plus the binding's NAME, which the cycle and poison messages have to say — built by `__lazy` and read through `__force`, whose states are pending → running → done | poisoned, with `running` as the cycle trap and a panicking thunk poisoning the cell rather than retrying. Both helpers carry their interpreter arms in this commit, which is the equivalence gate: a macro body runs in the native evaluator, and a pin drives a lazy call through one to prove the two answer alike. **Twenty-four pins, twenty-two of them in a new `inference/lazy.rs`**, behaviour-first: a counting side effect proves the memo, its absence proves that a parameter never read never runs, the forcing order proves the force is the first READ and not the call, a three-hop chain proves the single memo and an eager hop proves the force, and two emission pins cover what behaviour cannot distinguish (a forward that re-wrapped would print the same thing). Beside them: each of the three restrictions with its steer, both capture rules, both directions of the trait mismatch and the agreeing impl dispatching lazily, all three grammar homes, the compositions `lazy` refuses (`own` or a view, `mut`, `...`, a closure parameter, an `external fun`), the formatter's round trip in all three homes (`formatter.rs`), and the hover (`vilan-lsp`). Five ledger rows `NEW`; four new parser rule statements. The tour gains a "Lazy parameters" section. A100 S1, `proposal/lazy.md` §1/§5.

**Reference identity is an intrinsic that stamps a cell on the first ASK, so a program that exposes nothing stops minting an id per signal — and the eleven goldens A92 moved come back.** A92 gave `SignalCell` an `id: i32` field, filled by `fresh_id()` at construction, because the rpc runtime's dynamic exposure has to recognise a source it has already exported (two views calling one getter are one channel, one capability and one forward, not two of each). The KEY is right; the eagerness was not. A cell's identity is a fact about the cell, not a field it has to carry, and paying for it at construction means every `SignalCell` in every program — a counter's, a form field's, an SSR render's — mints an id for a dedup almost none of them use, and every corpus golden carries a `fresh_id()` call and a module-level `next_subscriber_id` cell to prove it. **`Shared::identity(): i32` is where the answer belongs**: `Shared` is the one place reference identity exists in the language (it is not deep-copied, so two handles are one cell and nothing else in the value says so), and the lowering is `cell.__id ??= next++` — the stamp goes on the cell object beside its `v` slot, the first caller mints it and every later one reads it, and a cell nothing ever asks about carries no property at all. `SignalCell` loses its field; `cell_identity(cell)` in `std::reactive` is `cell.value.identity()`, the value cell's, which is the signal's because copying the struct copies neither of its two `Shared`s; `expose_dynamic` and `expose_keyed_cell_dynamic` read it at the four sites that dedup. **The numbers, in instructions rather than seconds** (callgrind over `node --jitless`, 100,000 constructions against an identical control program, the control legs 0.016% apart — the noise floor): a `SignalCell::new` plus one `get` costs **3,556.6 Ir before and 3,043.2 after, −513.4 Ir, −14.4%**. On the owner's own application the shape is cleaner than the average: kolt's CLIENT, which exposes nothing, drops `fresh_id()` out of the constructor and emits no `__shared_identity` at all — it pays nothing, not less — while the server, which does expose, carries the helper and mints lazily at its four sites. **Eleven corpus goldens return to their pre-A92 shape** (`blanket-impl`, `element-syntax`, `reactive`, `reactive-flatten`, `reactive-on-change`, `reactive-owner`, `reactive-selector`, `reactive-turns`, `signal-update`, `spread-parameters`, `ssr-render` — nine of them byte-identical to the file A92 rewrote, the other two differing only in drift since), and `element-syntax` and `ssr-render` lose `fresh_id` and `next_subscriber_id` entirely: a program that renders and never subscribes now emits neither. The item said twelve; A92 moved eleven, and these are those eleven. Pinned in `std_surface.rs`: two handles to one cell and a `clone()` answer one number, two cells holding equal values answer two, asking twice answers the same, and a `SignalCell` copied into a struct field keeps its identity while a second signal on the same value does not. The interpreter carries the same sentence over an `Object` cell, with a PER-RUN counter (a macro world is torn down between expansions, and an identity that outlived one would make a program answer differently depending on what ran before it). `std/cells.md` gains the method and the paragraph. Tracker M66, R8 at Order 36's GO.

**A two-entry package where one entry uses element or `css` syntax builds again: the base cache's key carries the modules an entry's own SYNTAX seeds, not only the ones a `std::` path names.** An element desugars to `std::ui`'s `view` and a `css` block makes `std::style::prelude` ambient inside itself; both are pushed into the load beside the written imports and both land in the world — and neither is named by any `std::` path in the entry's text, which is all `BaseCacheKey::std_seeds` was reading. WHICH entry failed depended on which sorted first — rename the element entry so it leads and both build, which is what makes this so easy to mistake for something about the file. The `css` twin says "cannot find 'style' in this scope". One line: `collect_std_item_modules` joins `collect_module_paths(.., "std")` in the seed list the key is built from, through the same `seed_module` resolution, so a desugar seed is keyed exactly as a written import is. **The same shared state is what made two `inference` tests read red under plain `cargo test`** — `an_element_needs_no_view_import_at_all` and `b270_a_shadowing_view_does_not_capture_the_element_desugar`, after any std-free program had been analyzed in that process; nextest's process-per-test hid it, and the whole `modules::` filter (285 tests) now passes under `cargo test` too. Pinned in `base_cache.rs` on the DIAGNOSTICS rather than on a hit delta (an element entry compiles macro worlds, and those consult the cache on their own account): the plain entry then the element entry, the element entry then the plain one, and the `css` twin, each analyzing clean and emitting — red-proved, the pin reading back the "cannot find 'view'" the repro does. Found by hygiene-36 chasing N84's flake. Tracker B341.
