**A module opened as the entry, whose own package imports it back, stores its world under a key that says which module the world excludes — so the files a cycle reaches stop being uncacheable.** A front end hands the analysis the file in front of it, so a package's modules are analyzed AS entries; when the load reaches `pkg::<entry>` the loader aliases that name onto the entry's own (global) scope rather than loading the file twice (B226/B239), and the world that comes out is missing the module it was built for. B239 answered that by storing nothing at all, and nothing else ever mints those keys — so those files could never be served, not once, however warm the process. **On kolt that is SEVEN of eighteen `src/*.vl`, and the probe says which and why**: a three-keystroke walk with an unbounded cache (`base_cache_keystroke_cost_across_a_sibling_checkout`, release) recorded `hits: 0` for `app_context`, `app_overlay`, `prefs`, `sidebar`, `styles` and `theme` — the cycle files — and for `store.vl`, which is a `[service]` entry and bypasses the cache for its own documented reason (a correction to the item, which counted it with the other six). The key gains `entry_open_module`, the entry's own canonical path, set for a file-mode entry that seeds a sibling at all and `None` everywhere else — so every world stored before this field existed is unchanged, std-only worlds go on being shared across files, and an entry-shaped world is offered back to the file it was built for and to nothing else. The world travels with its `entry_is_open_module` flag, which is what makes a hit reproduce B239's deferred order instead of discovering it again. **What it is worth, and what it is not.** Paired in one process, the same file both ways, five edits each (release, loadavg 16–42): `sidebar.vl` 344 → 184 ms (−47%), `styles.vl` 1,251 → 1,103 (−12%), `theme.vl` 1,234 → 1,121 (−9%), `prefs.vl` 612 → 557 (−9%), `app_context.vl` 530 → 489 (−8%), `app_overlay.vl` 580 → 543 (−6%) — against 31–46% for the files that could already be served. The gap is the half this does NOT recover and the item did not separate: an open module's world is stored UNRESOLVED, because the pre-entry `resolve_world` is exactly what B239 defers, so a hit saves the module LOAD WALK and the post-entry `build()` still pays the resolve on every keystroke (`vilan check` phase marks, quiet box: `theme.vl` load+walk 191 ms, base 0, build 161, checks 240, against `views.vl`'s 141 / 145 / 11 / 312). Splitting the import fixpoint out of `resolve_world` and running it before the store was tried and reverted: it accounts for 0.4 ms of that 150 — the cost is the preludes, the `use` drain and the constraint fixpoint, which read scopes whose chain reaches the entry's. The remainder is filed. **M19's per-module checks record is deliberately withheld** from an entry-shaped world on both legs: those records are of checks that ran over a RESOLVED world, and they are keyed by every source's content but the entry's — which is sound only while module checks do not depend on the entry, and through the alias they do. **Pinned red-first** in `base_cache.rs`: a three-module fixture with a cycle through the entry stores one world, HITS on its second analysis with a fresh build's diagnostics and JS, evicts by content when a sibling is edited, and — the assertion the key exists for, which fails with a HIT where a MISS belongs the moment the field is taken out — is not served to a different file of the same package with byte-identical seeds. The cost is the six worlds themselves: kolt's unbounded session retains 12 → 18 worlds and 272 → 494 MiB of nominal weight, nominal because M50's 24× factor was measured on RESOLVED worlds and the derived tables it is mostly made of are the ones these worlds have not filled. Tracker M70.

**`Style::attribute`'s and `Style::within`'s `Option<str>` enters its one-release deprecation window, with the condition value as the steer, and the estate moves ahead of it.** A89 gave the two combinators `value: Option<str>` so a PRESENCE condition had a spelling at all — `Some(v)` the exact match `[name="v"]`, `None` the bare `[name]` — and A95 makes that argument unnecessary rather than merely unfashionable: `attribute(name)` IS the presence condition and `attribute(name).eq(value)` the exact one, so the `Option` every call site has had to spell since A89 disappears from the surface instead of staying as a second way to say one thing. Ruled as one release of `[deprecated]` and then removal (style-conditions.md §12 (iv)), so **nothing breaks today**: both methods still compile, still emit exactly the stylesheet they always emitted (pinned beside the warning, the sugar's rules asserted equal to the value form's), and both now carry a steer naming the replacement AND where the `Some` went — "use .on(attribute(name), inner) — or .eq(value) on the attribute for the exact form". **The estate moves now rather than at the removal**, so the tree does not spend a release warning at itself: the corpus's three styled programs (`style.vl`, `theme.vl`, `css-block.vl`) and the spec's one prose example are rewritten to the value form, and every corpus program builds with the deprecation warning at 0. The rewrite is also where the condition SET earns its keep in a real program — `let dark = const within(attribute("data-theme").eq("dark"));` is named once and summed into four rules — and it turned up the correction the guide and the reference now both carry: a named set must be bound `const`, because a `const` expression reads only compile-time-known bindings, so the paper's `let interactive = hover() + active().not();` is `let interactive = const hover() + active().not();`. The `inference/styling.rs` fence pins deliberately keep the deprecated spelling: they pin the SUGAR's six nesting refusals, which are exactly what the sugar is for as long as it exists. Three pins (the two steers, the unchanged emission, the value form's silence); no `.css` golden moves, and the two corpus `.mjs` goldens that do move carry the new `const` bindings and nothing else. **One find, fixed here because the deprecation is what surfaced it**: `print_func` had no arm for `[deprecated("use …")]` at all, so `vilan fmt` SILENTLY BAILED on any file carrying one — the whole file handed back unchanged and `--check` calling that clean. Nothing in std, the corpus or the docs had ever declared one, so `formatter_never_silently_bails` had nothing to catch it on until `style.vl` grew two. The attribute now prints first, as the ordered prefix has it, on a free function and an impl member alike, with its own pin (both positions, `[must_use]` behind it, and the fixed point). Tracker A95 (S5), and the formatter gap.

**A call written with NO RECEIVER means the FREE function, even inside the `impl` block that declares a method of the same name.** `fun when(self, ..) { self.child(when(condition, body)) }` did not compile: the bare `when` resolved to the METHOD it sits inside, and the call reported the method's arity (``  `when` expects 3 arguments, but got 2 ``). That is not a shadowing decision, it is a resolution that cannot be right — a method needs a receiver, and `self.when(..)` is how one is written — and there was no qualified escape from inside a package either: `pkg::ui::when(..)` answers "`pkg` is a namespace, not a value" and a self-import is a cycle. std lived with it: its positional value forms had to construct their struct literal inline instead of being the one line of sugar the paper promised (positional-slots.md §3b, and A99 has since retired the methods that needed it). Ruled at Order 36's GO, R4: **the free function wins.** **Narrow by construction, three ways.** It fires only for a CALL SUBJECT, so a bare mention of the name as a VALUE still resolves to the member it always did (and is still refused, because a method has no value form — which is what proves the rule did not move it); only when the enclosing `impl` body's own declaration TAKES a receiver, so a receiverless ASSOCIATED function still shadows, since a bare call to one IS a call to it; and it resolves from the impl body scope's PARENT rather than jumping to the module, so an intervening binding still wins. A name no outer scope binds falls through to the ordinary walk, and the method's arity error is reported exactly as before — a program with no free function to mean is not one this rule can fix. Read where every other name is read (`resolve_prepped_local`'s drain, after the walk), so it is ORDER-INDEPENDENT: the method may be declared below the body that calls the free function. Four pins in `inference/traits.rs` — the shape with a user impl (the std exhibit is gone), order independence with the two narrowness controls in one program, the no-free-function control, and the value-mention control — two of them red with the rule disabled. Tracker B334.

**A keyed run's order pass leaves an unmoved row alone: an append costs no cut at all where it used to cut and re-insert the whole list.** A91 made the reconciler's unit a REGION — one empty-text marker per row, a row's extent running from its marker to the next boundary — and its order pass cut EVERY live row out by span and re-inserted it before the anchor, in the new order, whether or not the row had gone anywhere. That is correct and it is oblivious: one `extractContents`, one marker move and one content move per row, on every change of the list, for a thousand rows of which one was appended. **What is settled is now decided first.** A row is settled when its previous index reads as part of an INCREASING run across the new order — those rows already stand in the document in their new relative order, so leaving them where they are and threading every other row in before the next settled row's marker produces exactly the new order. `Region::insert_row` and the new `Region::open_row_before` take that marker as an `end` bound (`open_row` is `open_row_before` at the anchor), and a `None` in the cut table is the whole test for "this row did not move". **Two linear scans, and the better of them wins.** A forward greedy run keeps the earliest row of each increasing chain and is optimal when one row moved backward (a row dragged to the end); a backward run keeps the latest and is optimal when one row moved forward. Neither is the maximum increasing subsequence — that is a patience sort — and the two agree with it on every shape a real list takes, differing only on a reshuffle, where nearly every row has to move whichever set is chosen. **The numbers, on 1,000 rows between a static header and a footer** (rows cut / rows built, per pass, counted at the DOM stub; the tree's own order printed beside every count, so a cheaper pass that lost the run is a wrong answer and not a smaller number):

```text
pass                    before            after
append one row          cut 1000 build 1  cut    0 build 1
prepend one row         cut 1000 build 1  cut    0 build 1
remove the first row    cut 1000          cut    1
remove a middle row     cut 1000          cut    1
change one row's value  cut 1000 build 1  cut    1 build 1
move the last to front  cut 1000          cut    1
move the first to last  cut 1000          cut    1
reverse (the control)   cut 1000          cut  999
```

Callgrind Ir over the whole harness under `node --jitless`: **23,276,320,737 → 9,033,205,462, −61.2 %**. That figure is honestly STUB-DOMINATED and is not a claim about a browser — the stub's `insertBefore` is O(children), where a real host's is not — which is exactly why the item asked for the node and call counts and why they are the table above. Per-row node cost is unchanged (2,005 nodes for 1,000 rows): the marker is what buys a row of any shape, and A98 is about what the pass DOES with it. `place_each` and `place_each_by` both take the change; the `@process` twin gains `open_row_before` for the surface gate and calls it nowhere, as it does for every other `Region` member. One pin, eight edits, both halves asserted per edit (the cost and the resulting tree), non-vacuous against the skip removed. Tracker A98.

A method's content lands at the parent's current end, always, so a conditional or a keyed run among static children needed a wrapper element — which is the defect positional slots were filed to remove, and which a surface offering both spellings keeps offering. **The rewrite is mechanical, and there are two spellings of it**: `parent.swap(s, r)` becomes `parent.child(swap(s, r))` — byte-for-byte what the method did — or `{swap(s, r)}` in a child hole, which is what to reach for when position matters. Pins: the six refusals with their steer on both twins, a user type's own `bind_each` drawing none, the `child` rewrite rendering what the method rendered, the gate reachable under the free `swap_split`, and two in `vilan-lsp` for the fix and its negative. **A `context` clause is recorded on a CALL's own type and on a closure literal's, from the callee's declared return and from the landing — the two faces of one gap.** `let body: (|| void) context c = make();` was refused even where `make` declares exactly that return: `expr_type_ids` holds the type an expression PRODUCES, and a clause is not part of it — the solver records the clause against the binding's annotation and never against the call that fills it — so `clause_carried_by` could not see one. The declaration is the answer, and it was already in hand: a function's return type is a promise about the value it hands back, and a clause on it is part of that promise. `call_return_clause` reads it, at all FOUR landings (a binding's initializer, a struct field, a return, a call argument), and `clause_carried_by` consults it too, so a call carrying a DIFFERENT clause now earns the mismatch message that names both rather than being told what the position takes. Only a direct call to a named function: a call through a value has no declaration to read, which is the same reason `value_type_of` prefers a declaration over a recorded type. **The mirror shape from slots-35 is ADOPTION at the other landings.** `let wire = || { … };` did not carry the clause of the field it later lands in, though an annotated `let` does — and an argument binding has ADOPTED a parameter's clause since B309. The predicate is now `adoptable_closure`, shared, and the arm sits at the field and return landings beside the parameter's: an unannotated local binding whose initializer is a closure literal takes the clause of the position it lands in, and the literal is born under that extent exactly as one written at the landing would be. std's own route gate is the exhibit — `browser/ui.vl` writes `let wire: (|| void) context owner_scope = || { … };` into `Swap`'s `wire` field, and the annotation was doing work the landing can now do on its own (the annotation stays; it is no longer load-bearing). **Neither refusal is weakened**, and two controls say so: `make(): || void` promises nothing and its binding is refused exactly as before, and a binding annotated with a DIFFERENT clause is still the mismatch at a field rather than an adoption. Four pins in `inference/macros.rs` beside the two they narrow. No ledger row: the two messages are unchanged, and the change is which values reach them. Tracker B333.

**`const let` and `const fun`: a compile-time binding may hold a CLOSURE, and a const function's promise is checked where it is made.** `const let NAME[: T] = EXPR;` is `let NAME = const EXPR;` plus the one addition `const-eval.md` §11 now states — the result may be a closure over plain data — and it is a STATEMENT, so it is legal at module level and inside a body alike (R3). `const fun NAME(..) { .. }` declares a function whose body is const-evaluable; `const mut` is refused with a curated parse rule that names both spellings that do work (`const let`, or `mut name = const ..;`). **The snapshot is the closure's OWN body, with its captures baked.** `const fun scale_step(rem) { |n| rem * n }` + `const let space = scale_step(0.25)` folds `const space(2f)` to `0.5` and emits, for the runtime call, `const space = (n) => 0.25 * n;` — one arrow, no IIFE, no wrapper. That shape falls out of B340's framing (a closure is a callable struct of its captures) and out of one fact about the pass: a const site is lowered by a TRANSFORMER OF ITS OWN, whose generated names are that world's, so emitting its arrow into the real output would reference declarations the output does not have. What travels instead is the analyzer's closure ENTITY plus the captured values, and the real emitter walks the closure itself with each capture substituted for the binding it closed over — so the arrow is monomorphized and named like every other, and `0.25` stands where `rem` did. The captures arrive keyed by the const world's names, which is the one thing the two emitters cannot share; the world hands the program its `Id → name` table beside the results and the emitter finishes the translation. **The `const fun` gate reads the call graph, transitively.** A body that reaches a host `[extern]` binding or one of the five impure intrinsics (`scan`, `args`, `env`, the two randoms) is refused at its own declaration, spanned on the name, NAMING the capability — and a `const fun` three calls above one is told the same thing about itself. Not a colouring requirement: a plain `fun` is still const-callable under §9.2's transitive rule, and a `const fun` is still an ordinary function at runtime with runtime arguments. **Both existing refusals gain R2's steer and a quick fix.** "`space` is a runtime value; a `const` expression reads only compile-time-known bindings" now adds "Declare it `const let space = ..;`" — but only where that is possible, so a parameter or a `mut` gets the refusal alone (B83); and "a `const` result must be plain data; this evaluates to a closure" at a `let x = const ..` names the declaration that admits one. The editor's **Declare it `const let`** fix is ONE arm for both, keyed on the two steer constants the analyzer builds its messages from rather than on a second copy of the sentence: at a read it inserts `const ` in front of the binding the message names, and at a closure result it MOVES the keyword to the head of the declaration. **The raw leak is gone**: `const let x = ..;` used to parse as the `const` prefix over a `let` STATEMENT and die in the evaluator with `statement node in expression position: ConstVariable(Variable { .. })` — an internal message reaching a user through the failure envelope. The mark is on the INITIALIZER now, so there is no statement in expression position to leak. Eighteen pins in the new `inference/const_eval.rs` (the fold, the local form, the annotation, `const mut`, the snapshot at both times, the emitted arrow, both steers and the evidence rule behind one of them, the capability gate direct and transitive, and the two "still an ordinary function" controls) plus one in `vilan-lsp`; spec §9.6 and the editor appendix. Two ledger rows `NEW`, one re-keyed, one curated parse rule added. RULED 2026-09-14 (R1–R3). Tracker G24.

The coercion is recorded at the EXPRESSION, in `infer_type_inner`, which is the one place a value's own type and the type its position wants are both in hand; an allow-list of value forms keeps it off the declarations and blocks an expectation forwards through, so an `if`'s two branches each take their own wrap rather than the `if` taking one around both. Offered only for a GROUND `call` signature, for the reason a generic `fun` has no value form. **The field rule (Q2).** `a.b(c)` stays method lookup whatever `b` holds, so a `Callable` field is called `(a.b)(c)` — exactly the rule a closure-valued field already has, so it is the same steer, widened to name both value forms rather than a second message about the same mistake. **`const` needs no arm**: a `Callable` value is plain data, the lowering is the method call the analyzer already resolved, and `const Scale::new(0.25)(4f)` folds to `1`. Nineteen pins in the new `inference/callable.rs`, written against kolt's `src/lib/scale_step.vl` shape — the file that carries the use case with a `FIXME: Make into call operator overload when supported` — plus the core-traits reference page. Two ledger rows `NEW`. RULED 2026-09-14 (Q1, Q2). Tracker B340.

**The std cache prunes itself at materialization, and `vilan cache prune` is the gesture for the times that is not enough.** An installed binary carries std as data and writes it out once to `~/.vilan/std-cache/<content hash>/`, so the compiler and the editor read ordinary files. The key is the std's CONTENT, which is what makes the cache impossible to serve stale — and what makes a new tree land on every build of the toolchain. Nothing deleted the old ones except `vilan upgrade`, and a developer's toolchain refreshed from source never runs `vilan upgrade`: every lane binary and every order's release build left a tree behind forever. On the owner's machine that is **374 entries and 316 MB since 19 July**. **The moment the cache grows is the moment to sweep it**, and it is the only moment worth sweeping at — an existing entry returns before any of this — so `materialize_into` runs the same seven-day `prune_stale` `upgrade` runs, right after the atomic rename of a NEW entry. Safe by construction rather than by ordering: an entry's directory mtime is its creation time and nothing touches it after the rename, so the tree written a moment ago is the youngest thing in the root and survives its own sweep, as does anything a compile started this week might still be reading (std files are read lazily, which is the whole reason the guard exists). **The `malloc_trim` at the analysis-landing seam is conditional on how much the release handed back, and what it costs there is measured instead of estimated.** M64 asks glibc to return the heap's retained-free arenas after every release, which is unarguable at a document CLOSE and is asked far more often than that: the dependency sweep re-analyzes every open importer of an edited file, each of those landings releases the program it just brought (the document is not one of the focused few), and each release walked the arenas.
```text
floor    landings skipped   CPU saved   resident size forgone
 4 MiB        0 / 12           0 ms            0 MiB
16 MiB        5 / 12        33.6 ms          107 MiB
32 MiB        7 / 12        67.9 ms          251 MiB
64 MiB        7 / 12        67.9 ms          251 MiB
```

Three megabytes of resident size per millisecond of a background thread is not a trade a server whose reported footprint was 4.13 GB should take. What `TRIM_MIN_RELEASED_BYTES` (4 MiB) is for is the release that cannot pay for the walk at ALL — glibc walks its arenas in proportion to their own size, not to what was just handed back, so a few hundred kilobytes has nothing page-shaped to give and still costs the whole walk — and no landing in a kolt-sized session is that small, which is the measurement's verdict and not a disappointment. The corpus goldens: `style.css` 23 of 69 and 31.4% → 0 of 46; `css-block.css` 9 of 31 and 29.1% → 0 of 22; `theme.css` 3 of 10 and 24.1% → 0 of 7; `style-when.css` and `preflight.css` had none and have none. **Three `.css` goldens MOVE and they move by SUBTRACTION only** — 23, 9 and 3 lines removed, none added, none changed, the surviving lines in the same order — and the same holds for kolt's sheet line for line, which is what says the drop reaches only the dead. **The mechanism is late emission, not retraction.** A rule cannot be un-emitted through a write-only channel, which is what made B308 "not implementable as ruled" when a lane first priced it; the answer is not to emit it yet. `asset::stage(kind, token, line)` records a contribution against a LIVENESS TOKEN without writing it, `asset::staged(kind)` hands back the ones whose token the build still names, and the pairing with `asset::schedule_at_end` (G23) is the whole machine: `Style::rule` stages each rule under its class and asks for the finaliser (idempotent on the function's identity, so asking once per rule is a set membership test), and `flush_stylesheet` emits what survived. The registry is host-held because it has to be — a const pass gives every site its own interpreter scopes, so no vilan global can span two `const` expressions — and it reads back in `(token, line)` order, deduplicated on that pair, so the answer stays a function of the SET of contributions and never of the order they were made in (build-hooks.md §5.1's rule, which the registry is no exception to). **What "still names it" means, stated rather than assumed**: the token appears in a value some `const` expression evaluated to — as one of its strings, as a whitespace-separated word of one (`class_list` renders a joined list, so a `const` ending in it names every class at once), or as a substring of one (a class glued into a larger word by interpolation or `+`). That is the right question here because every class is minted at const time and every `Style` that dresses an element reaches the program through a const result: `class_list` and `+` are runtime code that can only read classes already in a const-built map. It is an OVER-approximation in the safe direction on purpose — a const result later removed by dead-code elimination still names its tokens, and a string that merely looks like one keeps a rule alive — because the opposite error would delete a rule an element still wears. `asset::staged` refuses to answer before evaluation has finished, naming the hook that is the right place to ask, since until the last `const` expression has run a token may still be about to be named. The band order is untouched: these lines reach the channel exactly as they did when `rule` emitted them and `assemble_assets` sorts them by first byte and media width as ever (B35, ui-styling.md §0bis.6). The retraction design §5.4 priced is withdrawn and not built. Five pins in `inference/styling.rs`: B308's own nested exhibit emitting exactly the composed rule (with the `:root` token line, which names no class, still there), the standalone condition style as the control, the family-covered slot, the registry's own token rule away from styling, and the refusal on reading it too early. `hmr_css_matrix`, `ssr_differential`, `style_when`, `style_chain_order`, `examples` and `split` green. Trackers B308, G23.

**Const evaluation gains an END-OF-EVALUATION HOOK: `asset::schedule_at_end(f)` runs `f` once, after every const evaluation of the compile has finished, in a const context of its own.** The asset channel could only ever be written FORWARD — a line emitted at the moment it was minted, with no way to take it back — so a system that mints values and later discards some of them has no choice but to ship the discards, which is exactly the shape `std::style` is in (every intermediate `Style` a condition combinator wraps puts its own rules on the sheet although the class never reaches an element). The fix is a hook rather than a retraction: a module accumulates while the program evaluates and processes and emits the whole result in one go at the end, which dissolves "X is already emitted before Y is known" instead of unwinding it. `schedule_at_end` is the request, and it is the sixth verb of `std::asset`'s const-only channel — a runtime call path reaching it is refused like every other. **The function's NAME is its identity**, which is what makes the request safe to make from a chokepoint that runs thousands of times: three requests for one function schedule one finaliser, and the order finalisers run in is the order they were first asked for. An anonymous closure is refused, and the reason is structural rather than stylistic — a closure's captured scope belongs to the evaluation that made it and is torn down with that run (`clear_scopes`), so there would be nothing left to call. **What "the end" is, settled and written down**: the end of ONE COMPILE's const pass, per leg, like every other const fact. Under `run --watch` that is the end of the ROUND — the legs the round recompiled re-schedule and re-emit, and a leg the round did not touch neither re-schedules nor re-emits, keeping the sidecar the previous round wrote through the artifact record every other asset already rides (B276/M59). Without that half, a late-emitting styling system would blank an untouched leg's stylesheet on the first edit anywhere in the project, which is the pin that says so. A finaliser may schedule another (it runs in the same pass, since the walk is by index over a list that may grow) and one that re-schedules itself does nothing. A finaliser that panics fails the build naming the function, at the site that scheduled it — the only span the pass has, since the interpreted tree carries none. **The mechanism**: the interpreter records the emitted name of each scheduled function (one name generator serves the whole const pass, so the emitted name IS the function's identity — `resolve_trace` has rested on the same fact since the shared world landed), the const pass collects those across sites, and after the last `const` expression it re-enters each one through a site of its own: the scheduling site's reach and prelude, with a synthetic body `const __const_result = flush();`. The scheduling site is the right seed because it REFERENCED the function, so its emission record already requires it and the reach closes transitively over everything the finaliser calls — no second walk, and no way for a finaliser to reach code its scheduling site could not. One carve-out from §2's value-escape rule, as narrow as it can be written: the ARGUMENT of a `schedule_at_end` call may name a compile-time-only function, because that name is handed to the const pass and never becomes a runtime value. Five pins — idempotent scheduling read off the RAW contribution vector (the flush deduplicates by `(key, line)`, so a finaliser that ran three times would still write one line and the mistake would be invisible in the file), run-once-at-end as an ORDER assertion over two sites and the finaliser, the panic naming the function, the const-only refusal, and the two-leg watch round in `assets.rs` holding both halves of the HMR answer. One ledger row. Tracker G23.

**Organize Imports prunes an unused impl selector, rewrites an emptied statement to the selector its file actually needs, and completion answers inside one.** B318 S3's tooling third, and the place where E168 and E169 turn out to have been the same predicate one construct early. **The prune.** A selector is a TERMINAL the organizer asks `keep` about, at its own `(impl …)` span — and its question is not rule (1)'s ("does this file spell the thing this leaf binds"), because a selector binds nothing at all. It is rule (2)'s, narrowed from a FILE to an IMPL: does this file resolve a method to an implementation this selector admits? That is strictly easier to answer than the provenance guess rule (2) makes, because the analyzer banked exactly that member set when it resolved the selector, so the organizer reads an answer instead of deriving one. A selector whose block the file calls a method from survives beside a dead name in the same set; one it never uses fades and prunes, and the fade and the prune describe the same element, which is E114's contract. **The rewrite.** E168's own item said its `import pkg::a;` would be "re-pointed at B318's selectors later", and this is later: `keep_module` answers a verdict rather than a bool — no rescue, the module, or a SELECTOR — and the selector is chosen when everything the file gets out of that module's file is the members of ONE subject's `impl` blocks. `import pkg::a::b;` with `b` unused and only `Widget::make().bump()` reaching into `a.vl` becomes `import pkg::a::{ (impl Widget) };` rather than `import pkg::a;`: the precise, minimal statement of what the file needs. The module form is still what a file using more of the module gets, and the E168 pin that produced it now produces `(impl i32)` — which is the paper's own exhibit for the form — with the statement's own `still builds` property pinned beside it, because a selector RESTRICTS and an organizer that narrowed past what the file needed would break the very build it was rescuing. **Completion.** Inside a selector the candidates are not names the module offers: after `impl ` they are the impl SUBJECTS the module's file writes, and after `)::` (braced or not) the selected block's members, `self` methods included — which is the half `Importable::statics` deliberately leaves out and exactly the half a selector's `::` tail takes. Both read the parse cache through the new `module_impl_blocks`, with no analyzer, which is the property the whole import-path family rests on: the module being selected from is one this program may never have loaded. The position is read before the path split, since a selector's own text is not a path and `import_path_segments` declines it; a subject holding parentheses of its own (a tuple type) closes by depth rather than at the first `)`. **A closing tag straight after text is a tag again, and the `>` of an attributed opening tag is a tag delimiter wherever it sits.** Two defects in the TextMate grammar's element rules, both found in the first minutes of E163's tokeniser and both invisible to the regex pins that stood in for it. **`<span>hello</span>` painted `</span>` as a generic argument list.** The generic list's begin is a `<` glued to an identifier character; `hello` ends in one; and the element rule's own atom-position guard (`(?<![A-Za-z0-9_])`, E161 — a tag `<` OPENS an atom, so a `<` glued to a name before it is an argument list) REFUSED that `<` for exactly the same reason, leaving it to the list. **Scope completion on a BLANK LINE offered only globals — the one position where a user actually asks for it.** `fun main() { let start = 1; ▮ }` did not offer `start`, while `st▮` one character away did, and the reason is that `scope_at` asked the wrong question: "the scope of the entity AT, or nearest before, the offset". On an empty line the innermost entity containing the offset is the enclosing FUNCTION, and `entity_scope_map` holds the scope an entity is DECLARED IN, so a function answers the module scope — the popup then walked module → global and never reached the body at all. (One character to the left it worked by accident: the half-typed accessor is its own entity, and it lives in the body scope.) The question is the innermost scope the offset sits INSIDE. A scope has no span of its own — `Scope` is a name map with a parent — so its extent is read off its members: the union of the spans of the entry entities filed under it, folded up the parent chain because a scope's text contains its children's. The union reaches the closing brace because the parser's filler for a block with no trailing expression is an `Expr::Void` spanning that brace (S3), and this walk deliberately keeps the one entity `entity_spans` excludes: without it a blank line after the last statement falls outside the body it is written in. Entry entities only, by the entry's own id ranges, so a scope shared with a loaded module cannot union spans from two coordinate spaces; computed at most once per query, beside the edit anchor, and only where something asks. The nearest-entity path stays as the fallback for an offset no scope contains — fresh text past the last top-level item, where there is no enclosing body. Tracker E165.

<!-- family: tooling -->
**The "Convert to a `css` block" refactor never fired on real code — the seed it demanded is the one spelling the estate does not write, and any typed link refused the whole chain.** Two gates, both closed. The SEED was a bare `style()`, matched as `Node::Accessor("style")`; the web prelude publishes the MODULE, so the templates, the docs and kolt all write `style::style()` and every chain in an app was refused at its first token. The rule is syntactic now — a path whose last segment is `style`, called with no arguments — which reads `style::style()`, an aliased `s::style()` and a bare `style()` alike off a raw parse, resolving nothing. The LINKS were the deeper half: `render_css_items` knew `raw` and the condition table, so `.color(c)`, `.flex_row()`, `.padding_x(..)` — every shorthand, which is to say every link an app writes — returned `None` for the whole chain. A typed link is converted by INLINING its std body: a shorthand in `style.vl` is a chain of `with_length`/`with_color`/`raw` links over `self`, so `.padding_x(space(4))` writes `padding-left: {space(4)}; padding-right: {space(4)};` and `.radius(Length::px(4))` writes `border-radius`. Inlining rather than a second table beside `STYLE_PROPERTY_METHODS` because it cannot DRIFT — the body is the answer — and because a method whose body is not such a chain (`raw` itself, `with_border`, `background_gradient`: anything with a statement in it) has no declaration spelling and says so by not being converted. And one unconvertible link no longer refuses the chain: it SPLITS there, everything before it becoming the block and the rest a postfix chain on it (`css { … }.select_off().hover(…)`, which parses and types), because chain order is merge order and the tail keeps its order relative to everything the block holds. A chain with nothing convertible in it is still not offered — a `css { }` with the whole chain hung off it is not a conversion. What proves the inlining is not the block's text but its style: `style_chain_order.rs` builds a typed chain and the block the refactor produces for it and holds the two to the same stylesheet and the same resolved slots, which is the same two assertions the chain sort's own twins make, and for the same reason — a class name is a content hash of the slot key and the declaration, so one wrongly inlined body moves a hash. Tracker E167.

**Organize Imports broke a green build in one direction and could never clean up in the other, and both were the same question asked of the wrong set: what does a MODULE import bring, on its own?** An `import` carries every `impl` in the module's file with it, whatever leaf it names — that is what kolt.local 004 established, and rule (2) of `Document::import_leaf_is_used` implements it for a module LEAF. A NAMED leaf never reached that test. So `import pkg::a::b;` with `b` unused faded as "unused import" and the action DELETED the statement, taking `a.vl`'s `impl Style { fun select_off(self) … }` with it, and the very next analysis said "Style has no method 'select_off'": an editor action that starts from a green file and ends at a red one (E168). The action rewrites the statement to `import pkg::a;` now instead of deleting it — a second predicate, asked only of a statement the leaf question emptied out, answered at the module SEGMENT's own span from the same reference table the leaf question reads, and rendered through the printer `vilan fmt` uses so that the two cannot undo each other. The fade stays on `b`, which is genuinely unused. The truncation refuses to leave an ORIGIN (`import pkg::a;` does not become `import pkg;`), a `use` is deleted rather than widened (it binds a name out of a namespace, and a namespace with no name taken out of it binds nothing), and a brace set with one live member prunes to that member exactly as before. The opposite failure is the same test counting too much: `import pkg::a;` beside `import pkg::a::b;` with only `b` used was kept forever, because the file does resolve something declared in `a.vl` — `b` — although it is `b`'s own leaf that provides it and the module import brings nothing the file spells (E169). Rule (2) subtracts what this file's other import leaves bind, aliases included, and what remains is what the module import ALONE carries: the methods of the `impl`s declared there, and anything reached by `a::` qualification, which writes the module's own name and is rule (1)'s question. A definition reached BOTH ways keeps the module import, which is the edge that stops the refinement from being "a module import beside a named one dies". `organizing_never_breaks_a_green_build` gains both shapes, and the fmt/organize agreement pin gains the rewrite. Tracker E168, E169.

<!-- family: performance -->
**Closing a document gives its memory back to the OPERATING SYSTEM rather than to glibc's free list: `libc` is a normal dependency of `vilan-lsp` on Linux now, and `malloc_trim(0)` is called after a document closes and after an analysis is dropped.** The measurement this answers is E106's second half: closing kolt's open `src/*.vl` returned 418 MB to the ALLOCATOR (heap in use 738 → 320 MB, free-but-retained 3 → 421 MB) and 62 MB to the system, so a session of opening and closing files ratcheted resident size up and never brought it down — and nothing inside the server could release it, because as far as the program is concerned the memory is already free; it is glibc holding the arenas. `malloc_trim(0)` is the ask, it has no `std` spelling, and hand-writing an `extern "C"` block for a call in the SHIPPED server is the wrong posture — so the ruling (Order 34, R4) promoted the dependency. It costs no third-party surface: `libc` was already in `Cargo.lock` (this crate's own dev-dependency for the thread clock, and several crates' dependency), so `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt` already covers it; the edge is declared for `cfg(target_os = "linux")` and the two glibc-only symbols are gated again on `target_env = "gnu"`, so a musl build links neither and every other host gets a no-op. It is called at the two moments there is a whole analysis to hand back — a close, and M63's release — and never per keystroke, where the walk is proportional to the arenas and the memory it found would be reused by the next analysis anyway. Measured on kolt's nineteen files (release): a session that opens all nineteen and closes them sat at 928 MiB resident with 606 MiB of it free-but-retained, and returns to 363 MiB with the trim — the same 336 MiB of genuinely live heap either way, 270 MiB of which is the analyzer's base cache and no document's to give back. The pin is `closing_every_document_returns_the_process_to_its_opening_size`, stated against the resident size of the session at its retention capacity rather than against the empty process, because that floor is what a process keeps by design. Tracker M64.

**`Vilan: Show Language Server Status` reports memory now — resident size, heap in use and heap retained-free — beside the cardinalities it always had, and says how many of the open documents still hold a program.** The status page was built (E106) on `leak_tally`'s standing ruling that RSS is too noisy to ATTRIBUTE anything to, and that ruling is right for attribution and wrong for a status page: E106 itself was found by reading RSS beside `mallinfo2`'s in-use/free split, and the field reading that started the whole thread was a resident figure off the owner's own server. A page that reported cardinalities and no bytes meant the next report arrived without the numbers. Three figures, in MiB with one decimal, on one line that diffs cleanly against the next: `memory: rss=508.1 MiB heap_in_use=498.3 MiB heap_retained_free=98.5 MiB`. The split is what makes the reading honest — resident size that stays up while in-use bytes fall is the allocator's to hand back (M64's trim), not the server's to free — and a reading the host cannot take prints `?` rather than a zero, because a missing reading and an empty heap are different facts. `programs=` joins `documents=` on the retained-state line, which is M63's own number: on a settled session it is at most two, and a larger one is the retention rule not holding. Linux-shaped and no-op elsewhere, through the same `libc` edge M64 declares; the leak tally's outstanding balance is deliberately NOT here, because it is thread-local and every analysis runs on its own spawned thread, so read from the request thread it would report that thread's reclaims and nothing about the session. Tracker E166.

<!-- family: performance -->
**The language server keeps a whole analysis only for the file you are in and the one before it: every other open document drops its `Program` to its editor tables and re-analyses when you come back, which takes kolt's nineteen open `src/*.vl` from 1,090 MiB resident to 510 MiB.** A `Document` held its analysis — the program, the entry text and tree it borrows for `'static`, the overlay-served module copies — for as long as the editor held the file, and that is ~23 MB per file on a real application: 1,090 MiB resident with nineteen open, 855 MiB of it live on the heap, against the owner's own server read from `/proc` at 4.13 GB eight hours into a working day (E106's measurement, M63's item). Nothing there was a leak; it was the design, and the ruling (Order 34, R4) bounds it at `RETAINED_PROGRAMS = 2` — the focused document and the one focused before it, which is what a working session alternates between. What a released document goes on answering is the whole of the work: its diagnostics (captured with every `SourceId` already resolved to a path, so a background tab's squiggles survive any republish), its outline, its semantic tokens and inlay hints (E121's keystroke path was already served from a capture and never touched the program), its `depends_on` edge (the source list is kept, so the dependency sweep stays exact rather than falling back to "sweep everyone" and paying the program back one save later), and — the sharp edge — its half of a cross-document find-references AND rename: the reference index is a table already, and the two questions `ReferenceIndex` asks a program (which file a source id names, what a definition is called and what kind it is) are captured beside it, with the std and dependency source sets a rename may not rewrite. A rename that silently skipped the files the user is not looking at would be the partial edit set kolt.local 034 exists to prevent, and it is pinned in both directions. What a released document cannot answer until it is focused again is the program walks — hover, go-to-definition, type-aware completion, the dead-item gray — and focus re-analyses: M58's warm path, 1,066 ms of CPU on kolt's `app_context.vl` at loadavg 35 against the 1,302 ms its cold analysis cost in the same process. Focus is read off the traffic that follows the CARET — `didOpen`, `didChange`, hover, completion, definition, references, rename, code actions — and deliberately not off the requests an editor sends for every VISIBLE document (tokens, hints, the outline), which a released document answers from its tables anyway and which would otherwise make three visible editors evict each other. The rule is applied at two seams, `Backend::focus` and the landing of every analysis, the second because the dependency sweep re-analyses background importers on every save. Measured on kolt's nineteen files (release, loadavg 33–41): resident 1,090 → 510 MiB, heap in use 855 → 500 MiB, and the marginal cost of opening one more file 48 MB → ~5 MB. What is left is not the documents': 336 MiB of heap survives every document being closed, 270 MiB of it thirteen retained worlds in the analyzer's base cache, whose own budget is 512 MiB resident (M24/M50) — which is why the item's "under 300 MB" is not reached here and is now a base-cache question rather than a per-document one. Tracker M63.

**An HMR swap no longer throws one websocket error per remote source, and no longer leaves the dead bundle's connection redialing beside the new one's: the duplex's teardown closes it for good instead of only closing its socket.** The swap's teardown list runs in REGISTRATION order and a `SocketDuplex` registers its at DIAL — before the mount that owns every mirror, which is the order an app writes (kolt dials at `client.vl`:47 and mounts at :60). A teardown that only called `socket.close()` therefore left `duplex.state` reading `Connected` while the browser socket was already CLOSING: the mount teardown that ran next disposed the root owner, every `RemoteSource` lease released, each release's `Unsubscribe` passed `SocketDuplex::send`'s `Connected` guard, and a `transmit` on a closing socket is the console error "WebSocket is already in CLOSING or CLOSED state" — one per source, on every swap. Then `onclose` found `Connected` too, and `handle_drop` did what a dropped connection deserves: reject the in-flight calls with "connection lost" and redial with backoff — so the DEAD bundle's duplex reconnected against the still-running server and lived on, unreachable from the new bundle, one zombie connection per swap. `close_for_good(duplex)` writes `Closed` FIRST, which is what makes the rest order-independent: the late releases drop at the send guard (the server drops the connection anyway, so those frames were waste), `handle_drop` stops at its own state guard, and `on_terminal` runs the disposal a torn-down session owes. Pinned end to end in `hmr_swap.rs`, where a WebSocket stub RECORDS a send on a non-OPEN socket instead of printing it — the browser's console error, made assertable — and the app under it dials two mirrors before it mounts, exactly as the item's exhibit does: after a swap, no transmit on a socket that is not OPEN, the old duplex `Closed` and never `Reconnecting`, one fresh dial and one live connection, and the new bundle's mirrors resynced from the server. Proven red by replanting the bare close: two `Unsubscribe` frames transmitted on a CLOSING socket, the old duplex going `Reconnecting` then `Connected` again, three sockets dialed and two connections left live. Tracker A96.

An instrument like that is unbuildable while the binder gives up on correct code, so the arm is settled first and the backstop is its own item. **The ruling is the universal reading** (B4 / `method-resolution.md` §10): the position is a requirement, the value either meets it or does not, and which side the reconciler happened to put first is not part of the question. A supertrait IS the promise that every `Doubler` is an `Add`; the sub-trait is the more specific side and is what the unification keeps. A value that does not implement the trait is refused as before, and the bare-trait PARAMETER an author writes is untouched — B186 makes that an implicit generic before this arm is ever reached.

(`Quad with Doubler with Add`), a default forwarding a `Self`-typed parameter to

binding its argument from the value's own impl, and two controls — a value that
does not implement the trait, and two traits with no clause between them. NOT
red-first, and that is the item's own point: no program's compile outcome moves,
because a later check already accepted everything this arm refused. The arms are
proven to FIRE rather than to change an answer — instrumented and counted over
the B72/B186/B210/B220/A86/B306 pins, eight hits on the concrete side and two on
the supertrait one. Tracker B316.

Emission now (a) resolves the splice decision through the active substitution, where it used to read the element's type as written, and (b) recomputes a positional read's offset and width from a LAYOUT-FREE path the analyzer records beside each access (`tuple_index_paths`: the root subject's tuple type and the chain of element indices that reaches the element, `deep.0.1` folding to the root plus `[0, 1]`), so the two halves can no longer disagree; a tuple PATTERN carries its elements' types for the same reason, and the width is computed where the binding is known. **A string argument inside an interpolation hole can be written with its quotes escaped now — `i"{get(\"k\")}"` — and lexes to the same token the plain spelling does.** A hole is lexed from the source bytes and the enclosing literal's quotes never reach it, so `i"{get("k")}"` has always worked. The spelling an author reaches for, having escaped a quote inside a string everywhere else, did not: `\` is in no hole charset, so the hole was refused as malformed by B247's message — which names braces nobody wrote — and the working idiom was to bind the argument to a local above the literal. It cost a lane an iteration, which is how it was found. `\"` opens a literal that closes at the next `\"`, and its body is kept raw exactly as `read_string` keeps a plain one's, so the escapes in it are interpreted at code generation and `\\` still takes its pair — which is what lets a body end in an escaped backslash without eating its own delimiter. An embedded quote has no escaped spelling, and the plain form (`"a\"b"`) is the one that carries it: the single place the two spellings are not interchangeable, and it is written into the spec rather than left to be discovered. The RECOVERY differs in one place too, and has to. An escaped literal that does not close ends the hole at the QUOTE rather than at the backslash, so the body scan resumes inside the literal's text and meets the same line break the plain form's scan meets, and the i-string states the rule once (diagnostics-standard B5); ending it at the backslash resumes ON the quote, which reads as the i-string's own closing one and loses the break entirely. Seven pins: the two spellings lexing to one identical token stream, a raw body carrying `\n` and a trailing `\\`, both spellings compiled and RUN end to end (and the `i"""…"""` hole beside them, which goes through the same scanner), the formatter's verbatim round-trip of the escaped spelling, a lone `\` still refused by name as the control — the fix opened one spelling, not the backslash — and the unclosed case stating the break once. `spec/lexical.md` loses the implementation note that said nested quoting inside a hole "is currently a parse error" and states the rule in its place. Tracker B278.

**`__with_finally` and `__guarded` cost a browser bundle 241 raw bytes, 94 minified and 10 after gzip — measured, and left alone.** B292's two runtime seams are emitted into any program that reaches them, and the worry was that `Owner::dispose` makes that every program that touches `std::reactive`. The numbers, taken on kolt's browser entry (216,076 bytes as emitted) and on the split fixture's eager `app.js` (22,207): both helpers are 241 bytes of source — `__guarded` 156, `__with_finally` 85 — which is 94 bytes minified (esbuild 0.28.1, `--minify --target=es2022`) in either bundle, since the helper is fixed-size and the bundle is not. Gzipped, kolt pays 10 bytes minified-then-gzipped (24,073 → 24,063, 0.042% of what a browser actually downloads) and 37 unminified; the toy fixture, where 94 bytes is 0.92% of a 10 KB bundle, pays 27 minified-and-gzipped. Left as two helpers, for reasons the number only confirms: they are a `try`/`finally` and a `try`/`catch` answering a value, so folding them into one means a mode argument paid at every CALL site (three in kolt) to save part of 94 bytes, plus a second interpreter arm to keep the macro evaluator honest. The other half of the item — "emit only the one a program reaches" — is already how it works, and that is worth recording: a program that only READS a signal gets neither helper, a program that writes one gets `__with_finally` (the drain) and not `__guarded`, and a program with no `std::reactive` at all gets nothing. Tracker M61.

**`nested_nurseries_join_inside_out` asserts the nesting it is named for instead of an interleaving nothing promises: the set of lines, plus the four orderings a nursery actually guarantees.** The pin compared stdout byte for byte — `inner-body/inner-child/inner-done/outer-child/3` — and failed once under full-suite load with `inner-body/outer-child/inner-child/inner-done`, passing in isolation and on the next full run. The ruling is that the ORDER IS NOT PROMISED and the runtime has no race to fix: the two children are independent TIMERS, 25 ms out there and 10 ms in here, started one statement apart, so a 15 ms stall between two adjacent spawns — one loaded box, one scheduler quantum — starts the 10 ms sleep after the 25 ms one is already due and inverts the interleaving. Two sibling children of two different nurseries have no ordering between them at all; promising one here would promise it everywhere. What a nursery does promise is causal and is what the pin reads now: every line printed exactly once (no child dropped, none run twice, the value still `3`), the body running to its own end before a child it spawned resumes, the INNER join waiting for the inner child before `inner-done`, and the OUTER join waiting for both the inner nursery and its own child before the value. Proven not to be a weakening that asserts nothing: with the two sleeps reversed — the inner child slow at 200 ms, the outer fast at 5 ms, the interleaving inverted on purpose — the four invariants still hold, which is exactly what a byte-comparison could not say. N35's class, and the second pin in it. Tracker N72.

**The element-head sorter's bargain is written down where the people it affects will read it: sorting an element head moves WHEN its attribute values are evaluated, and that is accepted rather than checked for.** E151 put an element head's items in a canonical order, and an attribute's value is an arbitrary expression, so moving `title(a())` past `id(b())` moves when `a()` and `b()` are called. **`Vec2::length_squared` — `x² + y²` under the name the comparison wants, with `length` now stated in terms of it.** A pointer-move handler's whole arithmetic is "did this travel further than the threshold", run on every event, and it needs no square root: `sqrt` is monotonic, so comparing squared lengths against a squared threshold decides exactly what comparing lengths decides. The advice was already in `length`'s doc comment and in the book, and what it pointed at was `v.dot(v)` — correct, and a name that says the arithmetic instead of the intent, so every call site had to re-explain itself. `length` is `self.length_squared().sqrt()` now, which states the relationship in one place. It is a name for a comparison and not a faster `length`: take the root when the NUMBER is the answer. No `Mul<f64>` — `scale` stays the scalar half, for the reason recorded at its definition.

**`Color::var` and `Length::var` refuse a custom-property name without its two leading dashes at const time, instead of rendering a reference no browser resolves.** `Color::var("button-color")` emitted `var(button-color)`, and that is not a broken reference — it is not a reference at all: `button-color` parses as a keyword, the declaration is dropped, and nothing anywhere says so until the page renders the wrong colour. The name is now checked where every other style token is, at const evaluation, with the fix spelled in the message (`var("--button-color")`); the fence is the attribute name's plus the dashes, so a space, a quote or a `:` — which would run past the `var()` call the name is written into — is refused too, and a bare `--` names nothing and is refused by the first check. `view.style_var(name, source)` deliberately does NOT take the check: it appends a whole declaration rather than a `var()` reference, and `style_var("width", ..)` over a plain property is correct code. Nothing in std, `vilan/examples`, the corpus or the docs is newly refused — every shipped call site already carried its dashes.

**`Style::attribute` and `Style::within` take `value: Option<str>`, so a PRESENCE condition has a spelling — `attribute("data-selected", None, ..)` is `.sX[data-selected]` — and the new `not(inner)` marker negates the condition immediately enclosing it, which is what finally spells "hovered AND not disabled".** `[disabled]`, `[data-selected]` and every other boolean attribute is a presence condition in the markup that carries it, and the exact-match form was the only one std had: `attribute("data-disabled", "false", hover(..))` worked only for an app willing to carry the state as a VALUE, and anything else reached for `child_relation("[data-selected]", ..)` as a raw-selector escape hatch and hit its v1 fence ("takes an unconditioned style") the moment a `hover` nested inside. `Some(v)` renders `[name="v"]` exactly as before and `None` renders `[name]`; `within`'s value takes the same `Option` for the ancestor, `[data-collapsed] .sX`. Negation is a MARKER rather than a pseudo head, because which selector is negated is a fact about the condition OUTSIDE it: `not(inner)` emits nothing and marks the inner's slots, and the enclosing `attribute`/`within`/`hover` family/`pseudo` emits its own selector negated and clears the mark — so `attribute("disabled", None, not(hover(s)))` is `.sX:not([disabled]):hover` (the hover kept, the attribute negated), `hover(not(s))` is `.sX:not(:hover)`, and `within("data-theme", Some("dark"), not(s))` is `:not([data-theme="dark"]) .sX`. `:not(x)` carries x's own specificity, so the composed rule is (0,3,0) over its (0,2,0) parts exactly as the un-negated one is; the one thing a negation moves is a guarded rule's cascade BAND, since `:not([..]) .sX` opens with ':' where `[..] .sX` opened with '[', which is written at `render_rule` and pinned. A `css` block reaches all of it through the name-blind nested-rule rule — `.attribute("disabled", None) { .not { .hover { … } } }` resolves to the same class as the chain, and the desugar was not touched. Three refusals fence the marker: an unwrapped `not` fails at APPLICATION naming the wrap it needed (it emitted no rule, so applying it would be silence), `not(not(..))` is refused rather than cancelled, and a media condition cannot be negated in v1 — `@media not (..)` is a grammar of its own. BREAKING: every `attribute`/`within` call site passes `Some(..)`; std has none, and the corpus, the docs, the spec and the inference pins are swept in this change. `pseudo` now refuses a name opening with `!`, the grammar's negation marker, and `children`/`divide`'s refusal steers a state on the element itself to `attribute(..)`.

**An `[rpc]` method may now return a `KeyedCell<K, T>`, and its stub hands the client a `KeyedSource<K, T>` — the keyed row of the handle mapping, in the same sync unleased shape as the plain one.** `fun tasks_in(self, workspace: str): KeyedCell<i32, Task>` answers `KeyedSource<i32, Task>` at the client: no `Result`, no await, no call until something leases it, and then one call, one capability and one ELEMENT-GRAINED forward — a `Reset` seed and one `Patch` per change, the ops the mutation recorded rather than two snapshots diffed. This is the half `[expose(keyed)]` cannot do: there is one field per exposure, and a per-workspace or per-conversation collection is not a set the compiler can name. The mirror gets the plain form's whole lifecycle — its `origin`, the re-mint at the next 0→1, the reconnect replay and the owner hook — with one difference the keyed type forces: a per-KEY lease is a first demand too and mints the channel exactly as a whole-collection one does, and the channel is withdrawn when the LAST demand on it goes rather than the first, because a keyed channel carries one forward per demand. The contract surface names the mapped type (`tasks_in(str)->KeyedSource<i32, Task>;`), the reply is the same plain `i32` channel id the other forms send, and `Option<KeyedCell<K, T>>` is deliberately not a handle return in v1 — a keyed absence would need both `Absent` and an answer for what a per-key absence means, and neither has been asked for, so it falls to the ordinary non-Wire return refusal.

**BREAKING: the stub of an `[rpc]` method that returns a source is now SYNC and answers the mirror itself — `fun get_message(self, id: str): RemoteSource<MessageBody>`, where it answered `Result<RemoteSource<MessageBody>, RpcError>` before — and it makes no call at all until something leases it.** Every handle stub's type moves, in both written forms: `SignalCell<T>` and `Option<SignalCell<T>>` both answer `RemoteSource<T>`, so `client.get_message(id)!` becomes `client.get_message(id)` and the `Option` form's `match` at the call site goes. The mirror is minted UNLEASED — no channel, no capability, no frame — and the first 0→1 lease runs the shipped re-mint path (`acquire` → `remint` → `rebind`), which is what makes the first mint free rather than new machinery: a hundred handles held and ten watched is now ten calls and ten forwards, where it was a hundred calls and ninety-one capabilities standing for the life of the connection. Migrating: drop the `!`, drop the `Option` unwrap, and read `status()` where you read `Err`; `std::memo::Memo<K, V>` (new) is the one-line way to keep one handle per id, `bodies.get_or(id, || client().get_message(id))`.

**A `Debounce` whose nursery was cancelled is still a `Debounce`: the driving loop's bookkeeping is now cleared on every unwind, not only on the loop's own end.** `run` set `running` synchronously before spawning the loop — the guard that stops two calls in one tick from spawning two — and the loop cleared it when it ran out of work. **A throw out of an observer no longer turns the reactive graph off for the rest of the session: the drain restores its scheduling state under a `finally` and lets the error keep unwinding, and a disposal group now finishes past a throwing cleanup.** `drain` set `draining = true`, pushed the turn onto `draining_turns`, and restored neither on the way out of a throw — an observer that panicked, or a host API that refused its argument (Chrome's `insertRule` on a selector it will not take). The turn then stayed DRAINING forever and stayed on the stack, so every later write that resolved to it — a settled capture's late path, and EVERY no-ambient-turn `set` or `at_settle`, which join `draining_turns.last()` — enqueued into a queue nothing would ever flush. One error, no second error, and a dead graph. vilan has no exception syntax, so the catch seam is runtime glue in the shape `std::db`'s migration path already uses: `__with_finally` (a `try`/`finally`, nothing allocated per call) and `__guarded` (a `try`/`catch` answering `Option<str>`), both with native arms in the interpreter so the macro evaluator agrees with node. The drain takes the FINALLY and rethrows nothing — the original error keeps its type, its message and its stack and leaves from where it was thrown, and the rest of its wave is abandoned, because a throwing observer means the graph is mid-update and the write that started the settle is the honest place for the failure to land. `Owner::dispose` takes the opposite guard for the opposite reason: a disposal group is a list of independent promises, so every cleanup runs and the first failure is raised after the group is released — and without that, B291's idempotence would have made a throw leak every cleanup behind it permanently. Measured on a drain benchmark under callgrind: the guard costs about 1.3-1.4 kIr per DRAIN and nothing per notify, which is +0.44% of total program instructions at 16 observers per turn and +0.031% at 256. Tracker B292.

**An `Owner` now has a DISPOSED state, so a `take` or a `defer` that lands after its owner is gone releases on the spot instead of parking a cleanup on a list nothing runs again.** `Owner::dispose` emptied its cleanup list and kept no flag, so a registration from an async continuation whose scope was torn down first — a route switched away before a handle's reply, a `bind_each` row rebuilt while its first fetch is in flight — sat there forever: the effect fired on every later write for the rest of the session, and only a SECOND `dispose` released it. A registration is a promise to release, and after the extent has ended the only way left to keep it is to keep it immediately, so `take` disposes the item at once (still returning it) and `defer` runs the cleanup at once; `dispose` is idempotent, with the flag raised BEFORE the cleanups run so a cleanup that registers back into the same owner is disposed on the spot rather than appended to a list the loop has already snapshotted. `Owner::is_disposed` reports the flag. **`KeyedCell<K, T>`: a keyed collection whose WRITES are the deltas, so a keyed channel stops paying for the size of the collection on every change.** Exposing a `SignalCell<List<T>>` keyed makes the server DIFF two snapshots per change — `keyed_diff` re-keys both and compares every retained element — and it pays that once per SUBSCRIBED CONNECTION however small the change is. A position index makes `update` and `remove` a lookup rather than a scan on both ends. **Nothing on the wire changes** — the same `Reset` seed and the same element-grained `Patch` per change, whole-collection and per-key alike, the same `KeyedSource<K, T>` on the client, and the SAME CONTRACT HASH as the `[expose(keyed = K)] SignalCell<List<T>>` spelling, so a service may swap one field for the other without breaking a deployed client. `[expose] items: KeyedCell<str, Task>` is a keyed channel: the cell names both types itself, so `keyed` is redundant on it and `keyed = K` has nothing to add, and `T: PartialEq` — the diff's way of learning that an element changed — is no longer required. Hand-wired: `ReactiveServer::expose_keyed_cell(cell)`, a distinct name rather than an overload because a cell IS a `Source<List<T>>` and would otherwise satisfy `expose_keyed`'s bound and take the diffing path silently. Tracker A54.

**Rule 2's last-use elision can see a `Shared` CELL: a binding fed by `cell.read()` may keep naming the cell's storage when nothing can mutate that storage while the binding holds it.** Rule 2 (§6.2) skips a copy when the SOURCE dies at the read — that is the only reason the aliasing it leaves behind can never be observed — so `is_elidable_copy` accepted a plain local binding and nothing else. A cell does not die: `let previous = row_views.read()` leaves the handle holding the same storage and every later read reaches it, which is why B256's ruling stalled on cost. So the question is asked from the other end, and every part of the answer is syntactic. **The cell's own writes are the hazard, and they come in two shapes.** `h.write() = x` REBINDS the slot — a fresh value is installed and the old one is left exactly as it was — so it can never reach back into what a read handed out; every other spelling (`h.write().push(9)`, `update`'s `mutate(self.value.write())`, a component write) mutates the storage the read shares. A cell no write mutates in place is safe outright, which is `bind_each`'s `row_views`/`row_owners`; a cell some write does mutate is safe when a rebind ORPHANS the read first, on the declaring block's own straight line with nothing that could reach a write in between — which is `drain`'s `let wave = turn.pending.read(); turn.pending.write() = [];`, where the clear that looks like the hazard is the thing that ends it. **Cell identity is a union-find over SLOTS, not a root comparison**: two slots can hold one cell (`let g = h.clone()`, `Subscription`'s `subscribers` field initialized from `SignalCell`'s, a handle passed to a parameter), and a handle moves between slots at exactly four forms — a binding's initializer, a construction slot, an assignment, and `clone()` — so unioning there and dropping every other position into one `Unknown` component covers the relation without an alias analysis. **The binding is guarded too**: it may not be mutated in place (`mut c = h.read(); c.push(10)` would grow the cell), may not sit at a value seam, and may not be one the last-use walk is opaque about — which is how a closure capture refuses, since a capture reads the binding from another region. And a binding the rule admits joins B53's shared captures as one rule 2 must refuse to move OUT of: it owns nothing of its own, so it has nothing to donate. **On its own this moves no emitted byte** — a shared read is not yet a copy site, so there is nothing here to elide, and the corpus goldens and the copy-elision census are unchanged — and that is the point: it is the unblocker the B256 ruling asked to land first, and the fix below is what it pays for. Five pins in `borrows.rs`: the two std shapes, the different-cell control, and — ignored until B256 lands beside it, because until then nothing copies here to elide — the in-place write before the rebind and the closure-captured binding. (tracker B267)

**`View::show(condition)` was a silent NO-OP on every flex container — on every element an app gave a `display` at all.** It set the `hidden` PROPERTY and nothing else, leaving the hiding to the preflight's `[hidden]{display:none}`. That rule is emitted inside `@layer vilan.preflight`; a compiled `Style`'s own rules are UNLAYERED, and an unlayered author declaration is the highest-priority author layer there is — so `.sX{display:flex}` beat the reset whatever its specificity, and `show(false)` painted the row exactly as before. kolt's `child_relation("not([hidden])", "display", …)` is that defect wearing a HACK comment (`views.vl:132`). **No cascade layer could fix it**: "above unlayered" does not exist, so a `vilan.overrides` layer declared last would still lose, and `!important` is refused permanently (css-block.md §10). **So `show` writes the inline `display` instead**, which beats every rule in the sheet: `display: none` when the source is false, and on true the element's own inline `display` — captured once, before the first toggle, because `show` owns that slot from then on (`set_style_property` with the empty string REMOVES the declaration, so an element that had none ends with none). The `hidden` attribute is still set, so selectors and assistive technology see it, and `Element::remove_attribute`'s sibling `Element::style_property` (`style.getPropertyValue`) is the read that makes the restore exact. The SSR twin makes the same two writes, so a server-rendered hidden element is hidden on the first paint rather than painted until the client's first toggle takes it away. Two consequences worth naming: `show` now works on an SVG subtree (SVG honours `display`, and ignores the HTML-only `hidden` attribute), and an app that writes this element's inline `display` itself after binding `show` loses that write on the next toggle — style through a `Style` and the two never meet. Two pins in `ui_rows.rs`, both red first: the flex container hidden and restored, asserted beside the emitted stylesheet that shows why the attribute alone cannot do it, and the server render. (tracker A60)

**`vilan fmt` canonicalizes an element HEAD — the import and style-chain sorters' third sibling: undotted attributes lead in `id`, `name`, `type`, `for`, `href`, `src` order and then alphabetically, `on:` handlers follow them alphabetically, and a dotted chain link is a BARRIER that never moves.** The desugar is the whole argument. An undotted `name(value)` lowers to `.attr("name", value)` and an `on:event(h)` to `.on("event", h)`, each filling the slot its own first argument names, so they commute — with each other and among themselves — while a dotted item splices VERBATIM and may write whatever it likes (`.styled(s)` writes `class`, `.child(…)` appends in order, a user method is unknowable). So the rule is the style sorter's barrier rule one construct over: a link holds its position absolutely, items sort only within the runs BETWEEN links, no link moves relative to another, and the sort is STABLE — which is the whole of the last-wins story, since `class("first") class("second")` renders `second` and the reverse renders `first`. A head with a COMMENT inside it is refused outright, as a style chain is, because a reordered head would carry its comments to the wrong item. **The safety net gets its twin**: `format` re-lexes its output and compares tokens, so a printer that MOVES tokens needs a token-level pass that reduces both sides to one sequence — `sort_element_heads` joins `sort_import_runs` and `sort_style_chains` in `normalize`, and is deliberately conservative (a head it cannot read to a `>` or `/>` is left as written, which can cost a reorder and never produce a wrong one). **The commutation is proved, not argued**: `crates/vilan-cli/tests/element_head_order.rs` builds AND RUNS a fixture written out of order in every shape a wrong rule would break — the barrier in both directions, two `.child` links whose order is the document, a last-wins pair, every leading name backwards, hyphenated and keyword-spelled names, handlers before the attributes — and the two documents must be equal once each tag's attributes are sorted, which is the one difference a legal reorder may produce because an HTML start tag reads its attributes as a set. A second assertion compares the emitted JavaScript as two multisets, which is the only cover an `on:` handler gets (a server-rendered element discards its handlers, so the rendering cannot see one). Ten pins in `element_head_layout`. One consequence is named rather than left to be found: an attribute value is an arbitrary expression, so moving the item moves when it is evaluated. In the tree exactly one head reorders (`element-syntax.vl`'s `<input>`, golden regenerated); kolt — read-only evidence — reorders four, three of its 57 hand-written heads and the one `<svg>` frame in its generated icon library.
