**`fun main() { if flag { ret; } … }` compiled clean and then died at load: `SyntaxError: Illegal return statement`, the whole module refused before a line of it ran.** `main` is INLINED at module scope — that is what makes a vilan program a flat ESM file rather than a function call wrapped around one — and a `ret` in it lowered to a bare `return` out there, which no JS parser accepts. Every spelling was affected: a guard clause, a `ret` nested in a loop, a valued `ret` in a `main(): i32`. **The lowering is a labeled block**, not a function: `main`'s body is wrapped in `main: { … }` and each of those `ret`s becomes `break main`. The alternative — emitting `main` as a function invoked once — was measured and declined: it moves **115 of the 124 corpus goldens** (+5,282 bytes) and re-plumbs the split seam, to fix programs the corpus contains none of, where the block is emitted only when a `ret` is actually there and the corpus is byte-identical without it. A `ret` in a loop breaks the LABEL, not the loop, which is the distinction a bare `break` could not make; a valued `ret` assigns the exit-code temp on its way out so the `process.exit` after the block still sees it; a `main` that owns a resource keeps its `try`/`finally`, and the break runs the teardown on the way out. **A `--watch` round decides each leg's freshness at that leg's own turn, and compiles a leg that writes another leg's input first.** Both watch loops — `vilan build --watch` and the HMR round — decided "fresh" for every leg BEFORE any leg compiled. A round now orders its legs so a producer compiles before the leg that reads its output, and a leg downstream of one that recompiled recompiles with it (`watch_leg_reuse::a_leg_that_reads_another_legs_artifact_recompiles_in_the_same_round`). **A self-call bound by a `let` and read in an unannotated recursive body's return position resolves.** `fun g(n: i32) { if n == 0 { ret 1; } let x = g(n - 1); x + 1 }` failed "type of variable 'x' could not be resolved", on the binding and at every call, where the direct-tail form `g(n - 1) + 1` had always worked. It was a deadlock: `x`'s constraint waits on `g(n - 1)`, which waits on `g`'s inferred return, which reads the tail `x + 1`, which read `x` — and a binding whose type slot is still `Unknown` answered "not yet" instead of looking at what it was bound to. Deferring is right when someone else is going to land the type and wrong when this ask is what that someone is waiting for, so an UNANNOTATED binding with no type yet is now read through its initializer, which is the hop B185 gave `unfilled_closure_parameter` for closure parameters. The re-entrant ask then answers `never` — evidence that constrains nothing — and the other return evidence decides, exactly as it does for the direct-tail form. Two guards ride along and are pinned: an annotated binding is not followed (its annotation is its own answer and outranks the initializer), and the existing cycle guard ends a binding cycle (`let p = q; let q = p;`, writable because module bindings resolve in any order), which stays the ordinary refusal. Mutual recursion and a chain of rebindings are pinned beside the exhibit; the spec's return-type-inference paragraph says a binding in between changes nothing. B126's residue, orphaned since 2026-08-22, closes with it (B191).

<!-- family: feature -->
**The guard clause: `if !(slot is Some(let n)) { ret; }` binds `n` for the rest of the block.** The owner's ruling off B171's scope question — "`if !(x is Some(let y)) { return }`, would the binding be accessible after?", yes. B195 already knows which captures a condition binds on its FALSE path, because that is the set it hands an `else`; when the `if` has no `else` and its then-branch provably diverges, that false path is the *only* way past the `if`, so the same set is published into the enclosing scope from the end of the `if` onward. They land there as ordinary declarations, so a later `let` of the name shadows them and the scope is the block the `if` was written in, not the function. All three conditions carry weight and each has its own pin: an unnegated `if x is P(let n) { ret; }` reaches its continuation exactly when the pattern did *not* match; a then-branch that can fall through reaches it on a miss; and an `if` with an `else` reaches it through whichever arm did not diverge, which is a wider rule nobody has ruled. Divergence is the type checker's own analysis (`Divergence::checker` — `ret` and `jump` are its leaves, `jump break`/`continue` inside a loop included), so the guard and the editor's unreachable-code paint cannot disagree about what "dead" means; `panic(..)` is a leaf for the paint and not yet for the checker, so a panicking guard is pinned `#[ignore]`d against B204 and the spec carries the gap as an implementation note. The spec's `is` section, the tour's control-flow page and the "cannot find" entry in the error appendix all state the shape (B187).

<!-- family: miscompile -->
**An `is` capture reached through a call argument is unbound in both branches.** `if always(maybe is Some(let n)) { print(n); }` compiled and printed `undefined` — a read of a payload slot the subject does not have — because the branch bookkeeping travels the condition's boolean spine (`!`, `&&`/`||`, the `is` test) and *dropping* it for anything else meant falling back to the plain then-branch default. A call's truth proves nothing about a test inside its argument, so the capture now reaches neither branch: stepping off the spine narrows the capture's visibility to the subtree it stepped into rather than clearing the frame. The one rule that survives the step is `&&`'s, and only inside that subtree — `always(maybe is Some(let n) && n > 1)` still binds its own right operand, because `&&` short-circuits wherever it is written. The same cap closes `always(maybe is Some(let n)) && n > 0`, which read the missing payload from the `&&` written around the call. The spec's `is` section states the spine rule (B199).

<!-- family: performance -->
**A superseded analysis now STOPS. A keystroke burst used to run one whole whole-program analysis per debounce window and throw all but the last away at `land`; ten keystrokes on kolt's `views.vl` cost 989 ms of CPU each and now cost 127 ms — one complete analysis and nine cancelled, measured through the real notification handlers.** E117 stamped every analysis with the world revision it read and taught `land` to DROP a result the world had moved past, which closed the ghost-diagnostic hole — but it closed it at the end: the superseded analysis still ran to completion on its 128 MiB thread. The analysis now carries a cancellation token, installed on that thread and read at the phase boundaries the `VILAN_PHASE_TIMING` line names (the entry walk, `build()`, the check sequence, and the post-passes' `contexts+graph` and `const-pass`), plus per call site inside `check_generic_bound_satisfaction` and per function inside the move scan — the two loops the `checks` phase is mostly made of, which is what bounds the cancel latency at one call site rather than one whole-program sweep. Measured on the generated 1,791-function exhibit at loadavg 87: a token set 10–75% of the way through a 249 ms analysis stops the thread in 13–69 ms. **Every checkpoint sits downstream of every process-global store** — the base world cache is written before the entry tail begins, the parse caches hold one complete module each — so no cancel can leave a shared cache holding a partial value; a macro world's nested compile is exempt outright, because its world is cached for the process and a half-built one stored there would be read back by a later analysis as whole. **The cancelled analysis answers `None` rather than a truncated program**, which is not a nicety: a checkpoint that fires before `build()` leaves type slots the constraint fixpoint would have filled, and the extraction tail reads them by hard index. Nothing here is what correctness rests on — `land` and `plan_publish` keep their revision-stamp checks unchanged, an analysis that outruns its own cancellation is dropped exactly as before, and removing every checkpoint changes what the editor shows not at all, only how long it took. **`did_open` registers its generation like an edit does.** E123 routed the open through the same scheduling but it registered nothing, so an edit arriving before the open's analysis finished did not supersede it — the two ran side by side and the revision stamp decided which landed last; the edit now cancels the open. **The dependency sweep supersedes each dependent** instead of awaiting one full analysis per dependent with no supersession check between them, and it abandons itself when the world moves under it, which on a shared module is worth an entire analysis per stale round. The dependents it schedules are marked `dependency_moved` for the window between the module's edit and their own re-landing, which fills the seam the keystroke path shipped with a hard-coded `false`: inside that window the verdict is `Stale` — whole-file syntax-only tokens, hints still served (Q1/Q4). The session trace grew a line to say what the scheduler did — `analyses: started= landed= cancelled=` — and it is a diagnosis, not a counter: cancelled climbing with started while landed does not is a session typing faster than it can analyze. Numbers, release, loadavg 85–87, ten keystrokes a debounce window apart: the generated exhibit 80 → 13 ms of CPU per keystroke (6.0x), kolt's `views.vl` 989 → 127 ms (7.8x), against a warm complete analysis in both cases so cancellation is not credited with M21's saving. **`diagnostics_budget` holds and is now CPU-clocked**: 59 ms of process CPU (310 ms of wall) on the 1,791-function exhibit at loadavg 92, against the 500 ms mandate the paper measured at 925 ms — it stays behind the same `#[ignore]` its sibling gate has, for its subject's size rather than its verdict. Backlog M26.

<!-- family: performance -->
**The language server's base-world cache has a byte budget and evicts least-recently-used, instead of growing for the life of the session.** The cache retains one resolved pre-entry world per distinct key shape, and since M21 the key includes the entry's package root and its sibling set — so an N-file package can mint N keys from one editing session, and the only eviction the cache had was per-key overwrite. The retention was already measured (`base_cache_retained`, and the `BaseCacheWorld` leak-tally site); it is now bounded. Worlds carry the bytes the store recorded and the tick of their last store or HIT, a store evicts least-recently-used worlds until the total fits the budget, and the world just stored is exempt — so a single world larger than the budget bounds the cache at one world rather than turning it off. The default is 512 MiB, generous on purpose; `VILAN_BASE_CACHE_BUDGET_MIB` overrides it in mebibytes, read once at server start, with a value that does not parse reported on stderr and ignored. An evicted world gives back everything it was holding: its recorded bytes, and the claims it held on analysis-owned overlay copies.

<!-- family: performance -->
**Editing a file that imports an OPEN sibling no longer rebuilds the whole pre-entry world on every keystroke.** The language server caches the resolved world every analysis starts from, and since M21 a `pkg::`-importing entry is eligible for it — but a world that had loaded a module served from the open-document overlay was refused the store outright, because those copies are owned by the analysis that parsed them and freed when it is superseded (`leak-soak.md` §7.9.4a; §7.9.2 proved the naive form unsound — a stored world borrowing analysis-owned text is a use-after-free reachable by pressing ctrl-Z). That is exactly the shape a real session has: kolt's `client.vl` imports `pkg::views`, `views.vl` is an open buffer, and every `client.vl` keystroke paid `base` 1,357–2,713 ms while its two siblings, which import no open file, paid `base 0.0 ms`. Ownership is a reference count now: every party that holds a reference derived from an overlay-served copy holds a *claim* on it — the analysis that parsed it, and any stored base world built over it — and the copy is freed exactly when the last claim is released. A stored world takes its claims inside the analysis that still holds the originals; a cache hit hands the world's claims to the receiving analysis under the cache lock, before the clone escapes; an analysis with nowhere to keep a claim (the CLI, the wasm front end, a transient reader, a macro-world compile) is served a miss rather than a borrow nothing keeps alive. Per-keystroke growth stays zero, and an unchanged open buffer is now parsed once for a whole run of analyses instead of once per analysis.


<!-- family: fix -->
**A trait-conformance refusal now advises a signature the author can actually write. `impl P with PartialEq { }` said ``declare `fun eq(self, b: PartialEq): bool` `` — and `PartialEq` is a trait, so that line names a type no value can have; the advice was unfollowable at the one moment the reader most needs to follow it.** The cause is the `= Self` default. `trait PartialEq<B = Self>` resolves `B` to the very same type as `Self` — both are `Type::Trait(PartialEq, [])` — so a signature rendered from the RESOLVED types cannot tell a declared `b: B` from a declared `Self`, and printed the trait's own name for both. `function_signature_label` now renders FOR the impl, by the WRITTEN name, which is the rule B29's own conformance check already applies (`ambiguous_position_expectation`): `Self` is the impl's subject, and a parameter's own name is the matching `with`-clause argument, falling back to the subject when the clause supplied none — precisely what `= Self` means. So `impl P with PartialEq` advises `fun eq(self, b: P): bool`, `impl Meters with Combine<Feet>` advises `fun merge(self, b: Feet): Meters`, and an ordinary `name: str` is untouched, because only a position resolving to the DECLARING trait's own abstract type is ambiguous at all. **B197's arm rendered its own signature to route around this, and that duplicate is gone**: one rendering serves both arms, so an operator trait whose shape is not `fun m(self, b: B): Self` can no longer be described wrongly by a template that assumed it was. Hover is deliberately unchanged — there is no impl in hand there, and `Self` is what the author typed. Five pins (`PartialEq`, `Add`, a user trait's `= Self` default, a written `with`-clause argument, and the ordinary-parameter control); the two B197 pins that read the signature go red without the fix too, which is the routing under test.

<!-- family: fix -->
**`self.add(self)` written out in a trait default over a supertrait resolves. `trait Doubler with Add { fun twice(self): Self { self.add(self) } }` was two errors on a program with no mistake in it — `Expected Doubler, but got Add instead.` at the call and `Expected Add, but got Doubler instead.` at the argument — while the OPERATOR spelling of the same thing, `self + self`, has dispatched since B193.** Inside a default body `self` is the trait's own abstract type (`Type::Trait(Doubler, [])`), and a member reached from a SUPERTRAIT is declared in that trait's terms: `Add::add` is `fun add(self, b: B): Self` with `B = Self`, and both of those resolve to `Type::Trait(Add, [])`. So the argument was refused against a parameter naming a different trait, and the call's type was refused by the enclosing default's own declared `Self` return. A supertrait's `Self`, reached through a sub-trait, IS the sub-trait's `Self` — the lookup now records the pair, and both halves rebind it: the argument check, which reads a parameter type straight off the declaration, and the `Self`-return specialization, which already substitutes structurally for a concrete receiver and simply did not count a sub-trait receiver as one. **The rewrite has to be structural rather than a substitution entry, and that is the interesting constraint**: types are not interned, so a member's `b: Self`, its `Self` return and the trait's own `Self` binding are three distinct ids for the one type, and no id-keyed context can reach all three. **It applies only to an argument-less `with` clause**, which is the whole rule rather than a convenience: with no argument written, every `= Self` position and every `Self` mean the sub-trait and a blanket rewrite is exactly right, where `with Add<i32>` parts them — `b: B` is `i32`, the `Self` return is still the sub-trait — and nothing in the resolved types tells them apart. That shape is untouched. Four pins: both spellings side by side in one trait, two impls proving the default dispatches per specialization, a two-level `Base`/`Middle`/`Top` chain on a user trait (whose chained call also proves the CALL came back as the sub-trait), and the control that a method no supertrait promises is still refused.

**A refused `[expose]` now generates NOTHING — no contract entry, no client mirror, no `session.expose` call — so `[expose] tasks: i32` is ONE diagnostic instead of five. B189 took the pile from six to four; the residue was two `cannot infer 'T' … ': Wire'` and two `cannot find type '_'`, and `_` is not a type: it is the `service` expansion's own placeholder, handed to an author who never wrote it.** The expansion reads an exposed field's element off the field's SOLE type argument — it runs before any type resolves, so the `Source` impl the compiler reconciles against is not there to read — and when it could not read one it pushed the literal `"_"` and carried it into all three places the element is named. It is refused instead, at the field, naming why: the mirror's element is read from the annotation's sole type argument, so spell the source with its element there. The accepted set is exactly what it was — that program never compiled — and the message is now one an author can act on. Five pins, red-proven in two halves (the placeholder restored; the refusal removed), plus the `Feed<Note>` control that A32's own shape still exposes.

**A `[derive(..)]` on a type declared inside an inline `mod` now generates its impl INTO that `mod`, where the type it names is in scope. `mod shapes { [derive(PartialEq)] enum Kind { .. } }` was four diagnostics on a program with no mistake in it — `cannot find type 'Kind'; import it first` twice, plus a follow-on per variant raised inside a body the author never wrote.** Expansion is unified, so a derive rides the same channel a macro attribute does, and every generated list walked into the FILE's module scope whatever scope the deriving item was written in. B190's fixture drops the hand-written `impl Kind with PartialEq` it had been standing the derive up with.

A parameter an enclosing `fun`, `impl` or `trait` owns is now RIGID: it unifies with itself and nothing else, and only the parameters a site is inferring — a callee's at a call, a struct's at a literal, an enum's at a constructor, a declaration's own at an `impl` head — are open. A bounded parameter still SATISFIES a trait-typed position through its bound (satisfying is not binding), and an identity mapped type `(U in T: U)` now reduces to its source instead of being bound to it. One estate program changed verdict: a tuple-comprehension pin declared `: T` where its body produces `(U in T: i32)`, and now says so.

**One module declares a name once, and a bound names a trait.** Two `struct N`, two `trait N`, a `struct N` beside an `enum N` or a `trait N` were all accepted with no diagnostic: the scope's lookup index keeps one entry per name, so the LAST declaration won and `x: N` resolved by declaration order — `trait N` first made `N` the struct and ran; `struct N` first made it the trait and failed at a struct literal with `cannot initialize a non-struct: N`, which names neither declaration. A duplicate top-level declaration of any sort is now refused at the second site, with a note at the first; two *modules* may still each declare `N`, a module being a namespace. Separately, `fun f<T: S>(…)` with `S` a struct was accepted and surfaced only as `cannot access field 'v' on type T` somewhere downstream; a struct or enum in bound position is now refused where it is written, naming the sort and steering to a similarly named trait when one is in scope.

**A tuple receiver resolved NO method at any arity — not an inherent impl, not a trait impl, not `impl (i32, i32) with Add`'s own `add` — so `(1, 2) + (3, 4)` ran and answered `4` / `6` while `(1, 2).add((3, 4))` was "cannot call method 'add' on (i32, i32)".** One impl, two spellings, and only one of them reachable. B170 made a tuple reachable as an impl SUBJECT and the operator path has dispatched through it ever since; the METHOD path never looked at a tuple receiver at all. **Nothing about the lookup needed teaching, and that is the shape of the bug.** The operator path finds a tuple impl by scanning the implementations and comparing the receiver against each `implementation.subject` with `compare_type`; the method path's candidate collector scans the by-member index and compares with the *same function* over the *same table*, using the same identity (arity, then elements structurally). What was missing was one level up: method resolution dispatches on the receiver's SHAPE, its arms are the nominal types, a bare trait `self` in a default, and a bounded generic — and a tuple fell to the catch-all "not callable", so it never asked. Adding the shape to that arm is the whole analyzer fix; everything the arm does is already shape-agnostic, including binding an impl's generics by reconciling its subject against the receiver, which is what types `impl (type T: Display, T)` at both `(i32, i32)` and `(str, str)`. **Three more nominal-only receiver sets sat below it on the way to a running program, and each was reachable only once the one above was fixed.** The transformer's re-dispatch — how a trait default specialized for a concrete type finds the impl that provides its requirements — admitted nominal receivers only, so `impl (i32, i32) with Tagged`'s inherited `label` walked past the impl to the trait's *bodyless* `tag` (caught by the emitter's never-silent check rather than shipped as an empty function). And the arm that lets a value satisfy a trait-typed slot listed the nominal shapes too, which is exactly how `PartialOrd<B = Self>` declares `lt`'s operand when an impl writes no argument: `(1, 2) < (3, 4)` ran while `(1, 2).lt((3, 4))` was "Expected PartialOrd, but got (i32, i32) instead" — the operator/method asymmetry again, one level below the fix that removed it. A tuple's own trait membership was never in doubt at any of these sites: `smaller<T: PartialOrd>((1, 2), (3, 4))` already ran through a bound. **What does not change:** a tuple's arity is part of its type, so an impl answers only for the arity its subject names (`impl (i32, i32)` gives `(1, 2, 3)` the ordinary "(i32, i32, i32) has no method 'first'"), and a tuple has no member surface of its own — `(1, 2).len()` is still refused. The operator path is unmoved and travels with its method twin in the same pins. This is what the tuple-comprehension paper measured when it found "the suite as methods" blocked one level BELOW variadic generics: the block was not the generics, it was that a tuple had no methods to be variadic over. (tracker B210, from `proposal/tuple-comprehension.md` revision 2 §R1.2; docs `spec/types.md` §5.7)

**`for x in tuple` compiled, ran, and bound `x` to `any` — so `for x in (1, "two", true) { print(x + 1) }` printed `2`, then `two1`, then `2`, and a `&mut` walk over a tuple silently discarded every write. The loop is now refused.** It was never designed: it was a fallthrough. A flat tuple IS a JS array at runtime, so the native `for...of` lowering ran, and the element-type lookup — which has arms for `List`/`Set`, `[T; n]`, a type declaring `next(&mut self): Option<T>`, a trait default's `Self`, and a trait-bounded generic — had **no tuple arm**, so a tuple fell to the give-up default written for an empty, never-pushed list: `any`. The spec produces `any` at host boundaries only, and a tuple literal is not one, so this was a conformance hole rather than an ergonomic gap. It was unsound three ways and the guards around it were inconsistent, which is the tell that nothing decided any of it: native binary operators went through (`x + 1` at three types, no complaint — and NOT a case the generic-left-operand rule can see, since `any` unifies with everything in both directions by spec), an ordinary annotation laundered it (`let s: str = x` was **accepted** and printed `undefined`), and the lending walk `for e in &mut xs { e = e + 1 }` compiled to `__replace(e, e + 1)` with `e` bound to a JS number — `Object.assign` on a primitive coerces to a wrapper, so the tuple slot was never touched and `xs.0` was still `1` afterwards, with no diagnostic anywhere. Meanwhile *field* access and *method* calls on the same binder were already refused ("cannot access field '0' on type any"), so a nested-tuple loop reported the one broken loop twice. **The refusal is the conservative half of two answers, and it is the forward-compatible one.** The other is to UNROLL the loop — check and emit the body once per element, each at that element's own type — which is the same elaboration the tuple comprehension's concrete arm needs and would deliver fold, reduce, any, all and for_each with no new syntax; that question is open, and every program this change rejects is one an unroll would accept, so it can replace the refusal without a migration where `any` could not. The message names the rule and then the spelling that works, which differs by which tuple you wrote: over a **concrete** tuple, positional access and destructuring work and the comprehension does not (`(x in t => e)` over one answers "must be a mapped tuple"), so it says so rather than steering at a form that would refuse the reader again; over a **mapped** tuple `(U in T: F<U>)` it is exactly inverted — `t.0` is refused while `T` is abstract and the comprehension is the shipped form for that source — and that half was a live miscompile of its own, printing `[ 0, 1 ]` and `[ 0, 'two' ]` for a pack of `Option`s. The binder's give-up type is narrowed with the refusal so the reader gets ONE diagnostic: `any` absorbs inconsistently and restated the same broken loop in the body, where the analyzer's own "no answer here" stands down. **The estate census found exactly one site**, and it was a test asserting the bug: a pin listing the deliberately-native iteration forms ran `for item in (5, 6)` beside `List`, `str`, `[T; n]`, `Set` and `Bytes`, and checked only that it *ran*. Being natively iterable is a fact about the emission; having one element type is what the loop's typing asks, and only `[T; n]` answers it — the tuple line is gone and the array's is pinned in its place. Zero hits in std, macro_std, the corpus, the docs fences, the examples, the benchmarks or the templates. (tracker B209, from `proposal/tuple-comprehension.md` revision 2 §R1.1; docs `spec/grammar.md` §3.5, `spec/types.md` §5.9)

<!-- family: feature -->
**`panic(…)` evaluates to `never`, and `never` ERASES: it yields to whatever it meets in every join — `if`/`else` arms, `match` arms, a block's tail against the type expected of it, an operator's operands (`never + i32` is `i32`), a call's argument against its parameter — so a body that ends in a `panic`, or in a `for { … }` nothing breaks out of, owes no return value, and programs the compiler used to refuse now compile.** The bottom type was already in the solver and `panic(..)` already had it; what did not agree was the checker's DIVERGENCE analysis. E114 gave the editor's unreachable-code paint two leaves it deliberately withheld from the checker — a `panic(…)` call, which lowers to a `throw`, and an endless `for { … }` — because widening the checker is a language change and not a paint lane's to make. It is made: `Divergence` has ONE constructor now, so the statement the editor grays and the statement the checker treats as dead are the same statement by construction rather than by two walks agreeing. Return-position checking and R4/R7's diverging-leg exemption gain both leaves with it, so `fun f(): i32 { panic("x"); }` and `fun serve(): i32 { for { tick(); } }` check without an unreachable value after them (std's `rpc.vl` carried `0 - 1 // unreachable — the panic throws` for exactly this; N48, beside this entry, deletes it). **Erasure removes the diverging participant and nothing else** — `let v: str = if c { 1 } else { panic("no") }` is still a mismatch, reported at the `1`, because the arm that survives still has to agree — and `never` never reaches emission as a value, since the expression that had the type leaves before anything can read it. **The endless-loop leaf is conservative in the direction that matters**: a `jump break` binds to the nearest enclosing loop by span, so an inner break leaves the outer loop endless, while an unspanned (desugared) loop and a `for cond { … }` — the `while` — are left out of the set and their tails still owe their value. Both leaves are settled ONCE per resolution phase, from facts the WALK banked rather than from the call table, which fills in as calls resolve: reading a callee from there made "does this body diverge?" depend on fixpoint order, and a return-type constraint that resolved before the panic call it sat after saw a body that did not. Twelve pins, each red-proven against a planted tree — four different plants, because the erasure half and the divergence half fail in different places — and the three controls (a plain void tail, a loop with a break, a `while`) are pinned red-side too. The type system chapter states `never` and the erasure rule where it lists the types, the return-position rule where it lives, and the memory chapter's R4 names what a diverging leg is.

**A chunk that reached another chunk's function had no sound way to name it — the emitted preamble snapshots its dependencies once, at evaluation, so a chunk that lands first binds `undefined` and keeps it — and cross-chunk references are now emitted as registry reads AT THE USE, with the by-value snapshot kept for the names the partition proves EAGER. Nothing about a chunk's *sibling* has that order behind it, and the failure is silent and permanent rather than a race that sometimes works: a `const` initialized from a slot the sibling has not filled is not a live view of that slot, so it stays `undefined` after the sibling registers and the call throws `TypeError: … is not a function` with the function sitting in the registry beside it. No lazily-filled local was needed: there is no hot path to spare yet, and the read is what buys the order-independence. The rewrite is scope-correct rather than name-correct — a reference is rewritten only where no enclosing declaration inside the chunk binds that name, which the whole-program scope rename makes unreachable today and which a rewrite depending on that silently would get wrong the day it is not. The emitter also stopped computing its own partition: `transform_split_with_plan` takes one, `transform_split` passes `chunks::plan`'s, and where a chunk's membership came from is the planner's business — which is what lets the pins hand the emitter the partition the route planner cannot make (`docs_double` moved into a chunk of its own, leaving a reference in each direction) and then evaluate the two chunks IN THE WRONG ORDER under node: the dependent lands first, its provider registers second, and the call resolves. **`shapes::Dot { x = 1 }` parses. **An editor keystroke no longer rebuilds the standard library's world just because the file imports a sibling module. Any `pkg::` import used to bypass `BASE_CACHE` outright, so kolt's `views.vl` and `client.vl` paid a full pre-entry world build on EVERY analysis — the `base` phase read 156–586 ms per keystroke (loadavg 10–30) — while their sibling `theme.vl`, which imports no sibling, hit the cache at 0.0 ms.** The bypass was syntactic and it was standing in for the wrong fact. What is true is that sibling modules LOAD INTO the world, so a world built for one sibling set is not a world for another — and that is a KEY, exactly as the entry's `std::` reference set and its dependency seeds already are. The key gains the entry's package root and its sorted, interned `pkg::` reference names (`None` for a sibling-free entry, so every key a world was already stored under is unchanged and std-only worlds go on being shared across packages), the seed names are interned like every other name that reaches a stored world's maps, and the hit is content-validated per source exactly as before — an edited sibling hash-mismatches and evicts, which is the E12 rule and not a new one. A SECOND bypass a level down went with it: the entry-expansion hoist rebuilt the world for ANY generated `pkg::` reference, which was an affordable conservatism while such entries never reached the cache and would have handed the whole saving back now that they do; the world carries the entry package's loaded module names and the hoist asks the question it already asks of `std::` — is this a module this world never loaded? Measured on kolt through the language server: `base` goes from a miss on every keystroke to `0.0 ms` from the second analysis onward (9 of the first 10 analyses hit, against 11 of 47 before, and every one of those 11 was `theme.vl`'s). Four pins, red-first: the hit, observation-identity against a cache-cleared build, a DIFFERENT sibling set missing, and an edited sibling evicting by content. Backlog M21.

**A generic bound is now evaluated once per (type, trait, arguments) instead of once per call site, which takes the whole-program bound check off the per-keystroke curve it was on.** `check_generic_bound_satisfaction` walks every recorded call site of the whole program on every analysis — including every site in every module the edit never touched — and asks, per bound, whether the value's type satisfies it. On kolt with its 636 KB generated icon module that is 1,791 unchanged functions re-asked on each keystroke, and the check is 63% of the `checks` phase they dominate. The answer depends only on the resolved types involved, never on which call asked, so it memoizes — and the key has to be the resolved `Type`, because ids are minted per OCCURRENCE and an id-keyed memo memoizes nothing (the same finding, and the same fix, as the `refined_edges` selection memo one cycle earlier). Both memoized calls read their subject only as a resolved type plus a trait id, so equal keys have equal answers by construction. Pinned by a counter, not a clock, for the reason its neighbour is: the memo changes no diagnostic, so no behaviour test can see it, and a timing assertion on a shared machine is not a test — sixteen extra calls at one type add sixteen evaluations without it (12 → 28) and ZERO with it (12 → 12). This is the first tranche of backlog M19; what remains — reusing an UNCHANGED module's analysis across analyses — needs a cache keyed on module content that one `Analyzer` over the whole program has no seam for, and is the paper's to sequence.

**E114's remaining two classes ship, and the third one in the item is RULED OUT rather than deferred: a local binding nothing reads is now faded, every statement after one control cannot fall through is faded, and an unused top-level `fun`/`let`/`struct` is not — because Vilan has no private declaration for the item's "unused private declarations" to be about.** The item asked for "a private fn/let/struct with no references (pub/exported items exempt)", which is Rust's rule written down by analogy. The language does not have the distinction: `pub fun helper()` is a *parse error* here, and its curated rule is the reason — "a module's items are importable as they stand" — while `module_importables` will bind any top-level name an `import` asks for. So a top-level item is module surface, a file the editor never analyzed may import it, and fading one on the strength of a single entry's analysis would be a guess about a world this analysis cannot see. That is pinned, not just documented: a fixture whose `fun unreachable_helper` and `let spare` are referenced by nothing in the program — the emission pruner would emit neither — asserts that both stay lit, so a later refactor cannot quietly widen the rule. **A function body is the one scope the language genuinely closes**, so that is where the declarations class lands: nothing outside a body can name a `let` declared inside it, which makes "unreferenced here" mean "dead" with no invisible world attached — and it costs no reachability walk at all, since the reference index the imports third already reads answers it. Exemptions are the ones the scope earns: an `_`-led name never fades (`let _ = …` is what the `[must_use]` rule tells you to write, and fading it would gray the very gesture that says "I meant this"), a parameter never fades (it is signature, not a local — an impl must take what the declaration takes), and a binding whose reference index dropped a use site is kept, since an incomplete tally is no evidence of zero. **The unreachable class reuses the CHECKER's divergence analysis rather than opening a second opinion about what "dead" means**: `Analyzer::block_diverges`'s three private methods moved to one `analyzer::Divergence`, which the analyzer's own R4/R7 and return-position checking now call and the editor calls beside it — so `ret`, `jump` (the loop tails), an `if` whose every arm diverges *and* has an `else`, and a `match` whose every arm diverges arrive already agreed on. Paint asks for two leaves the checker does not have, and the asymmetry is deliberate and one-directional: a `panic(…)` call, which lowers to a `throw`, and an endless `for { … }` (the language's only endless-loop form — `for cond { … }` is the `while`) that nothing breaks out of. Paint may see MORE divergence than the checker safely, because paint decides nothing; widening the checker the same way would be a language change, since `expr_diverges` gates the diverging-leg exemption and return-position checking, and a body ending in `panic()` would newly satisfy a declared return type. A `jump` carries no label, so it binds to the nearest enclosing loop by span, and a loop whose nesting is ambiguous is simply left out of the endless set — the conservative direction, which paints the statement after it as live. One faded range per dead block, not one per statement, because what died is the REST of the block and N grayed lines say that N times. Both inherit the imports third's conservatism whole: nothing fades while the buffer is ahead of the analysis, nothing fades in a file carrying a diagnostic — which is also what makes the platform-colored case safe, since a browser-only file analyzed under the wrong color is a file full of diagnostics, and the fade is already off. **Seventeen pins, eight of them watched red against the live implementation** (eight of the nine unreachable pins failed before the synthesized-tail rule landed — a `fun f() { ret; }`'s trailing `Void` records the closing BRACE as its span, passes every span test, and is not code at all), with the exemptions proven non-vacuous by removing them one at a time and watching the `_`-led, top-level, and diagnostic-gate pins go red. **Cost, measured, because E114's neighbour E121 sets a 10 ms keystroke budget**: both producers are called from exactly one place, `publish::diagnostic_groups`, which is the debounced diagnostics path — nothing on the keystroke path pays for them — and no reachability walk was added, the emission pruner's answer being a whole-program question the honest scope above turned out not to need. (Absolute figures are from a machine at loadavg ~90 and are worth only the ratios in them; the ratio is the claim.) **Semantic highlighting, inlay hints and completion now describe the buffer on your screen instead of the last finished analysis, and their cost stopped tracking the size of the codebase. On a generated 1,791-function exhibit the whole-program walk every request used to pay costs 1.104 ms of thread CPU; the keystroke path that replaced it answers semantic tokens in 0.004 ms — 276× less — and inlay hints in 0.001 ms, with the whole three-provider burst at 0.828 ms against the 10 ms budget (release, 50 requests per window, loadavg 41.9 on 16 cores; wall 2.926 / 0.004 / 0.001 / 1.632 ms beside it and asserted on nowhere). On a read-only copy of a real 1,791-function application the same request went from 12.2 ms of wall and 10 ms of CPU to 0.30 ms and 0 ms, and from 12.3 ms measured from the keystroke to 1.8 ms — at loadavg 45 against the earlier reading's loadavg 11, so the four-times-busier machine makes those a floor rather than a ceiling.** The measurement that motivated it is `proposal/editor-latency.md` §1.4a: hold a file completely fixed and grow the codebase around it, and the cost of serving that file's semantic tokens grows 6.4× — 4.2 to 27.0 ms of CPU for one unchanged 468-token file as its import closure goes from 4 to 5,000 functions — because every request re-walked `program.functions`, `structs`, `enums`, `traits`, `variables`, `parameters` and the whole `entity_map` from scratch. The 10 ms budget was spent at roughly 490 reachable functions, and kolt's `views.vl` is at 1,791. The fix is to stop recomputing: an analysis now captures its own token stream, hint list and symbol index once, when it is built, on the analysis thread — and a request re-serves that capture through a byte-identical anchor plus one lex of the open file, whose result is used only inside the window being edited. The cost that remains is proportional to the file, which is what the mandate asked for, and independent of the program it belongs to, which is what it was not. Mechanically the path is three pieces in a new `crates/vilan-lsp/src/keystroke.rs`, and none of them type-checks, resolves a project context, or touches the filesystem. Positions come from a *two-sided anchor*, which generalizes B38's `compute_retained_tail`: everything before the first differing byte and after the last differing byte is literally the same text, so the landed answers there map onto the live buffer by a constant shift and are exact — B38's own honesty argument, now applied to the larger half it threw away. The middle window between the anchors is the region you are editing, has no image in the analysis, and is painted from *syntax alone*; a landed span that straddles a window edge is dropped rather than clamped, because half of it describes bytes that are gone. Whether the classification outside that window is still true is decided by a *declaration-shape stamp* — a hash of every token the lexer produces outside a function body, which is exactly the text that binds a module-scope name. An equal stamp means no top-level declaration was added, removed or renamed, no `import` line moved and no signature changed, so the landed names still resolve where they did; a changed one degrades the whole file's tokens to syntax-only until the next analysis lands. It is computed off the lexer rather than the parser, so it costs one linear pass and survives the mid-keystroke syntax error that would fail a parse, and every ambiguity in it resolves toward *changed*, which is the safe direction. Completion gains a *per-module symbol index* of declared names, kinds and signature labels, built from the landed analysis and grouped by `Program::source_of`, with the edited module's own entry rebuilt from live syntax on any keystroke that moves its stamp and skipped on every keystroke that does not — so a `fun` typed one keystroke ago completes, which no answer drawn from the last analysis can do. The three combine into three verdicts, and they are the honest vocabulary for what a mid-keystroke answer is worth: *exact* (an anchor exists and the stamp matches) re-maps the landed tokens and paints the window from syntax; *stale* (the stamp moved, or a module this file imports did) paints the whole file from syntax, because syntax is never wrong; *unusable* (a paste replaced the file, leaving no byte-identical line) paints from syntax and withholds every hint. Two owner rulings are wired in exactly as ruled. Tokens take the yes: the region your eyes are in is syntactic and therefore always right, and a briefly mis-coloured identifier outside it is cosmetic and corrects itself on the next landing — which is what makes the owner's own exhibit work, since the lexer emits no token at all for a comment, so commenting a line out removes its semantic colours on the very next keystroke instead of holding them for the 409 ms–1.1 s staleness window §1.5 measured. Hints take the split: withheld inside the edit window always, because a hint on the line you are typing is simultaneously the most likely to be wrong and the least useful, and a wrong hint is not a cosmetic error but a lie about a type; served unchanged outside it rather than flickered off, because the only "mark" VS Code offers is removal and a display that strobes across a typing burst is the larger harm. The gate is a pin family under the thread clock (M15), on a subject this repository GENERATES rather than borrows: kolt is never integrated into this codebase, so the exhibit is a synthetic module of one repeated shape sized like kolt-with-lucide, written by a generator in the test and not checked in. Its non-vacuity is structural rather than promised — every run measures the whole-program walk the path replaced, in the same process on the same subject, and asserts that the path beats it, so the planted regression §6.2 asks for is the code compiled beside the answer. A seconds-long smoke pin exercising every seam runs in the ordinary gate; the 1,791-function budget pin is `#[ignore]`d, as is the 500 ms diagnostics pin, which does not pass and is not this change's to meet — one keystroke still costs about 925 ms of CPU to diagnostics at that size, and M21/M19 are what close it. Found and NOT fixed, and the gate now says exactly where the remaining budget goes: with tokens and hints down to microseconds, essentially the whole 0.828 ms burst is completion, and it is the landed engine's own per-module `name_to_id_map` sweep and per-request `read_dir` that the index is built to retire and has so far replaced only for a `module::` path prefix. The scope arm's shape was settled by measurement rather than by taste — offering every loaded module's declarations there turned a 125-candidate scope completion on a real application into a 3,144-candidate one, so the index contributes the edited module's own declarations and nothing else, and reaching a name that needs an import stays auto-import's job, with the ranking tiers and the edit that inserts it; the arm now answers 124 candidates where the old engine answered 125, plus whatever the buffer has declared since the last analysis. What that leaves is worth stating as a number rather than a hope: on the same application copy the five-provider burst an editor fires is 12.0 ms measured from the keystroke, against 15.3 ms before and a 10 ms budget, and every millisecond of the remainder is now completion. One older pin is rewritten rather than kept: `semantic_tokens_answer_the_analyzed_snapshot_while_typing` claimed the whole token stream comes back byte-identical while you type, which is precisely the staleness the ruling overturns; it now holds the sharper and true property, that the anchors hold still and the window tracks the buffer, with nothing lost and no classification changed. (tracker E121 §2.1/§6, from Order 25's keystroke-path lane; `proposal/editor-latency.md`)

**The viewport semantic-token request now costs the viewport: `semanticTokens/range` computed the WHOLE file's token stream and then filtered it by line, so twenty visible lines cost 9.0 ms of wall and 10 ms of process CPU on kolt's `views.vl` against the whole file's 8.9 ms — a ratio of 1.01, which is the defect stated as a number (measured before E121's keystroke path landed, at loadavg 8.2–11.9).** It is the request an editor sends most and it was the one paying most: `Document::semantic_tokens` re-walks `program.functions`, `structs`, `enums`, `traits`, `variables`, `parameters`, the whole `entity_map`, `member_name_spans` and `type_references`, re-parses the file raw for the markup and CSS spans, then sorts and de-overlaps — and the range handler ran all of it before discarding everything outside the window, plus one line-index lookup per token in the FILE to do the discarding. **E121's keystroke path, which landed between this item's measurement and its fold, did not reach this request.** It moved `semanticTokens/full` and its delta onto the analysis's own capture — a walk paid once, on the analysis thread — and left `range` on the per-request walk, so the defect survived it intact: re-measured on the merged tree, a twenty-line window still cost **0.851×** the whole file (1752.71 ms against 2059.89 ms of thread CPU over forty rounds of a 12,000-token stream, loadavg 1.29). The window is now a SLICE of that same capture. E121's `LandedSnapshot` carries a `token_lines` table beside its tokens — the first token index at or after each line — so a window is a clamp and two indexes rather than a walk, and the answer comes from **one capture per analysis rather than a second memo of the same tokens**, which is the shape this fold chose over the standalone `SemanticTokenStream` memo the item was originally built with. **The invalidation rule is the whole safety argument, and it is a one-place rule.** The capture is a pure function of the analyzed snapshot — the `program`, the `analyzed_index` its spans point into, and B38's `retained_tail` — and those three move together in exactly one place, `Document::adopt_analysis`, which is where the capture is replaced and its line index rebuilt. A live edit deliberately does NOT invalidate it: `set_text`/`apply_change` move the LIVE snapshot alone and these tokens describe the analyzed one (S1), which is the same reason the answer was already allowed to be one analysis stale, and the reason `range` stays in ANALYZED coordinates while `full` answers the live buffer through E121's two-sided anchor. **B38's salvage tail is folded into the capture at that same point, and that is a repair rather than a translation.** The capture is built on the analysis thread, where the tail does not exist yet, and nothing folded it in afterwards — so since E121 the capture and the walk disagreed exactly on the salvaged region, and `semanticTokens/full` painted nothing below a parse break that `Document::semantic_tokens` would have salvaged. One rule (`fold_retained_tail`) is now applied at both moments the tokens exist, and after an adoption the capture is byte-for-byte what the walk answers. Three pins, gating three claims. The answer is unchanged — a window's bytes are compared against the filter-the-full-stream form they replace, over windows that start mid-file, end past the end, land on a line with no tokens and cover everything; planting an ignored end bound reddens it. The answer is unchanged across a salvaged adoption too, at both the capture and the handler; removing the fold reddens both of those and leaves the two older B38 pins green, which is what says they could not have caught it. And the cost follows the window — on a 1,500-function, 6,000-line synthetic module with a 12,000-token stream, forty rounds each of a 20-line window and the whole file, on M15's thread clock: **0.003×** (0.98 ms vs 286.26 ms) against a bound of 0.25, where planting the pre-fold mechanism reads the **0.851×** above. The bound sits between two mechanisms, not two tunings. Tracker E122, the editor-latency paper's §1.6 find; folded across the keystroke path in Order 25.

**Opening a file no longer parks a tokio worker for the length of its first analysis: a `semanticTokens/full` issued the instant after `didOpen` answered in 1270.7 ms before this change and 7.9 ms after, on kolt's `views.vl` at loadavg 8.2–11.9.** `did_open` called `Document::analyze` inline on the async handler, and that call joins a 128 MiB analysis thread — so the notification handler held its worker for the entire first analysis and every request behind it waited, which the server's own session trace had been reporting all along as `slow request: didOpen took 1252 ms`. Nothing else in the file does this: `analyze_and_publish` has always gone through `spawn_blocking`. The open now does what an edit does. It inserts the buffer synchronously — a new `Document::unanalyzed`, the text and its line index and nothing an analysis produces — so a query arriving immediately still finds the document and `land`'s invariant that a missing map entry can only mean *closed* is untouched; then it schedules the analysis through the same `analyze_and_publish` every other path uses, sampled and stamped with the world revision it read (E117) and landed only if it is still the newest view of the live text. `Document::internal_error`, the degraded document a panicked analysis lands on, is now that same constructor plus its one honest diagnostic. The trade is real and stated: the first token or hint request after an open answers EMPTY instead of waiting, which is the state the debounce window between an edit and its analysis has always had, and a `semanticTokens/refresh` pair follows the landing so the empty answer is transient. Measured over interleaved rounds per binary: the open-then-request latency **1270.7 / 1058.9 ms → 7.9 / 1.5 ms**, the `slow request: didOpen` trace line **two occurrences → none**, and the open's diagnostics still publish at the same magnitude (1270 / 1059 → 1408 / 1051 ms) because the analysis is unchanged work on a different thread. Pinned two ways on a current-thread runtime, which is what makes the ordering exact rather than statistical: a request issued while a fresh open's analysis is in flight is ANSWERED and the analysis has demonstrably not landed when it is — planting the inline analyze reddens that assertion by construction — and the open's diagnostics still arrive afterward; and an edit arriving during a fresh open is the analysis that settles, so the supersession the scheduling brings with it is guarded too. Three existing pins had to be told to wait for an open now that one does not block: the two package-recolor pins read a diagnostic straight after `didOpen`, and the session-leak loop went from tens of seconds to **88 ms** the moment its twelve opens stopped analyzing — a gate quietly becoming vacuous, so it now waits for each and costs 8.9 s again. Tracker E123, the editor-latency paper's §1.6 find.

**`[derive(..)]` on a GENERIC type now generates a real generic impl — `impl Handle<type T> with Wire` over `Handle<T>` — instead of an erased one that named the subject bare in every role, and the arity rule generated code was exempted from now applies to it.** Every generator spelled its subject by its bare NAME wherever a type was wanted: `[derive(Wire)]` on `std::arena`'s `struct Handle<T>` emitted `impl Handle with Json`, `Result<Handle, str>` and `fun rebuild(..): Handle`, and `[derive(Debug)]` on a `struct Pair<T> { a: T }` emitted a body calling `.debug()` on a parameter nothing bound. Those are under-supplied applications, and B188's erasure — the very hole B188 closed for written code — was precisely what let them type-check, so B188 shipped its arity refusal GATED off `DERIVED_SOURCE`: total over what a program writes, exempt for what a generator writes. The exemption is gone and the gate with it. **The macro reflection surface now carries the subject's own generic parameters.** `macro_std::meta`'s `StructItem` and `EnumItem` each gain `generics: List<GenericParameter>` — name, written bounds, and the default AS WRITTEN — plus the two spellings every generator needs from them: `subject()` renders the subject as an application of its parameters (`Handle<T>`, `Either<L, R>`), and `binders(trait)` renders the impl header's binder list. Both are used by the vilan derive macros (`Json`, `Wire`, `Debug`, `Default`, `PartialEq`, `Hashable`) and mirrored in the Rust fallback generator, because two backends that disagree about a subject's spelling are worse than one that is wrong. Path heads (`Handle::from_json_value(..)`), struct-literal heads and display text keep the bare name: each of those names a namespace or a word, not an application. **THE RULE is the derived trait on every REACHED parameter, and a bare binder for a phantom one** — a parameter is reached when some field type or variant payload is written in terms of it, at any depth, so `value: T` and `held: Option<T>` both reach `T` and `Handle<T>`'s `T` reaches nothing. That is a deliberate DEPARTURE from the default this was ruled with, which was Rust's rule: bind the derived trait on every parameter, reached or not. The census is what changed it. Exactly one derive over a generic subject exists in std — `Handle<T>` — and its parameter is phantom by construction, because a `[derive(Wire)]` type whose field is typed by a parameter is refused at its own declaration by the Wire boundary check. C7 rules that a handle is sendable whatever it names ("a name is not the thing it names"): the entity stays on the server, only `{ index, generation }` crosses, and `docs/std/cells.md` and `docs/guide/services.md` both say in so many words that a handle names entities whose type is not itself Wire. Rust's rule would emit `impl Handle<type T: Wire>` and make `Handle<Session>` un-sendable for any `Session` that is not Wire — refusing a program the compiler has a passing pin for. So for `Wire` the every-parameter bound is pure cost: the reached case is unreachable, and the bound buys nothing while breaking C7. Reachability is also EXACT in vilan in a way it cannot be in Rust, where `PhantomData<T>` mentions `T` and the compiler therefore cannot tell phantom from reached: a vilan phantom parameter appears in no member type at all, so "mentioned by a written member type" IS the test. A type form the reflection surface cannot decompose — a tuple, a closure, a reference — is read as reaching every parameter, which falls back to Rust's rule rather than to a bare binder over a body that will not compile. **What this buys is that one derive now serves every instantiation.** `[derive(Json)] struct Box<T> { value: T }` encodes and decodes at `Box<i32>` and `Box<str>` from a single impl; `[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Default)]` over a generic works the same way. All of that was a compile error before — `cannot call method 'to_json' on T`, reported inside code the author never wrote — so nothing ran wrong and nothing changes meaning; this is a capability, not a correction. An unmet bound is refused at the USE site, naming the concrete argument and the trait (`'Opaque' does not implement trait 'Debug'`), not at the `[derive(..)]` and not inside the generated impl. Nine pins, seven of them red against the live compiler before the change, including a MIXED subject whose reached parameter binds and whose phantom one does not, both directions pinned so the bare binder cannot quietly disable the check. **Two `DERIVED_SOURCE` gates deliberately stay**, because this rule does not make them redundant: B189's covered set suppresses a generated `[service]` subscription call restating an `[expose]` refusal already reported at the author's own field, which is diagnostic dedup on a different axis entirely and has nothing to do with derive bounds. B174's operator exemption is the one this DOES make redundant — it exists because `[derive(PartialEq)]` emitted an `eq` over an unbounded `T`-typed field, and that field's parameter is now bound `T: PartialEq` — and it IS lifted, in this same unreleased section: the b194-landing lane removed it once b174 had merged, so the derive surface passes the operator rule rather than skipping it. (tracker B194, from b188's STOP; `macro-engine.md` §3/§10, `claims-and-epochs.md` §6)

**A negated `is` test now scopes its capture to the branch that actually matched: `if !(x is Some(let n)) { … }` no longer binds `n` in its then-branch — the branch reached only when the pattern FAILED — and does bind it in the `else`, which is reached only when it matched. The program this stops compiled, ran, and printed `undefined`.** B171 ruled the scope of an unnegated capture a day earlier — then-branch yes, `&&`-right operand yes, `||` arms no, `else` no — and a negation is the case that sentence does not reach. `if !(maybe is Some(let n)) { print(n); }` emitted `if (!($a[0] === 0)) { console.log($a[1]); }`: the payload slot read exactly where the subject has no payload, which JavaScript answers `undefined` and prints, so the program produced a plausible wrong answer and reported nothing — the same shape and the same silence as the `||` arm B171 closed. **The rule is B171's then-branch rule MIRRORED, and it is ruled here rather than restated**: a `!` swaps which of the two branches the capture is bound in, so the then-branch of a negated test refuses and the `else` accepts — and on down an `else if` chain, since each `else` in it is still the previous condition's false path. Two negations cancel, because a swap applied twice is the identity. The `&&` rule is unchanged *inside* the negation — `!(x is P && use(n))` still binds `n` for the right operand, which the short-circuit reached by matching — but a negated capture does not cross an `&&` it sits to the LEFT of: `&&` carries only its left operand's true side, and a negated capture is bound on the false one. That last case is the one a naive parity counter gets wrong, and it was live unsound too: `if !(!(x is Some(let n)) && n > 1)` compiled and read the missing payload before this change. A capture under a `||` stays unbound in both branches, exactly as B171 left it. **The mechanism is B171's visibility range, extended rather than duplicated.** The walk carries the answer for a capture at even negation parity and the answer at odd parity as a PAIR, which is what makes `!` a plain swap of the two halves and what lets `&&` cut the half its short-circuit does not carry while leaving the other alone — no depth counter, and the nesting cases fall out instead of being enumerated. The `else` branch is a sibling scope the capture was never declared in, so the negated captures a condition binds are handed to the `if` walk, which declares them into that scope from its start; an ordinary `let` of the same name inside the `else` still shadows from its own point on, since the positional rule does not care where a declaration came from. The bookkeeping travels the condition's boolean spine (`!`, `&&`/`||`, the `is` itself) and stops there: a capture inside a call argument is bound by an evaluation the condition's truth says nothing about, so it gets neither a negated cut nor an `else` declaration and keeps precisely the answer B171 gave it. No new diagnostic — the refusals are the ordinary "cannot find" error, which the errors appendix now steers under, since a capture that is visible in the branch three lines down reads as a compiler mistake. Fifteen pins beside B171's, nine of them red against the live compiler before the change; B171's seven are untouched controls and stay green. **`if !(x is P) { ret; }` binding the continuation past the `if` is still NOT part of this** — the then-branch is refused by the rule above and the read after the `if` stays refused too, both pinned; B187 rules that shape. Found and NOT fixed, a B171-era approximation this change deliberately leaves alone rather than widening its scope: a capture reached through a call argument (`if always(x is Some(let n)) { print(n); }`) is still visible in the then-branch and still reads the missing payload — off the boolean spine the condition's truth proves nothing about the test at all, negation or no negation. (tracker B195, from Order 24's rulings-smalls lane; docs `spec/types.md` §5.7, `tour/control-flow.md`, `appendix/errors.md`)

Eleven witnesses seeded in `resource.vl` and three in `resource_exit.vl` to start, with floors that keep the mechanism from rotting to nothing while it is adopted file by file. **The docs twin of that finding: the resources tour opened by stating the law c8609287 REPLACED, two of its programs printed the exact opposite of the output claimed beside them, and the `OwnedNursery` example's background work never ran at all.** `tour/resources.md:10` called resources values "torn down deterministically when their owner's scope ends" — the pre-amendment sentence, in the first paragraph of the chapter a reader meets the concept in — while `spec/memory.md`'s "Drop timing and order" three clicks deeper had been amended a cycle earlier. **The two false outputs are F7/F8's shape in prose.** The chapter's opening `Guard` pair promised `body / dropped second / dropped first` and actually prints `dropped first / dropped second / body`: nothing reads either guard, so both drop at their DECLARATION, in declaration order, before the `print` the sentence hangs the reverse ordering on. **The wall-clock waits run one at a time now, the two bounds that were too small to be liveness bounds at all are liveness bounds, the union's stragglers start first — and the CPU-time cure the item proposed was measured against each family and applies to none of them.** Four unions have paid this: Order 20's close, Order 24's hygiene lane and Order 24's pre-seal union, each with the same 301 s red on `build_hooks`'s watch family at loadavg ~25 on a pin that costs 0.6 s alone; and two sibling lanes' unions, where the language server's `package_recolor_tests` pair went red under ten-lane load while passing at 19.7 s at loadavg ~85 and 13.8 s alone. **Three different fixes, because the numbers say they are three different faults.** (1) **A nextest group, `wall-clock-waits`, with `max-threads = 1`**, over the 38 tests that wait on a wall clock for work happening on another thread or in another process: every live `vilan build --watch` / `run --watch` session and its round, plus the two recolor pins, which have no watcher and no child process — a `did_change` on one open buffer, then a poll for the server's debounced re-analysis and package sweep to recolor a *different* open buffer. The suite is the only load this repository controls and it was piling that whole family onto itself inside an interleave already 16 wide. (2) **Two bounds raised to 300 s**, the value E39/E40 settled `WATCH_LIVENESS` on and for the recorded reason: `settled`'s 10 s (200 × 50 ms) is not too large for a healthy sweep when the sweep is a real re-analysis of a real package and the whole pin costs 13.8 s idle — measured here at 9.58 s for `removing_the_import_colors_the_file_back` on a quiet box, grazing the old bound — and `release_differential`'s `NODE_TIMEOUT` of 30 s is a fixed clock around running a corpus program, which is E32's disease exactly. Neither pin claims anything about time; a green run pays neither number. (3) **`priority = 100` for the stragglers**, the idiom the leak plateaus already use: `dependent_edit_measurement` was the sole survivor of a 5455-test union at 246.6 s, holding the run open about four minutes after everything else had finished, and `style_chain_order` and `release_differential` were the other >120 s members. **The CPU-time direction — M15's shape — was measured against every one of these and fits none.** For the watch rounds the subject is an EVENT delivered by a 300 ms poll loop that sleeps in between, not a computation: at loadavg 79 a watcher with nothing to do burns **0.030 s of CPU per 30 s of wall — 1.0 ms/s, set by the poll rate and not by the load** — against 0.33 s for round 1 and 0.02 s for round 2, so a CPU deadline is a wall deadline in different units and makes *starved* and *stuck* less distinguishable, not more. For `dependent_edit_measurement`, which looks like M15's shape and is cited as such, the wall clocks it computes are PRINTED and never asserted: all 27 of its assertions are on leak-tally BYTES, so there is no load-sensitive verdict for a CPU clock to rescue — it is long, not fragile, and scheduling is the whole answer. `style_chain_order` has no clock in it at all. **The filterset's name pattern does not stand alone**, since `test(/watch|round/)` is exactly what rots when somebody adds a pin without knowing it exists: `every_test_that_drives_a_watch_session_is_in_the_group` reads all nine suite files, finds every `#[test]` reaching `spawn_watch(` or handing `--watch` to the binary (comments dropped first — three tests only MENTION the flag in their prose), and reds naming any the filterset would miss, while `the_group_is_declared_the_way_this_file_reads_it` holds the config against the same lists including the two members outside this crate. That gate found `split`'s `a_watch_round_clears_the_chunks_a_build_left` and `serve_build`'s `run_watch_tells_its_child_it_is_watching`, neither of which a filter written off the HMR suites would have selected. The group also takes a `slow-timeout` of 120 s advisory / 8 minutes fatal, deliberately OUTSIDE the pins' own bounds: a hung round should be reported by the pin, which panics with the round counts and the watcher's whole log, and `terminate-after` is only for what a pin's own bound cannot reach — a child that never exits, a wait written without one. **The cost, and the limits, stated because a flake is easy to declare fixed.** Serializing the group puts a floor under the union equal to the family's own serial time: **100.9 s at idle**, measured as the sum of its members' idle durations, against a suite that runs in ~64 s idle — so the group becomes the critical path and the union's idle wall roughly doubles, while under load (where the rest of the suite is minutes) it is not the critical path at all. And the group cannot help a box loaded by something outside the suite, which is what three of the five strikes actually record: five union-shaped runs of the seven affected binaries at loadavg 33–79 *before* the change were 104/104 green, so the artificial load this lane could raise did not reproduce the red. What the change is proved to do is remove the suite's self-inflicted share of it — five runs after, at loadavg 106–143, 106/106 green each — and what it is proved not to have broken is the bound itself: with a round planted that never re-runs, the pin still reds at 300.2 s carrying `rounds.txt: 1 lines, ran.txt: 1 lines` and the watcher's log. **B198 ruled: a containment test resolves BOTH its sides or neither, never a case-folded root against a lexical child — and the defect turns out to be reachable on unix too, through a symlink, which is how it was red-proved.** A product its generator has not written yet is not on disk, so `canonical_path` degrades to a lexical normalization and keeps the caller's spelling, while the declared generated root — which IS on disk — comes back as the filesystem spells it. `covering_from`'s `resolved.starts_with(&root)` compares components byte-for-byte, so the two disagree and the file reads as outside its own generated root: `vilan fmt` rewrites a product, which is `build-hooks.md` §12.1's fmt↔hook loop, reached by a spelling instead of by a link. Audit run 7 found it on Windows against `gen` / `GEN` and filed the two obvious repairs as a ruling rather than picking one, because both are bad: folding case inside `covering_from` makes a deliberately platform-independent predicate platform-dependent in the one function whose whole point is that `vilan fmt` and format-on-save answer alike, and resolving the nearest existing ancestor inside `canonical_path` changes what that helper promises every caller it has. **Neither is what shipped.** `canonical_path` is untouched; `covering_from` folds nothing; what changed is the resolution the CONTAINMENT TEST uses. `util::canonical_path_of_unwritten` canonicalizes the deepest ancestor that is on disk and re-attaches the components below it exactly as they were spelled, and both the subject and the declared root go through it — so a resolved root is never compared against a lexical child, and a tree where nothing at all exists degrades to G17's spelled ladder with both sides lexical together, which is the same comparison it always was. For a path that IS on disk it costs exactly what `canonical_path` costs: the first attempt succeeds. **Case is only one of the ways a filesystem gives a path two spellings, and the other one is portable**, which is what makes this fixable-with-proof rather than fixable-on-faith: `a_product_the_generator_has_not_written_yet_is_covered_through_a_link` builds the identical tree on unix with `elsewhere/peek` linked at `package/gen`, and before the change the not-yet-written product under the link answered `None` while its already-written twin — the same tree, the same link, the same root, differing only in whether the file exists — answered correctly, so "not yet on disk" is the whole difference under test. The Windows pin `a_product_the_generator_has_not_written_yet_is_still_covered` flips from `#[ignore]`d to live and asserts the same property through NTFS's fold; it is **unverified locally** — no unix host can run it — and CI's Windows leg is its instrument, with `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` the compile proof that it and the new helper build for that target. **Windows' own link spellings — junctions, case folding, the `\\?\` verbatim prefix — are now measured by CI instead of inferred from the unix run, and `vilan fmt`'s cycle guard can finally say "I do not know what this directory is".** Order 23 shipped the symlink doctrine (`const.md` §9.2: a link is a supported spelling of project layout, resolved honestly, with every fence applied to the resolved tree) with every pin `cfg(unix)`, because creating a symlink needs a privilege Windows does not grant by default. Audit run 7 read the non-unix half and found the cycle guard's stop arm UNREACHABLE. `TreeWalk`'s identity for a directory was `util::canonical_path`, which never fails: where it cannot resolve, it degrades to a lexical normalization — the right answer for a comparison KEY over a path that may not be on disk, and the wrong one for an IDENTITY. `Some` was therefore the only value the arm could produce, so the `else { return }` that stops the walk on unix could not run at all. It is the failure case that this costs, and it is worth being exact rather than dramatic: while resolution SUCCEEDS the two helpers agree and an ordinary junction cycle is caught either way, but the moment it stops answering, the lexical fallback mints a distinct key at every level of a cycle — `src/l1`, `src/l1/l1`, `src/l1/l1/l1` — `visited` never collides, and the walk fans out with nothing behind it, since `TreeWalk::walk` has no depth cap and there is no ELOOP on that side. The fix is one call, `fs::canonicalize(path).ok()`, so that a resolution failure STOPS the walk instead of minting a fresh key — the same sentence the unix arm already says when `fs::metadata` fails — and the reasoning is written beside it, because the two helpers differ in precisely the property this one call site depends on. **Eight pins land with it, all `cfg(windows)`, and CI's Windows leg is the only instrument that can run them**: on a unix host they compile away, so a green local suite says nothing whatever about them. Four are built on JUNCTIONS, which need no privilege and which `fs::metadata`, `fs::symlink_metadata` and `fs::read_link` treat as links exactly as they treat a unix symlink (`cmd /S /C mklink /J`, where `/S` is load-bearing — without it `cmd`'s own quote-stripping pass mangles a quoted temp path): the cycle itself, under a 60-second timeout that asserts exactly one `would reformat` and kills-and-panics on a hang, since a pin proving a hang is gone must not be able to pass by hanging the harness; a junction inside a declared tree digesting UNFOLLOWED, re-pointed at a byte-identical tree so that following and not following disagree; a declared directory input reached through a junction staying fresh across three builds; and a product under a junctioned `generated` root surviving both of the exclusion's ladders across the `\\?\` seam. A fifth needs the privilege — a RELATIVE directory symlink is the one shape a junction cannot express, because a junction stores an absolute target resolved when it was made — and SKIPS with a printed note when the machine does not grant it, rather than failing or quietly passing. Three more pin hazards with no link in them at all: a generated root covering its products through a case-folded spelling (NTFS folds case and nothing in the predicate does, so the answer rests entirely on `fs::canonicalize` handing back the on-disk spelling), and the reopen caveat `strip_verbatim_prefix` documents itself out of — its doc justifies stripping unconditionally on the grounds that "the result is a comparison key, never a path we reopen", and three callers reopen it, so a path past `MAX_PATH` is now round-tripped through the stripped spelling and reopened in all three of their shapes. **One measurement is RED and lands `#[ignore]`d rather than fixed.** A product its generator has not written YET has no on-disk path to canonicalize, so a case-folded spelling keeps its case while the declared root canonicalizes to the one NTFS holds; `covering_from`'s `resolved.starts_with(&root)` compares components byte-for-byte, answers None, and the formatter would rewrite a product — §12.1's fmt↔hook loop, reached by a spelling instead of by a link. Neither repair is obviously right, which is why it is a ruling and not a patch: folding case inside `covering_from` makes a deliberately platform-independent predicate platform-dependent in the one function whose whole point is that two front ends answer alike, and resolving the nearest EXISTING ancestor instead changes what `canonical_path` promises every caller it has. (tracker B198; audit run 7's F6, Order 24 charter item 4)

**Every native operator now checks its LEFT operand, not just `+`: `true - 3` typed `bool`, `"12" - "3"` typed `str` and `Level::High ^ Level::Low` typed `Level` were each a number wearing a type it was not, and all three compiled clean in v0.40.0.** b148 gave `+` an admitted set on the native path and gated the check on `+` alone, arguing the gate in a SCOPE note: the other native operators "emit arithmetic on numbers, where `+` emits a rendering". That is a statement about a NUMERIC left operand and it is true of nothing else. Three native types are not numbers — `bool`, `str`, and a backed enum — and for those the argument inverts: the host operator returns a number, a binary takes its static type from the LEFT operand, so what comes back is a number wearing a type it is not. Same miscompile `+` was fixed for, entered by the other nine operators. **The three shapes, as they ran before this landed.** `let c: bool = true - 3` held `-2`, so `if c` took the TRUE branch while `c == true` printed false — a `bool` that is neither of its values, and a `fun takes_bool(c)` accepted it. `let s: str = "12" - "3"` held `9`, and `s.len()` on it was `undefined`. `Level::High ^ Level::Low` was `4` typed `Level`, a value matching no variant at all: `== Level::Low` and `== Level::High` both false, silently — its `-` sibling was louder only by luck, panicking in a `match` with "Level: 4 is not one of its values". The bitwise arm was the quietest of the three: `true & 3` is `1`, which prints as `1` and looks like nothing until something compares it.
