**A trait on a PARAMETER is now an implicit generic: `fun f(x: Trait)` reads as `fun f<T: Trait>(x: T)`, monomorphized per call like any generic you write out.** This is the reactive paper's §7.3, the half of B161 that did not ship with the `let` position — and it is a surface, not a semantics: the desugaring is exactly the spelling the language already has, so there is nothing new to check, emit, or explain beyond where the `<T: …>` went. Parameters are the bulk of the estate's trait-annotation sites (the paper's §5 census), which is what makes it worth a surface at all. **The two readings are one family and they are not the same reading, which is worth stating because the difference is invisible in the spelling.** A `let`'s annotation is a CONSTRAINT: one initializer, one concrete type, the binding keeps it, and the body reads the impl's own surface — `let d: Greet = Dog { name = "rex" }` still lets you read `d.name`. A parameter is QUANTIFIED: one type per call site, so the function is checked ONCE against the bound and the body reaches the trait's members and no others — `fun describe(subject: Greet)` refuses `subject.name` exactly as `fun describe<T: Greet>(subject: T)` always has. Both are "no widening, no `dyn`, static dispatch"; only one of them has a `for all` in front. **Three consequences, each pinned.** Each annotation is its OWN generic, so `fun pair(a: Greet, b: Greet)` accepts a `Dog` and a `Fox` together and a function needing them equal must write the generic and use it twice — more permissive than the concrete parameter it replaces, so no call anywhere breaks. A parameterized trait binds the trait's arguments (`cell: Holds<i32>` is bounded by `Holds<i32>`, and a `Cell<str>` is refused at the call). And the implicit parameter is APPENDED after every generic the declaration writes, so the positional generic-argument spelling this language has — `tag<Dog, Fox>(..)`, no `::<>` — keeps binding what it always bound; prepending would have silently re-pointed every explicit argument one slot left. **The paper's honest cost concern is answered by measurement rather than argument.** A silently-generic function changes its emission shape, so the census took three sites shaped like `std::ui`'s A33-widened bindings (`fun bind_text<S: Source<str>>(self, source: S)`) — one whose body resolves per impl, one whose body never mentions the bound, one more of the first kind — and compiled each estate at two types, written out and sugared. Naively that is six emitted copies; five land, because M16's emitted-body sharing merges the T-independent one, and **the sugared and written spellings emit byte-identical output** — the same 683-byte file, the same five bodies for the three sites. The sugar costs what writing the generic costs, to the byte, which is the negative A33 carried and now has an answer for. **Everything else stays refused, with a steer that now names the position that works**: a return type, a struct field, a generic argument (`List<Greet>`), and a CLOSURE parameter — a closure has no generic list for an implicit parameter to be appended to, so the one position that cannot carry the sugar keeps the error. `&Greet` is deliberately NOT in that list and is now pinned so it cannot drift: `&` is a call convention that `walk_type_node` erases, so there is no `Reference` type for a trait to be nested inside, and the annotation the reading sees is the trait's own. That is B161 as shipped — `let seen: &Greet = & dog` has always been the constraint form, keeping `Dog` — and the parameter now reads the same annotation the same way, which is what "reuse B161's machinery" has to mean if the two positions are to agree. The refusal keeps its single error identity and reads "a trait names a parameter's bound, not a value type; write `fun f(x: Trait)` for a parameter, or a generic for a field/return". Seventeen pins in the sugar's own section, nine of them red against the live compiler before the change, including a `View` extension bound on `Source<i32>` against the real `std::ui` — the shape the estate will be written in. Three of B72's parameter-position REFUSALS invert into acceptances here, which is that arc closing rather than a regression: B72's steer said to write `<T: A>`, and the parameter now means it. What B72 established is untouched where it still applies — the rule fires at the declaration with no call in sight, it is one rule rather than a per-position message, and its pins now read at a field or a return. Found and NOT fixed on the way through, pinned `#[ignore]`d: a PARTIAL generic-argument list (`tag<Dog>(..)` on a two-parameter function) leaves the unsupplied parameters uninferred and reaches emission abstract; supplying none works and supplying all works, and it reproduces on two written generics with no sugar in sight. (tracker B186; `proposal/reactive-traits.md` §7.3; docs `spec/types.md` §5.5, `tour/data-and-traits.md`)

**The language server's line-index cache no longer answers for text that is gone: an entry is served only while the file still matches the length and modification time it was built from.** `line_index_for` caches by path for any file that is on disk and not buffered, and it had no invalidation at all — documented as safe because it was "written for `std`, whose files do not change". Stability was never a property of the KEY, only of std, and the map holds whatever a cross-file definition or reference asks for. A workspace file is exempt from the cache only while a buffer is registered for it, so one that was cached before it was ever opened kept its pre-edit index through the whole open/edit/save/close cycle, and every later reference into it converted spans through line breaks that had moved: a wrong position, published, with nothing to correct it for the rest of the session. The fix makes the documented invariant true rather than assuming it — a hit must match the file's current `metadata`, and anything else re-reads. That is strictly more than the two remedies the report offered: a did-close hook would not have seen a `git checkout` or a generator's rewrite, and restricting the map to `std` would have gone stale on anyone editing std itself. It also keeps the win the cache exists for, because a stat is orders of magnitude cheaper than a read plus an index build — pinned in both directions, a changed file re-indexed (proven red against the stamp comparison removed) and an unchanged one answering with the very same `Arc`. The entry is stamped with what was read BEFORE the read, so a file that changes mid-read looks stale next time and is read again; the cache can waste a read, never answer a wrong one. A name with arguments attached them to the nominal type (`Option<i32>` → `Enum(option_id, [i32])`); a BARE name fell through to whatever the reference resolved to, which for a generic declaration is that declaration's own type — argument vector **empty**, the parameter erased rather than bound. Downstream, an empty argument vector reads as "nothing to check", so every later comparison was vacuous: `read(Holder { inner = "seven" })` unified, `h.inner` typed as the unbounded parameter, and the emitted `console.log("seven" + 1)` printed `seven1` with `n` declared `i32`. **The same hole had an internal-error twin.** Where the erased parameter carried a trait bound (`struct Holder<S: Get<i32>>`), the field typed as the abstract BOUND, so `h.inner.take()` resolved to `Get`'s body-less requirement and the transformer — which cannot emit a signature — bailed with "please report this program". One erasure, two symptoms; refusing the annotation removes the abstract receiver that put an unimplementable call there at all. **The rule is that an under-supplied application is refused in every position an annotation can occupy** — parameter, return type, `let` annotation, struct field, a nested generic argument (`List<Holder>`), an `impl` head subject, a trait-bound argument — naming the arity and handing back the spelling that fixes it: `` `Holder` takes 1 type argument, 0 given — write `Holder<S>` ``. Inference from context is deliberately not attempted: annotations are checked, never inferred (B161's family), so a missing argument has nothing to come from. A parameter with a **default** supplies itself, so `struct Holder<S = i32>` written bare is complete and still type-checked on the default — the refusal fires only where a missing argument is genuinely missing. **Over-supply is the same check's other direction and was never actually checked**: `fun read(h: Holder<i32, str>)` reported nothing at all unless some *use* happened to force a mismatch, so an annotation nothing used passed silently. One arity check now owns both directions, at the annotation, where the fix goes. **The estate census found zero hand-written spellings that relied on the erasure** — 223 `.vl` files across std, the corpus, examples and benchmarks, every docs fence, every `.vl` fixture and inline snippet in the Rust tests, the website and the playground: every bare use of a generic name turned out to name a non-generic type of the same name declared in the same program. Two spellings are exempt and both fall out of the word *written*. A path **head** (`Option::None`, `List::from_json_value(..)`, `math::min(..)`) names a namespace to look a member up in, not a type, so its arity is nobody's to supply. And **generated** code is not written by the author: today's derive generators spell a subject by its bare name in every role, so `[derive(Wire)]` on `std`'s own `struct Handle<T>` emits `impl Handle with Json` and `Result<Handle, str>`, and the erasure this change removes is exactly what let those type-check. Refusing them would report a *generator's* defect at a `[derive(..)]` the author cannot edit — and making the generators generic-aware is a ruling rather than a fix, because the reflection surface a macro sees (`macro_std/src/meta.vl`'s `StructItem`/`EnumItem`) carries no generic parameters at all, and a derived impl over a parameter needs bounds nothing computes (`impl Box<type T: Json> with Json`). So the rule is total over what a program writes, and the generator half is filed rather than half-shipped. Twenty pins cover the miscompile, the internal-error twin, each annotation position, the two-parameter and partially-supplied forms, both exemptions, and the four controls that keep the refusal honest — a correctly-supplied application, a defaulted parameter, `Self` inside a generic impl, and a plain non-generic struct. (backlog B188, found by the papers lane on B184's path; the same substitution-hole class as reactive-traits §8.1/§8.2; docs `spec/types.md` §5.6/§5.11, `tour/memory-model.md`)

**The playground's buffers get a real prelude, chosen by mode: the WEB set in the browser mode that runs your program, the base set in the server check mode, and a toggle that turns the ambient scope off.** A pasted single-file program has no `vilan.toml`, so B156's weakest-scope rule had no `[package]` to hang the key on — and the playground therefore taught the spelling the prelude exists to delete, while `vilan init`'s scaffolds demonstrated the ambient idiom. `vilan-wasm` now carries the missing half as a **synthetic package context** rather than as synthesized imports: `compile_program_with(source, platform, prelude)` sets `Workspace::entry_prelude`, the same field a manifest's `[package] prelude` lands in for every other front end, and the existing `seed_preludes` pass does the rest. §9.2's mandate is what makes that the only acceptable shape — the prelude binds at the weakest layer, so a pasted `enum Signal` still wins over the web set's ambient one and an `import std::style::style;` still beats the ambient module `style`, both silently, both pinned. **The defaults are per mode and the browser's is the web set, deliberately.** The playground's browser mode is not a program that happens to target the browser; it is a web app, which is the one corpus §3.3 showed the base seven never empty an import block for — so `Signal`, `SignalCell`, `view`, `View` and the modules `style`/`ui` are ambient there, and a counter or a view tree pastes in with no import block at all. The server check mode is a process program and takes the base set, exactly what `vilan init` would give it. **The wire is `compile_with(source, platform, prelude)`**, with `prelude` absent for the mode's recommended set, the word `"off"` for none, or a module path to pin one; the page feature-detects the export, so a glue built before it existed keeps calling `compile_for` and takes the same recommended defaults. The base cache already keys on the entry prelude, so flipping the toggle or the mode never serves the other one's world. **One thing the work found that the filing had wrong**: the BASE set was already reaching manifest-less buffers, because `Workspace::default()`'s `entry_prelude` is `PreludeSpec::default()` — bare `print` compiled in the playground at v0.40.0 and the examples' `import std::io::print;` was redundant rather than required. What was genuinely missing was the web set and the toggle. **One thing it found and did not fix**: the B4 import steer and its web-set arm are both silently dead in the playground, because the std module inventory they read is a `read_dir` (`analyzer.rs`, `std_module_files`) and there is no filesystem behind the wasm — so an absent `Signal` in server mode reports plainly and names no repair. That silence is currently the honest answer, since `web_prelude_steer`'s repair is a `vilan.toml` line a pasted buffer cannot write, and it is pinned as such: an overlay-aware inventory would light up exactly that misdirection and has to deal with it. (tracker K14, ruled door 1 with a toggle; proposal/prelude.md §5.3, §9.2)

**An operator that dispatches to your impl now checks the right operand against the `B` that impl declares — until this landed it checked nothing at all, and passed a foreign struct straight into a body typed for another one.** `impl Counter with Add { fun add(self, other: Counter): Counter }` resolved for `Counter { n = 1 } + Point { x = 1, y = 2 }`, handed the `Point` to a body reading `other.n`, and printed `2` — the `Point`'s first slot, read under the wrong type, from a program that compiled clean. B179 ruled the operand roles for a NATIVE left operand a day earlier: the operator belongs to its LEFT operand, so the right one must be a MEMBER of what that operand's `add` accepts. A nominal left operand is exactly where an impl gets to SAY what that set is, and the dispatch site never read it — so the rule B179 wrote held only for the half of the language that does not dispatch, and the half that does was wider open than the one it closed. Every operator the dispatch serves had it, all measured before the fix: `-` gave `7` and `*` gave `30` off the same slot, `/ % << >> & ^ |` all computed, `==` answered a plausible `true`, `<` answered `true` through `PartialOrd`'s inherited `lt` default, and `counter += Point { .. }` rode the desugar's second registration site into the same body. The check is one general reconciliation at the dispatch site rather than a rule per trait, because the `B` it has to read is the IMPL's, and that is three different things: a type the impl wrote (`impl Meters with Add<Feet>` admits a `Feet` and, this is the point, refuses a `Meters` — which used to read `other.f` off the `m` slot and answer `6`); one of the impl's OWN parameters, substituted through what the subject bound (`impl Bag<type T> with Add<T>` at a `Bag<i32>` wants an `i32`, and stored a `str` there before); or `Self`, whether spelled in the impl or reached through `Add<B = Self>`'s default, which interns as the trait's own type and would have left the check with no `B` at all for the overwhelmingly common impl had it not been resolved. A binder the subject does not decide is a hole the operand fills, which is acceptance rather than refusal, and the bound it carries is then what the operand is checked against. **A GENERIC right operand refuses here for B179's reason one level along**: a bound promises a trait's methods, never that the parameter IS the declared `B`, and a declaration is checked once for all of its instantiations — so `fun bump<T: Add>(counter: Counter, value: T)` is refused even though `Point` satisfies `Add` and the call type-checked (it printed `8`, `1 + 7`). The comparison had to be the RIGID one conformance uses, because the ordinary one treats a parameter as a hole and answers true to whatever is asked — which is how two unrelated parameters in the two positions passed each other. This is also what makes B179's second steer truthful: "put a left operand there whose `Add` declares a `B` that admits `T`" named a route that was broken while every nominal left operand accepted every parameter, and the spelling it means — the left operand's own type carrying the parameter, so its `Add` declares `B = T` — is now pinned green and running at two instantiations. Sixteen pins over thirty cases, twelve of them red against the live bug and four of them controls that were green before and after — because half of this fix is refusing what was wrong and half is not refusing what was right. Census clean: every corpus golden byte-identical, every docs fence still compiling, std's own `impl List<type T: PartialEq> with PartialEq` unaffected. (tracker B180, found by lane b179 the day B179 closed; docs `spec/types.md` §5.7 and `appendix/errors.md`, ledger row 346)

It is never asked of "is this type unknown": an unknown from another family — a name that failed to resolve — still refuses at every use, pinned in the same program as a refused field that stands down, and a second, independent offense in the same struct (an `[expose]`d element that is not Wire) survives untouched. **The second half of the same read is the report COUNT.** A multi-entry package's `check` is one analysis per ENTRY over one source tree, so a module every leg reaches produced its diagnostics once per leg — kolt's two refused fields are six of those 53 errors, the one report each is owed arriving once per entry. The module loader has refused to report a module's parse errors once per importing SEAM since E102, keyed on file, position and reason — all three of what an error is — and an entry is that seam one level up, so it takes the same key. `check` arms the ledger for its round (a `--watch` round starts clean, and every single-analysis path never consults it), and a repeat is dropped from the OUTPUT and not from the verdict, so a second entry can never emit over a module the first found broken. The workspace loop and the several-colors loop E113 gave a shared file both arm it, for the reason E113 gives: the file is the subject, not the number of legs or colors it took to clear it. **The third is the ORDER.** A diagnostic raised against generated code re-anchors at the whole declaration (standard A2), whose span opens before the field annotation inside it, so plain positional order printed the consequence and buried the cause. The rule is one sentence, written where the sort is: a refusal that CAUSED a stand-down prints ahead of every diagnostic whose span encloses it, and ahead of anything sharing its span. Only refusals move, only past diagnostics that contain them, and everything else keeps its own start — so no unrelated pair is reordered and the result is still one total, deterministic order. "Caused a stand-down" is observed rather than asserted: the stand-down sites record the refusal as they take it, and a refusal nothing stood down for never moves. **The counts.** The exhibit's smallest form — one `[expose] items: Signal<List<i32>>` field, no method bodies, nothing else in the file — reported three with the root printed LAST, and reports one. A kolt-shaped three-entry package with two refused fields and one `[rpc]` body goes 21 → 2, both of them the refusal. Eight pins. Seven were proven red by planting: dropping the provenance record reddens five at once (the smallest form, the cascade through a field's uses, the generated-code follow-ons, the ordering, and the refused half of the unrelated-unknown pin); making the stand-down a blanket over any unknown receiver at all reddens the unrelated-unknown pin and only it; disabling only the ordering rank reddens only the ordering pin; and disarming the round ledger takes the two CLI pins from 1 and 2 reports back to 3 and 6. The eighth is E104's CONTROL — the second, independent offense in the same struct — and no plant in this change can redden it, which is exactly why it is there: it is what would catch a stand-down widened into a swallow. **`T::default()` under a bound now types as `T`, not as the bound — which makes `List::sum` over a struct element actually add: it printed `4` for a wallet holding 40 and 2.** A trait's associated function has no `self`, and the specialization that makes a trait member's `Self` return concrete is driven by the RECEIVER — read off the member's first parameter. A plausible wrong answer, never a visible failure. The fix is the same structural substitution the receiver branch already performs, applied where the path named a BINDER instead of a receiver — the accessor records both halves when it resolves through a bound (the constraint, and the trait that provided the member), so nested occurrences of `Self` specialize with the bare one. **The `Trait::func()` path is deliberately untouched**: its subject is the trait itself, not a bound binder, so its `Self` stays abstract exactly as B162 ruled. **And the operator check's skip list loses `Type::Trait` with it** — the carve-out existed solely to keep std's own `sum` compiling over this wart, and with the wart gone a value typed as a bare trait gets a verdict like every other shape. It gets its own refusal rather than the standard one, because the standard one cannot be acted on: `impl Maker with Add` is not a declaration the language has, so the message names the rule (a trait is a bound, not a value type — vilan has no trait objects) and the spelling that does work (`<T: Maker>`). One trait-typed shape still skips and is filed rather than refused: `self` inside a trait DEFAULT body, where `self + self` over a supertrait `Add` still emits the host's `+`. Refusing that one would be advice nobody can take — the explicit `self.add(self)` does not resolve there either — so it is pinned `#[ignore]`d until both halves close together. **A blanket impl never satisfies a bound for an ABSTRACT parameter, and that refusal is now the promise rather than an open question: it is spelled in the spec, pinned as a negative, and the appendix entry says so.** `impl type T with Wrap<T>` covers every type, so `fun wrapper<T: Tag>(value: T) { consume(value) }` — where `consume` wants `W: Wrap<T>` — reads at a glance as though the bound were satisfied; the compiler refuses it with `generic parameter 'T' is missing the bound ': Wrap<T>' required by this call`, while the same call on a concrete `i32` compiles and runs. Answering "satisfied, via the blanket" at abstract time is an **over-approximation**: §5.4 ranks a blanket impl *last*, so a more specific impl appearing later would be the one the call actually reaches at instantiation, and the abstract body would have been checked against an implementation that never runs. Monomorphization is where the question has a real answer, so the concrete check is the one that counts and a parameter's own **declared bounds are the only thing an abstract call may lean on** — which is exactly what `satisfies_trait_bound` does for a `Type::Generic` value, now with the reason written beside it instead of read off the code. No exhibit was found where wanting the other answer makes sense; if one appears the ruling reopens, and until then the fix is the one the message already names — declare the bound (`fun wrapper<T: Tag + Wrap<T>>`), which admits the call. The `#[ignore]`d wish becomes three pins that state the whole rule: the refusal, the concrete caller that passes through the same blanket, and the declared-bound spelling that admits the abstract call. The negative was proven non-vacuous by planting the answer the ruling refuses — falling through to the impl search for a `Type::Generic` value — and watching the refusal disappear. (tracker B173, from Order 23's b168 lane; docs `spec/types.md` §5.4, `appendix/errors.md`)

The fourth did not, and it was the worst of the four to get wrong: `if maybe is Some(let n) || n > 1 { … }` compiled and emitted `$a[0] === 0 || $a[1] > 1` — a read of a payload slot the subject does not have, which JavaScript answers `undefined` and compares `false`, so the program ran, produced a plausible wrong answer, and reported nothing. `||` short-circuits: its right arm runs precisely when the `is` test FAILED, so nothing is bound there. Everything else keeps the old rule exactly — `FOREVER` is what every non-`||` binding gets — and the control that an `is` and its use inside ONE `||` operand still see each other (`(x is Some(let n) && n > 0) || flag`) is pinned too. The transformer inlines `main`'s body as the module's top-level statements — that is what makes the entry the entry — so `fun main(condition: bool) { if condition { … } }` emitted `if (condition) {` against a name nothing declared, and the program died at its first statement with `ReferenceError: condition is not defined`. It already shipped for the node leg and the browser leg refuses it by ordinary platform coloring, like every other process-only name; what this adds is the steer, the pins that RUN it, and the docs saying it is the *only* argument door. The check keys on the global scope's `main` — the same lookup the transformer's entry discovery makes — so a method named `main`, or a module's own, keeps its parameters. **Found shipping the pin, and fixed with it: `arguments` and `eval` were missing from the emitter's reserved-name list.** Neither is a reserved *word*, which is how they escaped it, but strict mode forbids BINDING them and an ES module is always strict — so `let arguments = process::args()`, the obvious spelling of the very call this steers to, emitted `const arguments = __args();` and node refused to parse the module at all ("Unexpected eval or arguments in strict mode"), before a line of the program ran. The corpus program that exercises `args()` had been in exactly that state, byte-identical to its golden and unrunnable; one golden moves (`process-env.mjs`, `arguments` → `arguments2`) and the program runs. That fixture worked by luck at `i32` and printed **`abab`** for `Holder { value = "ab" }.twice()` — one type argument from demonstrating the bug it was silently relying on; it now reads `trait Doubler<T: Add>`, still prints `42`, and the bound is orthogonal to what it asserts. **The rule is adequacy, not merely a bound, and that is the ruling's own refinement over the item as written.** `T: Display` promises `to_string` and not `add`, and before this it left the shape exactly as broken as `<T>` — the check that asked whether a bound provided the operator's method only ever *recorded* a dispatch and never refused its absence. The right operand already checked adequacy, so the two sides disagreed about what a bound has to prove; they no longer do. A bound reached through a **supertrait** counts, which is what keeps std's own `math::minmax<T: Ord>` (`a <= b`, whose `le` comes from `Ord`'s `PartialOrd`) compiling, and is pinned. The refusal follows the operand-role family's wording and names the bound that would admit the operand, because the left operand is exactly where a bound works: `` `+` on `T` needs `T: Add` — a parameter promises only what its bounds promise, and `T` is unbounded, so there is no `add` to dispatch to ``, closing with where to put it. When the parameter is a **trait's** own it says so — ``declared on `trait Doubler` `` — since that bound cannot be added locally: it moves the trait, and every `impl` of it and every bound that names it. **`&&` and `||` are the one family where "add a bound" is not the fix, so they refuse outright on either side.** They admit `bool`, they model no operator trait at all, and no trait names that set — so B181's shipped sentence serves the left operand unchanged, and the left half it deferred to this step is simply the same check with the side condition dropped. `both(Point { x = 1, y = 2 }, true)` printed the struct: JavaScript's `&&` yields its right operand when the left is truthy. **One boundary is deliberate, and it is B188's, drawn on the same generators for the same reason.** `[derive(PartialEq)]` on a generic struct emits an `eq` comparing a `T`-typed field, so the rule would refuse the derive surface wholesale — and the diagnostic anchors at the `[derive(..)]`, which is not where the bound goes, so it would name a fix from a span that is not the declaration. Generated code was exempted, the rule total over what a program **writes** (which is what the census counted), and the generator half filed rather than half-shipped. B194 shipped that half in this same section — a derived impl binds every parameter its body reaches, so the `eq` above compares a BOUNDED `T` — and the exemption is gone again with it: the derive surface now passes this rule instead of skipping it, and an instantiation that cannot supply the bound is refused at the author's own call site. Bounding the struct yourself works as it always did, and every half is pinned. The spec needed no new rule, only an exact one: `spec/types.md` already prescribed `<T: Add>` for a left-operand parameter and the compiler did not enforce it, so this is a conformance fix — the section now says the bound is required, that it must provide the operator's method, that a supertrait's counts, that inside a trait default it goes on the trait, and what the author of a generic `&&` is told instead. (tracker B174, ruled 2026-09-01, from Order 23's operators lane via audit run 7 and `proposal/generic-left-operand-census.md`; docs `spec/types.md`)

<!-- family: feature -->
**A server can call functions the CLIENT declared.** Until now the wire went one way: a browser called an `[rpc]` method and a server answered, and a server with news — a session revoked, a job finished, another user moving something on the screen you are looking at — had no way to say so that was not the client asking a hundred times to hear once. `[client_service]` on a struct in the browser half declares what the server may call; `[service(KoltClient, client = KoltHandlers)]` names it on the service; `connection.client()` hands the factory a typed `KoltHandlersProxy` the service holds as a field and reaches as `self.client.session_revoked(reason)`. The generator is direction-agnostic — `[client_service]` produces the SAME dispatcher a `[service]` does, because `Dispatcher`, `RpcProtocol::respond` and the whole `arg`/`reply` foundation never knew which end of a socket they sat on — so the browser half is generation, not runtime. The wire grows ONE LANE and no flags: text `s:<id>:<payload>` and binary tag `0x73`, carrying requests the SERVER minted, in the server's own id namespace. Reusing `r:` would have collided two `fresh_id()` counters and made `r:7:` ambiguous on both ends; with a lane per direction each side reads its role off the prefix and nothing has to carry a direction bit. **This version is notifications only.** A `[client_service]` method declares no return type: fire-and-forget needs no pending table, no correlation id and no reverse reply lane, it cannot deadlock a handler's turn, and it covers what a server actually wants to say to a browser. The handler still runs inside `turn(FlushPolicy::AtEnd, ..)` exactly as a server-side one does, so a notification that writes a signal three times publishes one wave. The contract hash covers BOTH directions — a service declaring `client = …` appends the handler surface to its own, so the two ends agree about the reverse direction or the connection is refused at `__contract`, before any `s:` frame could be sent — and a service declaring none hashes byte-identically to what it always did. Both attributes on one struct is peer-to-peer, one dispatcher, no new spelling.

<!-- family: diagnostics -->
**Two refusals for the reverse direction, both at the attribute and both in its own vocabulary.** A `[client_service]` method that declares a return type is refused: v1 is notifications only, so there is no reverse reply lane for a value to travel on and no pending table to correlate it with, and the message says to drop the return type or have the handler call back on the connection it already holds. And `[service(.., client = X)]` where no `[client_service] struct X` is declared in the same module is refused too — the reverse surface is read off X's `[rpc]` methods AT EXPANSION and folded into this service's contract hash, so a handler the expansion cannot see would hash as no handler at all and both peers would agree about nothing. Same-module is the constraint the message states, because same-module impls are the reflection the compiler does.

<!-- family: fix -->
**Two rpc frames that TCP coalesced into one read were serialized by the receive loop, so a handler awaiting anything the SECOND frame would have delivered waited for a message the loop was holding.** Frames arrive as chunks, and the socket's `data` handler parsed each chunk into events in a loop that AWAITED each event's `respond` before parsing the next. Across chunks there was never a problem — node calls the handler again whether or not the previous call's promise settled — but within one chunk two requests were a queue rather than two handlers in flight, and on a fast local link coalescing is the common case, not the rare one. A handler that suspended on state the next frame of its own chunk sets waited for it forever. The loop now STARTS each handler's turn and lets the event loop interleave; per-handler turns settle independently, exactly as they always did across chunks. **Reply order within a chunk is not promised** — replies carry their request id and arrive when their handler is done, so a slow first frame no longer holds a fast second one behind it. Nothing in the protocol ever depended on the order; this makes it visible. The pin drives the server from a raw socket, so the coalescing is the test's rather than the kernel's: two masked frames in one `write_all`, the first handler waiting on a flag only the second sets, and its wait bounded in retries rather than in wall time.

**`std::print` is gone, and so are the fifteen other alias-only re-exports that lived in `std/src/lib.vl`. Each name is now spelled at its real home — `std::io::print` — and the prelude carries the ergonomics the aliases existed for.** Every entry in std's package root was there for one reason: to let a caller write `std::print` instead of `std::io::print`. That is import brevity, and a package root is the wrong place to sell it — a re-export whose only job is to be shorter is a second spelling of a name with no rule for which one is canonical, which is exactly what the estate then split down the middle. With a prelude in the language the ergonomics are served properly, so the alias layer goes. **The census is the whole surface**: `lib.vl` is the only `lib.vl` in std and `export import` appears elsewhere in the package only in the two prelude modules this same order added, so six statements and sixteen names is all of it — `print`, `panic`, `assert`, `Default`, `str`, and the eleven numerics `BigInt`/`f32`/`f64`/`i8`/`i16`/`i32`/`i53`/`u8`/`u16`/`u32`/`u53`. Two findings from counting: **thirteen of the sixteen had ZERO uses in the entire estate** — nobody, in std or the corpus or the docs or the examples or kolt or the website, ever wrote `std::Default`, `std::str` or any of the numerics, and the numerics were doubly dead because they are §4.7 primitives that have been ambient with no prelude at all since before any of this; and **std never used its own aliases**, spelling every internal import `pkg::io::print`, so migrating std itself was a null change and `lib.vl` was the only std file that moved. **Each old spelling gets a curated diagnostic rather than the generic failure**, because `std::print` will be typed from muscle memory for a long time and "cannot find 'print' in the imported path" names neither the removal nor either way forward: `` `std::print` was removed: `print` is in the default prelude (no import needed), and its module path is `std::io::print` ``, with the prelude clause dropped for `panic`/`assert`/`Default` (in neither std set, so claiming no import is needed would be false) and replaced for the primitives with "is a primitive and is always in scope — delete the import". The arm fires only directly under `std`'s root, so a typo inside a real module (`std::io::prnt`) keeps the ordinary message. **The migration took two shapes and the split was deliberate.** The fixture corpora — 200 files of Rust test sources, the `vilan/test` corpus, the benchmarks — were **rewritten** to `std::io::print`, a pure textual substitution that preserves every fixture's meaning exactly and cannot depend on the prelude reaching that fixture's package; the corpus goldens are byte-identical, which is the negative this half is checked against. The teaching corpora — 47 files of doc fences, the examples, `README.md`, the CLI templates — had the import **deleted** instead, 159 lines of it, because a doc fence that imports what the prelude supplies teaches the wrong thing, and the docs gate compiling every one of those fences afterward is the prelude's best end-to-end proof. Hello-world now opens with `fun main`. Two things the sweep exposed and fixed at the root rather than around: the transformer looked `print` up in std's PACKAGE-ROOT scope, which only ever worked because the alias put it there, and now reads a `print_fn_id` the analyzer captures from `std::io` beside `panic`'s — a lang-adjacent function should say where it lives rather than ride a convenience re-export; and `std::number` and `std::string` were being loaded only as a side effect of `lib.vl` re-exporting their members for the `std::i32` / `std::str` short names, so they join `boolean`, `list` and the rest in the always-loaded core list, where the primitives they host say so themselves. **Migrating your own code**: delete `import std::print;` outright if your package uses the default prelude (the compiler will tell you, and Organize Imports now strips it for you); otherwise respell it `std::io::print`. `panic`, `assert` and `Default` are a respelling either way; the numerics and `str` are a deletion, since they were never needed. (backlog B156; proposal/prelude.md §10.2; docs `spec/names.md` §4.7, `appendix/errors.md`)

That is what makes them the right tool for protocol text (file extensions, mime rows, HTTP header names, HTML tag names, hex), where case-insensitivity is defined over ASCII to begin with. The two bugs both lived in `document.vl` and both came from the full fold. `skip_raw_text` carried a comment claiming the lowered copy shares indices with the original — false while the fold could change length (`İ` lowers to two code units), true now. And `is_name_start` — lower the character, then test `a <= c <= z` — answered TRUE for U+212A KELVIN SIGN, which the full fold lowers to a plain `k`, so a character HTML says can start no tag name opened one. Seven behavior pins in the inference suite cover the full pair's Unicode mappings and length changes, the ASCII pair's narrowness (the four letters untouched, the length preserved, the empty string, a full round-trip on mixed input), the Kelvin sign at both folds, and `heading_id`'s two branches; the four ASCII pins were proven red by planting the full-Unicode binding back into the ASCII implementations, and `heading_id`'s by planting the ASCII fold at markdown's Unicode site. **A `let` or `mut` REBINDING of a closure parameter waits for the parameter's type the way a mention of it does — so it keeps a container whole, and keeps the copy it owes.** `s.set_with(|values| { mut next = values; next.push(2); next })` refused with "cannot call method 'push' on unknown", and the copy-update-return idiom is precisely what `set_with` is FOR. The cause was one resolver out of step with every other. An unannotated closure parameter reads `Unknown` until the call site infers the closure against the callee's signature and fills its slot (B13's channel); every consulting resolver — a method call, a subscript, a `for`, a `match` — recognises that `Unknown` as a "not yet" and defers on it. The VARIABLE resolver did not: it took the `Unknown` for an answer and ground the binding on it, permanently, because the fill lands afterwards. So the rebinding was `unknown` for the rest of the closure while the parameter itself typed fine — which is why the direct spelling (`values.push(2)`) always gave the right refusal and the rebinding never did. Rebindings now count as mentions: the walk that answers "is this an unfilled closure parameter?" follows a still-ungrounded binding to its initializer, and the variable resolver defers while its value is one. That is the whole fix, and it is general — nothing about `set_with`, about traits, about default bodies, or about `mut`, all of which the discrimination had pointed at. A plain `let` lost the type identically; so did a closure passed to any generic function, a `sub` observer (a trait REQUIREMENT, not a default body), an inherent `SignalCell::update` view, and a `str` parameter — the "scalars are fine" control was an illusion of numeric defaulting grounding `next + 1` by a different route. A chain of rebindings resolves through the same walk, as does one inside a nested closure. The RUNNING half is why this is a miscompile rather than a refusal: an untyped binding reads as a scalar to the emitter, so it dropped the `__clone` that a `mut` rebinding of a List, a Map or a struct owes its caller. `apply(seed, |values| { mut next = values; grow(&mut next); next })` mutated `seed` in place and printed `2 2` where the annotated spelling of the same program printed `1 2` — a clean compile, silently sharing the value it was supposed to copy. Following initializers put the walk on a graph that can cycle (`let a = b; let b = a;` is writable, module bindings resolving in any order), so bindings already stepped through end it; the two module-level-cycle pins hung without that and are green with it. Found by the website migration's clean-build gate, whose four errors were all this one bug.

One callee is exempt, and the exemption is new spec text: a `[extern(…, retains)]` host keeps what it is handed past the call, and a temporary has no binding whose scope could hold it open, so such an argument is left to leak rather than freed under a host still reading it — the direction these rules always fail toward. Six pins, each red-first: the double destruction and the readable-after-move, the widened predicate at both callee kinds proven by re-planting the narrowing, the retains exemption proven by removing its guard, and the pre-existing `option_replace_returns_the_old_resource_for_the_caller_to_own` pin, which goes red on the widening WITHOUT the declaration fix — the two had to land together. **A resource held in an `if` arm, a `match` leg, a loop body or any nested block emitted a `try` that trapped a name read after it: accepted vilan that throws `ReferenceError` the moment the scope runs — live in v0.39.0.** S3 moved disposal from scope end to last use by wrapping the statements between an acquisition and its last read in a `try`/`finally`. That region lowers to a JS block, so every `const` a statement inside it declares dies at the closing brace, and the region must therefore be WIDENED until it covers the last read of every name declared within it. That rule shipped, was pinned, and worked — at a function body's top level, and nowhere else. The widening asks the dataflow, once per statement of the region being emitted, *what names does this statement put into the block I am about to wrap?*, and the answer arrives as a map the liveness pass keyed on the OUTERMOST statement enclosing each declaration. At a body's top level a declaration's statement chain has ONE element, so outermost and direct are the same id and the lookup hits; one level down they are different ids — inside an `if` arm the chain reads `[the if, the let]`, the transformer holds the `let` and the map holds the `if` — so every lookup missed, the fixpoint never ran, and the `try` closed over a `const` whose read followed it. `if flag { let r = Res { … }; let value = 7; print(r.tag); print(value); }`, with one ordinary statement after the `if`, emitted `const value` *inside* the `try` and `console.log(value)` after it. Nothing catches this before run time: the program type-checks, the emitted JavaScript parses, and it throws `ReferenceError: value is not defined` when the arm executes. The differential that isolates it is one statement long — the SAME `if` written as the function's TAIL widens correctly, because a tail is never pushed onto the statement chain and the arm's declarations key themselves, and adding a single `print("after")` after the `if` breaks it. The fix is the keying, moved on the map's side: `declared_binding_extents` now keys the INNERMOST enclosing statement, which is the coordinate its one consumer holds at every depth. That is the side that was wrong, not a second lookup bolted beside the first, because only a statement's OWN declarations can put a name into the block the region becomes — a name declared inside a nested construct is scoped to it and cannot be read outside it — so the direct statement is the only key that ever answers, and the outermost key answered at exactly one depth by coincidence of chain length. The three shapes that were already correct stay correct and are pinned or probed as negatives: a closure body is its own walk region, so its chains start at the closure; the function body is the one-element case; and an `own` resource parameter keys nothing at all, declaring at its body's entry with an empty chain. Six pins, five of them red first with a genuine `ReferenceError` — a compile-only pin cannot see this class, since the bad JavaScript is well-formed — covering the `if` arm, the `match` leg, the loop body, a block two deep, and the tail-versus-statement differential with both spellings in one program so neither can be fixed at the other's expense; the sixth is the closure-body negative. No corpus golden moves. (tracker B159, audit run 5's F1; docs `spec/memory.md`)

**`"here " + point` compiled and printed `here 1,2`: `+` never typed its right operand, and an i-string is that same `+`.** A binary expression takes its type from its LEFT operand, and the native types never dispatch — machine JS *is* their operator semantics — so with `str` on the left the whole expression was `str` no matter what stood on the right, and the emission was the host's own `+` over whatever the right operand lowered to. A struct lowers to a tuple, an enum to a tagged array, a `List` to an array, and the host renders any of those as its comma-joined elements: `Point { x = 1, y = 2 }` printed as `1,2`, `Some(5)` as `0,5`, a `(1, 2)` as `1,2`. B24 closed exactly this hole for the COMPARISONS, and the check it added sits in the same loop — but it was scoped to `==`/`!=`/`<`/`<=`/`>`/`>=`, the operators §5.7 was being written against when it was found, so `+` was left with nothing typing its right side at all. **The reason the garbage turned up far from any `+` a reader wrote is that two desugarings build one**, which is what made this general rather than a curiosity. An interpolated string is not a second mechanism: `lexing::emit_interpolated` lowers `i"here {p} there"` to `("" + "here " + p + " there")` before the parser exists, so `i"here {p} there"` printed `here 1,2 there` through the identical path — the spec's own §2.3 already said each hole "must be valid as a `+` operand with `str`", and nothing was checking it. A `css` block's mixed value is built to that same shape (`css::build_value`), so `padding: calc({space(4)} + 2px);` put a `Length`'s two-field tuple *inside a declaration*, sheet fragment and all — `calc(var(--space-4),:root{--space-4:1rem} + 2px)`. **The rule is now stated rather than inferred**, because the natives have no impl to read it off: `+` on a native left operand admits `str + x` where `x` is a `str`, a numeric primitive, or a `bool`, and `T + T` for a numeric primitive `T`, and nothing else. The concatenation arm is deliberately NOT the trait's `B = Self`, and it is the one place the asymmetry is load-bearing: an i-string hole is this expression, and std's own `impl i32 with Display` is `i"{self}"`, which is `"" + self` — a strict `B = Self` would have refused the language's own rendering primitive. What the arm demands instead is that the operand's host value already *be* its rendering, which the numbers, `bool` and `str` satisfy and nothing else does. The steer names the one fix that works — `to_string()`, with an `impl … with Display` if the type has none — and deliberately does **not** offer "or interpolate it", because the i-string is this same concatenation and would send the reader back into the same garbage. Three more refusals fall out of the same rule and each gets its own words. The MIRROR shape, `count + "!"`, used to type as `i32` while producing the string `1!`; the numeric steer ("suffix the literal") would misread the author there, so it says what is actually true — only a `str` LEFT operand concatenates, because the expression takes its type from the left. Differently-typed numeric operands (`ratio + count` at `f64` and `i32`) now refuse under `+` exactly as they have always refused under `<`, an unsuffixed literal still adapting to its peer. And `bool` and backed enums, which are native for `==`/`<` without being numbers, have no `Add` at all: `true + true` would have added the lowering and typed the `2` as a `bool`, and two backings sum to something that is rarely a variant. A backed enum is refused on the concatenation arm too, and that is a judgement rather than a consequence — `Size::Small` lowers to `"sm"` and *would* have concatenated as one, which reads as a display form the program chose when nothing chose it. **The family marker is `miscompile` on §7.2's own definition** — "wrong code emitted, or a program admitted that it must refuse" — and this is both halves at once: the accepted program rendered a runtime tuple into user-facing text. The numeric arm alone would be a `breaking` entry (`f64 + i32` computes a correct answer today), but it is not a separable change: it is the same `B = Self` sentence, it cost the estate nothing, and the entry's claim is the miscompile. **Scope, stated because the neighbours look identical**: this is `+`'s rule, not the arithmetic family's. `f64 * i32` and `str - str` still skip the check, and closing theirs refuses code that computes correct answers today — a breaking numeric-strictness change with a migration of its own (`as_f64()`), argued separately rather than smuggled in behind a miscompile fix. (`satisfies_trait_bound` solves the same problem by reconciling subject-first; this site could not simply follow it, because swapping the operands there would also change which impls match a bare-trait receiver.) **The refusal that remains is better than the one that went.** With the caller's parameter genuinely unbounded the call is still refused — the check did not go vacuous, it now reaches the right parameter — and the message names the parameter the author has to go and edit rather than the impl's, which through std used to surface as a bound missing from a `U` appearing nowhere in the program. **The three that waited widened together**, keeping their generic-parameter ORDER, because a split build's emitter rebinds the gate call's type arguments from `swap` onto `swap_split` and `chunk_preload` by position (`transformer.rs::rebind_by_position`); the process twin's `swap` moved in lockstep, as A33's eight did. Emission moved once and in the good direction: `swap`'s widened binder puts its body under the enclosing monomorphization's memo key, so a duplicate `Signal::get` instance merges and the split fixture's eager bundle emits 104 functions where it emitted 105 — the same program, one declaration smaller, every other artifact byte-identical and the chunk files and manifest untouched. Twelve pins. The `#[ignore]`d exhibit A33 left behind is un-ignored; four more edge cases join it, each proven red first by re-planting the defect — the caller's member reaching the callee through the bound, two bare-parameter bounds over an impl that writes its binders in the other order, the bound surviving two generic bodies of re-wrapping, and the non-vacuity pin that must still refuse; the constructed-argument control stays green either way. Four compile pins drive the widened signatures with a user `Source` that is deliberately not a `Signal`, one running pin shows the widened `swap` still SUBSCRIBES and still disposes the subtree it replaces (a `swap` that read once would type, build and pass every compile pin), and a concrete-`Signal` control holds the existing call sites. **A trait may now declare associated functions — a `fun` with no `self`, with a default body — and `Trait::func(..)` calls that body.** A trait's members were all methods: something with a receiver, reached through one. That left the CONSTRUCTOR out. A type whose canonical construction belongs to a capability rather than to one struct — `Signal::new(value)`, where `Signal` is the capability and `SignalCell` the canonical cell — had nowhere to put it, and `Trait::static()` did not resolve at all, with or without a body on the declaration (the state B83 probed and recorded rather than built). It resolves now, and to a ruled answer: `Trait::func(..)` is THE TRAIT'S OWN default body, always — never an impl's override, which is reached through the implementing type's own path, `Type::func(..)`. That is not an arbitrary tie-break. A `self` method's `Trait::method(receiver)` form exists to name the trait a RECEIVER dispatches through; an associated function has no receiver, so there is nothing to select between, and the two spellings name two bodies rather than one dispatch. The trait's own generic parameters bind from the call like any generic function's (`Signal::new(7)` binds `T = i32`), and a supertrait's associated function is reachable through the sub-trait, as its methods are. Two refusals ship with it, from day one rather than as a later tightening: `Trait::func(..)` for a declaration with NO default body names a per-impl requirement with nothing behind it — the shape that used to reach the transformer's "please report this program" guard — and is refused naming both spellings; and `Type::func(..)` where the impl declares no such member is refused with the trait's spelling named, because a body with no receiver is not inherited onto a type's path the way a method's is. `spec/types.md` §5.5 states all of it.

**A trait in a `let` binding's annotation is now a checked CONSTRAINT on the binding's inferred type — not an error, and not the binding's type.** `let count: Signal<i32> = SignalCell::new(1)` is the shape: `count`'s type is `SignalCell<i32>`, what its initializer infers, exactly as if nothing had been written — and the annotation asserts that whatever the initializer produces implements `Signal<i32>`, failing at the annotation when it does not. This is the bounded-generic rule in binding position, checked wide and kept narrow: reading `count`'s members reaches `SignalCell`'s own, fields included; a reassignment must still be a `SignalCell<i32>`; nothing is boxed, widened or erased. The refusal it replaces at this one position is NARROWED, not repealed — a parameter, a return type, a struct field and every nested spelling (`&Display`, `List<Display>`) still refuse, which is what keeps a heterogeneous container impossible. The holes that refusal was built to shut stay shut, by the semantics rather than by the ban; the destructor case is the clearest, since `let handle: Named = Handle { .. }` once compiled, ran, and silently never dropped the handle, and today it compiles AND drops it, because the binding is a `Handle`. The `if` case needed no rule of its own: the arms unify first, and the constraint meets the ONE type that unification produced, so two arms of different concrete types are refused at the arms as an ordinary mismatch even when both implement the trait — there is no widening for them to meet in. The reading is universal, for every trait name in the position, std's included.

**`impl type T with Trait<T>` is a real blanket impl now: it dispatches through a bound, and any constructor-headed impl outranks it wherever both match.** The form parsed, analyzed and compiled cleanly for as long as nothing called through it; the first dispatch died with an internal error asking the author to report their own program — "a call resolved to `MaybeSignal`'s requirement `bind`, which has no body". The cause was a divergence rather than a missing feature. The analyzer already resolves a blanket beside a specific impl by SPECIFICITY (B73's R3): `"x".show()` reaching `impl type T with Show` has worked for releases. But a call through a BOUND — `fun badge<V: MaybeSignal<str>>(label: V)` — cannot be resolved there at all, because the receiver is a type parameter until monomorphization binds it, so the transformer re-asks the question at emission — and it re-asked with a nominal head comparison that could not see a generic subject at all and ranked nothing. A blanket was therefore invisible to every bounded call, and, less loudly, a pair the analyzer DID rank was answered here in declaration order: `impl Box<type T: Marker>` beside `impl Box<type T>` ran the marked body at a direct call and the plain body at a bounded one, in one program, silently. Both are gone, because the two sides now ask one shared question (`crates/vilan-core/src/impl_select.rs`, following `dispatch_refine`'s precedent of a shared module owning a resolution its consumers merely ask), in three tiers the spec now states: **applicability** — the impl's subject PATTERN matches the concrete type, its binders read as holes and the type as rigid, and every binder's bound holds there; **instantiation** — where the caller knows which instantiation it wants, and a bound-directed call always does, an impl is kept only if the arguments it provides FOR THIS RECEIVER are those arguments; **specificity** — the impl whose subject the others match and which matches none of theirs wins, then, for subjects of equal shape, the one whose binders carry the stronger bounds. A blanket is simply the least specific tier, which is why nothing needed inventing: it is the order B73 already ruled, applied where it had never been asked. The pay-off is `MaybeSignal<T>` whole — one trait, one blanket static impl, one generic `Signal` impl, and a component parameter that takes `badge("static")` and `badge(signal)` with no call-site ceremony, static dispatch, and the signal leg reacting to a later `set`. It also keeps a case a negative bound would have deleted: under a `MaybeSignal<Signal<str>>` bound a bare `Signal<str>` is a legitimate STATIC value through the blanket, while the same value under a `MaybeSignal<str>` bound is the reactive source through the `Signal` impl — the instantiation is decided before specificity is consulted, so both readings of one type live in one program. That is the recorded argument for ruling `impl type T: (not Signal)` OUT of the grammar and not merely deferring it: the two impls provably never overlap at one bound (`T = Signal<T>` has no finite solution), so nothing needed excluding, and a negative bound would have inverted the rule that adding an implementation is additive — implementing a trait for your type would newly EXCLUDE it from every `not`-bound in the ecosystem, making an impl addition a breaking change. **And the accept-then-ICE is closed as a class, not as an instance.** Every call through a bound now reaches one implementation's member, or the trait's default where the winning impl declares none, or the program is refused before it runs. Two impls with the same subject were already refused at the second declaration — so a second blanket for one trait never reaches a call site — and two the order genuinely cannot rank (`impl type T: Alpha` beside `impl type U: Beta`, met by a type that is both) were already reported at a direct call but reached the internal error through a bound; they are now reported at the call that made the binding, naming both subjects and the fix, in the same words the direct spelling uses. Ten pins, each proven red first by re-planting the exact defect it removes — blindness to a generic subject (seven go red, with the original internal error), the ranking itself (four), and the bound-side refusal (one) — plus a corpus program holding the whole recipe. Const evaluation reaches trait dispatch, so it reaches the blanket, and is pinned to select the same body a runtime call does at both tiers. No corpus golden moves. **A package now declares its own ambient scope: `print`, `Option`/`Some`/`None` and `Result`/`Ok`/`Err` are in scope with no import, `prelude = "std::web"` swaps in an application set, and the whole thing is the weakest binding in the language.** The argument is one probe. `list.get(1)` hands you an `Option` — a lang item, manufactured by a construct you wrote without naming a type — and the compiler then refused to let you take it apart, because you had not imported names you never wrote. `?.` has the same shape. A language that can *manufacture* a value at a use site should be able to *name* it there, and that is what closes here. This is not a new mechanism: the spec's §4.7 already made the primitives and `List` ambient, `macros.rs` already made every std macro ambient with the shadowing rule written into its own doc comment, and `world_prelude_nodes` already made ten `meta` types ambient in every macro body — ordinary std values and types were the one namespace left out of a pattern the language applies three times. **std ships TWO preludes**, which is the census's own finding turned into the design rather than an observation about it: `print` is not the most-imported name in real vilan code, `Signal` is (21 of 42 application files against `print`'s 15), and nine of the top sixteen application names are the style/UI cluster — so no single fixed set serves both a test corpus and an app. The base set is seven names, each admitted by a rule and not by rank: universal (base layer, every target), language-level, unambiguous, and top-of-census in more than one corpus. The web set adds `Signal`, `view` and `View` as members and `style` and `ui` as **modules**. **Ambient module names are the design's real addition.** A member entry costs one ambient name and buys one; a module entry costs one and buys a namespace — sixteen style enums behind `style::`, for the price of one qualifying segment. It also cannot collide, which is how the census's one self-collision dissolves rather than being adjudicated: `std::display::Display` (the `to_string` trait) and `std::style::Display` (the CSS enum) both exist in the base layer and could not both be bare, so bare `Display` is the trait's alone and the CSS one is `style::Display`. **The enum never renames and nothing in the estate moves.** No new precedence rule was needed for any of it — `std::style::style` is a function whose name equals its module's and the estate calls it bare 60 times, and every one of those files carries `import std::style::style;`, which is an explicit import and therefore outranks the ambient module. The other half of that is pinned too: a file which imports the function no longer reaches the module, so `style::Display` stops resolving *there* — one name, one binding, the ordinary rule rather than anything the prelude adds. **The key is `prelude`, on `[package]` and `[library]` alike**, because std — which must declare `prelude = false` — is a `[library]`. Its value grammar is one rule: a module path, or `false`. `"std::prelude"` and `"std::web"` are not set names the compiler knows, they are real modules in std whose exports ARE the ambient names, written in vilan in the same mechanism a user's custom prelude uses — so there is no built-in list in Rust to drift out of sync with the docs, and a reader can open the file. Omitting the key means the base set, which makes it additive to every existing manifest with no edit. A custom prelude REPLACES rather than extends, and extension is spelled by re-export — one mechanism, no merge rules, and std does not get a mechanism its users lack (`web.vl` re-states the base seven rather than deriving them). `prelude = "std"` is refused by name, because after the alias sweep std's root exports nothing and accepting it would mean a silently EMPTY prelude; `prelude = true` is refused because an untagged string-or-bool accepts it syntactically and the affirmative is spelled by omitting the key. **Per package, never inherited** — not from a consumer to a dependency, not from a dependency to a consumer, not from a `[project]` root (which has no such key), not per platform layer. Two packages that disagree about what `Signal` means both keep compiling in one build, which is the property that makes this safe to ship before a registry rather than after. **The implementation is a resolution scope, and that was the one thing this feature could get catastrophically wrong.** In this compiler an explicit import BEATS a same-file declaration, silently — `world_prelude_nodes` says so in its own doc comment ("imports overwrite hoisted function bindings, so the exclusion is how the prelude yields") and filters every name a macro world declares out of its synthesized text for exactly that reason. So a value prelude spliced in as file-head imports would have *replaced* `vilan/test/match-patterns.vl`'s own `enum Signal` and `vilan/test/default.vl`'s own `trait Default` with std's — turning two non-events into miscompiles. Instead the prelude's bindings are copied into a scope with `or_insert`, in the one window where both halves hold: after the import fixpoint (so a prelude module's re-exports point at real definitions, and an explicit import is already there to yield to) and before any name resolves (so nothing has memoized a lookup the prelude would change). Items overwrite it during the walk, imports overwrite it just before — the weakest scope by ORDERING rather than by a precedence table. `record_reference` is deliberately not called for a prelude binding, or Organize Imports would start pruning real imports because "the prelude already references them". The pin that holds this is not the obvious one: the entry file is seeded before its walk, so ordering alone protects it and every entry-file shadowing pin stayed green with the fix removed — it took a *module* file whose own `print` has a disagreeing signature to turn the miscompile into something an analyze-only harness can see. **Tooling was half the feature and mostly fell out.** Completion and go-to-definition needed no code at all: prelude names are ordinary entries in `name_to_id_map`, so `scope_completions` offers them undecorated, `auto_import_completions` stops offering them by its existing "already in scope" filter, and go-to-definition lands in the std source exactly as an import does. Organize Imports gained one line and now **strips an import the prelude covers**, matched on the DEFINITION rather than the name — so `import std::io::print;` goes and `import my_lib::print;` beside an ambient `std::print` stays. `vilan fmt` is untouched, by its own standing rule that pruning is the editor's job. The unresolved-name diagnostic gained the arm the two-set design makes necessary: a base-prelude package reaching for `Signal` is told `` `Signal` is in the prelude of the web set — set `prelude = "std::web"` `` rather than being steered toward an import, and that index is read out of `std/src/web.vl` itself on a cold path so the steer can never drift from the module. The base seven are excluded from that arm, since both sets carry them. One defect was found and fixed by a pin rather than by review: the base-cache key did not include the prelude, so a stored `std::web` world was served to a base-prelude program — the key and the workspace fingerprint now carry the entry package's and every dependency's. Twenty-nine pins across the manifest, resolution and editor surfaces, the shadowing ones proven non-vacuous by planting the bug they remove. (backlog B156; proposal/prelude.md; docs `spec/names.md` §4.4/§4.7, `spec/appendix.md` §A.4, `tour/hello-vilan.md`, `tour/projects.md`, `appendix/errors.md`, `appendix/editor.md`, `appendix/glossary.md`)

The exhibit is kolt's `StorageSignal` — a signal with a place to hang persistence, `set` kept off the trait — which could subscribe, derive, and cross the wire, and could not fill an attribute. The widening is a bound on an ordinary generic parameter (`fun bind_attr<S: Source<str>>(self, name: str, source: S): View`), the spelling `expose<T: Wire, S: Source<T>>` has shipped with since the RPC arc, and it moves in **lockstep across both `ui` twins**: the same component source is compiled through the browser layer and the SSR twin, so a widening on one side alone would have made every custom-source component client-only. The gap is narrow and now pinned from both sides: `S: Source<List<T>>`, the bound's argument CONSTRUCTED over the caller's `T`, resolves fine — that is `bind_each`, and it shipped — while the bare-parameter twin is `#[ignore]`d until the solver closes it, with the note that the three signatures then widen together *in their generic-parameter order*, because the split gate rebinds their type arguments by position. **`attr` and `child`** dispatch through the `AttrValue` and `Slot` traits, whose reactive arms are `impl Signal<str> with …`; widening a trait ARM is a blanket impl and not a bound, so `<div href(source)>` still wants a signal and the element-syntax desugar — which builds `.attr(name, value)`, never `.bind_attr` — is byte-for-byte where it was. **`combine`** only reads too, and is held by the grammar rather than the semantics: its mapped-tuple parameter would need each element to be *some* `Source<U>`, a per-element existential the form has no place to bind (`(U in T: Source<U>)` is refused because vilan has no trait objects, and a single `<S: Source<U>>` names one type where the tuple needs a different one per element). **The negative this was checked against is emission, and it is worth reporting precisely, because "byte-identical" turned out to be the wrong claim by a hair in the right direction.** A generic function is monomorphized, so the widened binders moved out of the plain-named emissions into the generated-name pool — which renames them and shifts every generated name after them. Nothing else moved: a checker that reduces two bundles to a canonical form (duplicate declarations unified, generated names renumbered by a canonical traversal, statements compared in order and declarations as a set) reports every affected artifact as the SAME PROGRAM up to naming — one corpus golden, four split goldens, and six example bundles — and the process corpus program's stdout is byte-identical before and after. Exactly one corpus program's golden moves, out of a hundred, and every `.css` asset is untouched. The bundles are also *smaller*: the widening puts the nested `effect`/`observe` instances under the enclosing monomorphization's memo key, so two instances that used to be emitted twice now hit it once — 285 bytes off the reactive-ui example, 274 off the walkthrough client. **`window` is a listen target now, `listen` hands back the `Subscription` that unhooks a DOM listener, and an `Event` will tell you where the pointer is.** `std::dom` bound element listeners and nothing else, so anything needing a window-level event hand-rolled its own `external fun` — `std::router` had one for `popstate`, the website had a third, and a `message`, `resize` or `storage` event was a thing std simply could not deliver. The live exhibit is a sidebar-resize drag in the dogfood app, which had to hand-roll all three of the gaps at once, and a drag is the canonical case for why element-local `on_event` cannot carry it: the pointer leaves the element the moment the drag starts moving. **`window()` is a handle, not a suffix.** The obvious sketch was an `on_window` free function, but taken as written it grows a parallel vocabulary — `on_window`, `on_window_event`, then a `listen_window` beside `listen` — where the only difference from the element forms is *which object* is being listened to. That is a target, and vilan already spells targets as handles, so `external struct Window` carries exactly the three verbs `Element` does and the surface never has to answer why one of them is spelled differently. It also gives the next asks somewhere to land: window `resize` plus `innerWidth`/`devicePixelRatio` is what the canvas proposal's DPR path wants, and those are accessors on a handle rather than three more free functions. Nothing beyond the listen verbs ships, deliberately — an accessor no delivered event has a caller for is dead surface, which is the trap this gap was filed with. Acquiring the handle costs one runtime helper, because a global property has no function form; that is the same reason `location.pathname` has needed one since routing shipped. **Removal is a `Subscription`, and it is a new verb.** `on_event`'s signature does not change: it is the chaining form, it is what `on:click` lowers to, and it is fire-and-forget by design, because an element listener dies with its element and that is usually the whole answer. Nothing about the window ever dies, so removal has to be expressible — and the vocabulary already existed, since `Source::sub` has always handed back a handle whose `dispose` unhooks it. So `listen` is that shape on both targets, `[must_use]` exactly as `sub` is, over a new `Subscription::teardown(release)` constructor: a subscription over no signal, whose `dispose` runs the hook once and nothing else, riding the same one-shot release cell a remote source's lease decrement already uses — which is what makes disposing twice safe, and a drag disposes twice by construction. Two tiers, one rule: `on`/`on_event` are fire-and-forget, `listen` is the removable form. Making `on_event` return the handle instead would have turned every existing zero-ceremony call site into a `must_use` warning, and `View.on_event`'s chaining return has no room for it at all. Ownership stays the caller's, as `sub`'s is and unlike `effect`'s, and that asymmetry is the point: a drag arms two window listeners per `pointerdown`, so auto-registering with the ambient owner would push two dead cleanups onto the enclosing boundary on every drag, forever — the leak the owner model exists to prevent, entered from the other end. `get_owner().take(window().listen(…))` is the one-line idiom, and an owner-tied twin is recorded rather than built. The whole design rests on one host fact worth stating: `removeEventListener` is **identity-matched**, so `listen`'s teardown has to hand back the same closure the host was given, and that was probed against the real emitter before anything was built — a closure bound once, passed to a std function, used as an argument and captured by the returned teardown, emits as a single JS `const` referenced twice. **`retains` marks registration only.** `addEventListener` retains, because the host stores a vilan closure and calls it later; `removeEventListener` keeps nothing past the call and is left unmarked. The exhibit's hand-roll marks both, which is the over-marking a golden caught on `appendChild` during the retention audit, and this surface deliberately does not inherit it. **The coordinates are named for the pointer, not for the DOM's coordinate space.** `clientX`'s "client" means *viewport* for reasons that are pure history, and the mechanical transliteration would teach that history to every reader forever, so the accessors are `pointer_x`/`pointer_y`. The family objection is real and answered: if `pageX` lands later its name is `page_x` — where the pointer is *in the document* — which is self-explanatory on its own terms rather than as the second row of a coordinate-space table, and two good names beat four uniform ones. Page, offset and screen variants wait for a caller, as does `setPointerCapture`, which is worth designing alongside and is not a substitute: it retargets a drag's events to the capturing element, but `resize`, `popstate`, `storage` and `message` still have no element to hang on, and capture is its own surface with its own disposal question. `std::router` folds onto the new verbs and deletes its own hand-roll, which is one of the three the gap was filed over and the only one that lives in std; the split fixture's golden moves by exactly the two lines that says — the helper, and `window.addEventListener` becoming `__dom_window().addEventListener` — with every chunk byte-identical. Its `popstate` handler keeps its explicit `turn` wrapper, because the window verbs are raw exactly as `element.on` is. The acceptance test is that the exhibit rewrites onto std surface **alone** — its `impl Event` block and both window externs deleted, its `mut dispose` closure becoming two `Subscription::dispose` calls — and that rewrite is pinned end to end under a DOM stub whose `removeEventListener` matches by identity like a browser's, so a teardown that reconstructs its handler removes nothing and every negative assertion fails. Four browser-runtime gates, a fifth over the markings themselves (a declaration gate, because retention is not observable through a listener at all — a closure cannot capture a resource, so no drop order could move), two compile pins for the types, and the formatter and analyzer retention pins extended with the marked/unmarked pair this surface is declared in. Four plants, each watched red and restored: coordinates crossed, listener identity broken, the flag dropped from a registration, and the flag added to a removal — the last being exactly the exhibit's own over-marking. (backlog A27, kolt.local 037; proposal/router.md §5; docs `std/browser.md`, `std/reactive.md`, `guide/ui.md`)
