<!-- family: feature -->
**A file can now be read a chunk at a time — `Reader::of(File::open(p))` and `next(size)` — and every open mode has a scoped form whose close is awaited, which is the one that matters when you are writing.** These are the two halves the filesystem arc had left: the owner's vision named *"files can be opened, read incrementally"*, and until now the incremental half did not exist — `read_bytes` materializes the whole file, so a 2 GiB log had to be fully resident, and the only chunked reader in std read HTTP bodies. `Reader` is that loop, and the interesting thing about it is what it is built ON. Node's `FileHandle.read` keeps an implicit position when you pass none, and binding *that* as the primitive would have put mutable state under a loan where the move checker cannot see it: two loans of one handle, each reading, would silently move each other's position. So the handle stayed positional and stateless when it shipped, and the cursor arrives now as an ordinary vilan value layered on top — `next(size)` reads at a position this program owns and advances it, `position()` reads it, `seek()` moves it. A cursor can always be built from a position; a position can never be recovered from a cursor. The payoff is visible in one program: `reader.file.read_at(buffer, p)` reads anywhere in the file **without disturbing the cursor**, so a header probe and a sequential scan share one open file — the property the host's hidden position would have destroyed. A chunk is shorter near the end and **empty at end of file**, which is the loop's terminating condition and the one trap the docs state twice: stop on empty, not on short. That is `std::fetch`'s `BodyReader` loop with the mechanism swapped rather than copied — `BodyReader` answers `{ done, value }` because a `ReadableStream` may legitimately yield an empty chunk mid-stream, so emptiness cannot carry the end there; a file's read cannot, so a second field would be one the caller could always derive. Each `next` allocates and hands back a slice of exactly what was read, so a chunk is never a window on memory the next call overwrites — the reuse is what `read_at` is for. `Reader` declares no teardown of its own and needs none: it is a resource **by containment**, which buys the whole R-rule surface unmodified — it moves, no closure captures it, no `List` holds it, and dropping it closes the file it owns. One shape is deliberately absent and the reason is recorded rather than assumed: the position is a `Shared<i53>` rather than a plain field behind `&mut self` because the language *forces* it — `next` awaits the read, and an async function cannot take a `&mut` parameter, since the view would be held across the suspension. The sketch had guessed right for a reason it did not know it had. **The other half is the scoped form, which shipped read-only and was therefore available in exactly the mode where it matters least.** `with_file(path, |file| …)` awaits its close, so a close failure is a failure of the call — but a close failure is information almost exclusively on a *writing* handle: a write that resolved was handed to the OS, and the OS is entitled to report its failure at `close(2)` rather than at the write (a full disk, a quota, a network filesystem that defers), which is why POSIX warns that ignoring close's return can lose data you believe you wrote. Under the destructor that error goes to stderr and your program carries on. So there is now one scoped form per constructor — `with_file_create`, `with_file_create_new`, `with_file_append`, `with_file_modify` — the suffix naming the constructor it opens with, for the same reason five named constructors replaced node's flags string in the first place: a mode is a name here too, and threading an untyped one through `with_file` would have reintroduced what the constructors exist to prevent. All five delegate to **one** implementation, so the close-before-return ordering that IS the idiom is written once and a form added later cannot quietly drop the await; the emitted shape is `try { body; await close; return } finally { drop }`, so a throwing body still releases the handle through the safety net, and what it wrote before throwing is on disk. Nothing was needed from the compiler for any of it. Fifteen pins, against real files and against the emitted bytes: the chunk loop over a size that divides neither the file nor any prefix of it, a file shorter than one chunk, an empty one, the interleave, R1/R5/R9/R10 and the coloring refusal on the new type, the four writing modes proved by what each does to a file that already exists, the exclusive claim refusing an occupied path without touching it, the throwing body, and the descriptors coming back — plus a corpus program holding the emitted shape. The behavioural ones are plant-proven: a cursor that advances wrong reddens the three reading pins, a shared form with its `await` removed reddens all five scoped forms, a close taught to swallow reddens the seam pin, and the wrong constructor behind `with_file_append` reddens the mode pin. One honesty note the fd instrument earned: the descriptor counts prove release, not ORDERING (measured with the await removed, they still read zero, because the counting call itself awaits), so the ordering stays pinned on the emitted bytes, where the await is. (kolt.local 031 S5; proposal/filesystem.md §3.4's build note and §5.3; docs `std/process.md`, `guide/persistence.md`)

<!-- family: feature -->
**A static estate is now three lines of vilan: `asset::read_dir_all` enumerates it, `asset::bundle_as` places each file at a url its path does not spell, and `asset::digest` mints the content-hashed one.** `bundle`'s rule has always been *the path IS the url*, which is what makes it impossible for two files to claim one output name and impossible for anything to be renamed behind your back — and also what forced a path-pinned name (`/favicon.ico`, `/robots.txt`) to sit at the package root, and what made an estate a hand-written list of calls: the dogfood app spells twelve of them. Both costs come off without giving the rule up, because the rename is spelled AT THE CALL. `bundle_as(path, url)` is `bundle` in every other respect — same registry, same copy, same tracked build input, same `chunks.json` row, same `serve_build` route, same `--watch` recopy — so `bundle(path)` shares one implementation with it rather than sitting beside a second one, and is exactly `bundle_as(path, i"/{path}")` for any path free of `.` segments — the one divergence is that `bundle` skips a `./` in the SOURCE spelling when minting the name, where the target grammar refuses one, because the target IS the url. What the target must be is stated and refused with the fix named: it starts at the site root, it is `/`-separated on every host (a backslash is refused, never translated — kolt.local 017's ruling, since the target becomes an output name, a manifest row and a golden), and every segment must be a name, so an empty segment, a `.` or a `..` is a compile error. The reason is that the value returned IS the url the copy answers on: `/a/./b` is a different url to a browser while being the same file on disk, so a target that is not already the url it promises would be a lie the caller cannot see. The target passes the build-owned-name fence `bundle`'s does by reaching the same check — `<leg>.js`, `<leg>.css`, `<leg>.chunks.json` and the route-chunk namespace, for every leg, because `dist/` is one directory — and gains the one refusal the identity rule used to give for free: two files bundling to one url is a compile error naming BOTH sources, because a collision is a statement about a pair and naming half of it sends the reader to the wrong call. That check is per compile, so the same collision across two legs of a workspace — separate compiles into one `dist/`, where the second copy would silently have won — is caught at the copy instead, naming both again. Enumeration is the other half. `read_dir(path)` lists a directory's immediate files by bare name and `read_dir_all(path)` every file beneath it by a path relative to it, both `/`-separated on every host, with two deliberate divergences from `std::fs`'s versions and each forced by what a const result is. Entries are **byte-sorted, always**: a const result is compiled INTO the output, so host iteration order would make one source tree produce two builds, and determinism here is the property the whole const feature rests on rather than a nicety. And only **files** are listed: nothing in this channel consumes a directory — `read`, `bundle`, `bundle_as` and `digest` all take a file — and there is no compile-time `stat`, so a directory entry would be one the program could neither act on nor filter out, and the estate loop would break on the first nested folder. A symlink is classified by what it points at, so a link to a file is bundleable; the walk never follows one into a directory, so it cannot loop. The listed directory is a **tracked build input** on `read`'s doctrine, recorded per directory walked, which is what makes it compose: a file appearing or disappearing anywhere in a listed tree moves exactly one recorded key, so both directions invalidate — you drop a file into `static/` and the next build ships it with no source edit at all. The re-hash the per-leg watch skip performs learned one arm to match (a recorded directory re-hashes as its listing, not as a file's text), so an unchanged tree can still be skipped instead of disqualifying the leg by failing to read. `digest(path)` is the last piece: the file's sha-256 as lowercase hex, 64 characters, over the BYTES — a fingerprint of a font or a `.png` must be a fingerprint of the file and not of a decoding — tracked exactly as `read`'s input is, so an edit re-mints the url. It closes a recorded exhibit: the dogfood app's fingerprints were minted OUT OF BAND because `asset::read` is text-only and no digest was in const reach, and `bundle_as(p, i"/static/{stem}.{digest(p).substring(0, 8)}.{ext}")` is now spellable in the language that ships the file. Fuel prices are argued rather than picked: a listing charges 1,024 per entry (the directory itself counting as one, so an empty listing is not free), a quarter of `bundle`'s 4,096, because an entry costs the walk a listing row and the stat that classifies it where `bundle`'s charge prices a whole-file read on top of both (the count is the files returned plus one for the listed directory; the directories a recursive walk descends are not individually charged, a recorded open question) — which leaves the dominant per-entry cost to what the program does with the entry and keeps the binding fence on the work that copies bytes; and `digest` charges one per eight bytes, an eighth of `read`'s rate, because `read`'s rate prices the arbitrary-length `str` the program then computes over while a digest is 64 characters whatever the file weighs, so the charge bounds how much a build hashes rather than how large a value it holds. Nothing about plain `bundle` moved: the corpus goldens are byte-identical, which is the negative this slice is checked against. Why the const channel and not a manifest key or a build hook is the owner's own argument, recorded in the paper: a toml key walls off programmatic logic, and a hook exchanges no values with the program, has no manifest contract to serve through, needs the whole freshness machinery to approximate tracked inputs, and is first-party-only arbitrary execution where the const channel is fenced interpretation a library can safely ride. Fifteen behaviour pins in the inference suite and eight end-to-end in the CLI (the served target, the sorted listing, the tracked directory in both directions, the fingerprint against sha-256's canonical `abc` vector, every url-shape refusal, both collisions, the owned-name fence), plus a corpus program holding the whole recipe. (kolt.local 035; proposal/const-eval.md §3.1; docs `std/misc.md`, `spec/const.md`, `std/process.md`)

<!-- family: feature -->
**`db.migrate(steps)` carries a schema forward — the thing `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` cannot do.** An idempotent schema *ensure* is right exactly until the first schema *change*: add a `description` column and the clause is a no-op, so the deployed database keeps the old shape while the code querying it has the new one, and the choices left are hand-run SQL against production or deleting the file. `std::db` is batteries-included by doctrine and had no third answer. It does now: `Migration { name, sql }` steps applied **in list order**, the applied ones recorded in a `vilan_migrations` table the migrator owns (`name TEXT PRIMARY KEY`, `applied_at_ms INTEGER`), and the names it applied returned — so a boot log reads `applied 2 migrations` the first time and `applied 0` on every restart after. The design is one invariant and everything else follows from it: **a step is recorded if and only if its SQL committed**, because the record insert rides *inside* the step's own transaction. There is no window where the schema moved and the record did not, so a process killed mid-migration leaves a database whose recorded set exactly describes its schema and the next boot resumes there. The transaction is per STEP and deliberately not per run — all-or-nothing sounds safer and is worse, because a failure in the fifth step would then re-run the first four, and a first step that is not re-runnable (a `DROP`, a backfill that doubles) could never recover. Three conditions stop the boot loudly, all of them *before* a single statement is applied, so a database this refuses is a database it did not touch: a step whose SQL FAILS, named alongside SQLite's own diagnosis (`migration '002-bad' failed and was not applied: no such table: taks`) with nothing recorded for it and its half-applied DDL rolled back; a RECORDED step absent from the list, which is a rolled-back deploy about to run its old queries against a newer schema; and an UNAPPLIED step ordered before an applied one, which is two branches merged into an order no fresh database could ever reproduce. Names must be unique and non-empty, but they need NOT sort in order — the list's order is the authority, and the second refusal already catches every misordering an ascending-name rule would, on a fresh database vacuously and on one with history exactly. Deliberately absent from v1 and stated as such: down-migrations (roll forward with a new step, which is what production does anyway), locking beyond SQLite's own file lock, and diff-GENERATION, which wants the declared-schema question answered first. One documented requirement the surface does not check: a step must never contain `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`/`ROLLBACK` of its own — that commits the migrator's transaction out from under it, landing the schema change permanently while its record is still unwritten, the one way to break the invariant — and it is not checked because substring-scanning SQL is not parsing SQL (a comment, a string literal and a `commit_sha` column would all be refused wrongly, and a line break evades the scan). How an app COLLECTS its steps stays the const channel's business: `const asset::read("migrations/001-create-task.sql")` compiles each file's text into the bundle, so the deployed app is still `dist/` and every migration edit is a tracked build input. Five pins drive real SQLite files in per-test temp directories across two boots each, every one proven red first. (proposal/db-migrations.md, kolt.local 036; docs `guide/persistence.md` and `std/process.md`)

The name is the house one rather than a new coinage: `List::index_of(value)` already returns `Option<i32>`, and in this vocabulary `find` takes a PREDICATE, so `str::index_of(needle)` is the spelling that was missing rather than a second one. **Absence is `None`, never `-1`** — the whole reason this is not the host method renamed, and the same doctrine `substring` states: `-1` is an index nothing in the type system tells apart from a real one, and it would be reported one call later, by `substring`, about a number this call produced. The empty needle sits at each end, as it does in the host. Both live in `std::option` beside `strip_prefix`/`parse_i32`, so the always-loaded core `str` stays off the `option` chain. That last one is not a papercut for a generator: a CSS rule, a JS body or a JSON object writes braces on nearly every line. Pinned per case with the negatives beside them — `pub` still an ordinary identifier where it is one, the escaped brace still printing a brace, the misleading messages proven GONE rather than merely joined — and the std pair proven non-vacuous by planting the `-1` leak. **`Signal<T>` is a trait, so a signal can be your own — a clamping setter, a persisted cell, a debounced write.** `Source` reads (`get`/`sub`/`effect`) and `Signal` writes: `set` and `notify` are requirements, `set_with` a default of exactly the line std used to carry, and `new` a default-bodied associated function returning the canonical cell. A component bounded on `Signal<u32>` accepts the cell and accepts an implementation whose `set` clamps 1000 to 800 — after which the component, the owner and every observer read 800, because there is one value and the implementation decided it. The trait promises nothing about notification frequency; a cell that wants to skip an unchanged write says so in its own `set`. `update` is deliberately NOT on the trait: its value is in-place mutation with one notify, a generic default could only read-copy-mutate-write-back, and an implementation may want its own or none — so it stays inherent to `SignalCell` and general consumers are locked out of it. `bind_value` and its SSR twin bound on the trait, and the `Slot`/`AttrValue` arms element syntax dispatches through are now blankets over `Source<str>`, so `<p>{anything reactive}</p>` places and `<a href(anything reactive)>` tracks. std also gains `MaybeSignal<T>`, the static-or-reactive component parameter: one effect-shaped `bind`, a blanket for the static case and a `Source`-bounded blanket for the reactive one, chosen at the call with no runtime discrimination. **A module of a fullstack package is coloured by the entry that REACHES it, in the editor and in `vilan check <file>` alike — not by the manifest's default.** A `[entry.<name>]` package builds one leg per entry, each over the modules that leg loads, each under that leg's target; but a single file addressed by path took the `node` default, and the language server took its own imports' inference. Neither is what the build does, and the platform decides more than which functions may run: it selects `std`'s layer overlay, so it decides what the file's types ARE. Under the process overlay a browser module's `View` is `{ tag, attributes, children, text }`, `self.element` is a field that does not exist, and every browser-only module of a fullstack app was reported broken on correct code while `vilan build` was clean — the report this closes, against an app whose `default-entry` is its server. Reachability answers it: `platform_color::file_platforms` walks the loader's own `pkg::` import graph from each entry (`analyzer::package_modules_reachable_from`, the same `collect_module_refs` seeds and the same resolution the load loop uses), and a module reached by exactly one leg takes that leg's platform. Reached by SEVERAL, it takes each: a shared module is compiled once per leg and must type-check under every one of them, so `vilan check` on it reports the union its legs would and the editor publishes the union too, deduplicated to one squiggle per mistake — the mirror lie, passing a file the package check refuses, is now closed in the same place. Reached by NONE, the designated `default-entry` answers, which is the old behaviour kept where it is the only thing left to say. The two surfaces take one answer from one function: G20 had already unified them, on the manifest's default rather than on reachability. Found fixing it and fixed with it: file mode compiled every path it was handed as if it were the program, so `vilan check src/widget.vl` on a clean module answered "Cannot execute program without a main function" — a demand no module can meet, and the reason the fix could not be verified until it went. An ENTRY still gets the demand, because an entry without `main` is a build that cannot succeed.

**Clippy and `cargo audit` are gates now, which closes N21 — and getting there took 217 findings to zero, deleted two functions nothing called, and removed a test binary with no tests in it.** The `fmt` job shipped a release ago and the item's other two legs did not, so the tree had been accumulating lint findings with nothing to report them and rustc's own warnings with nothing to fail on. `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo audit --deny unsound` are jobs in `ci.yml` feeding the required `check`, and `rust-toolchain.toml` now pins `clippy` beside `rustfmt` — the clippy leg deliberately carries no `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN`, for the formatter's exact reason: the lint set widens every six weeks, and an unpinned gate that denies warnings goes red for a tree nobody edited, so a lint sweep belongs in the deliberate bump commit. The audit leg is the one that reverses that argument and says so in its comment: an advisory published against an unchanged `Cargo.lock` reds a commit nobody wrote, and it is wired to stop the line anyway, because a rustfmt default moving is a false alarm while a vulnerability in a dependency of a shipped compiler is a true finding that merely arrives on someone else's schedule. Its strictness is chosen rather than inherited — a vulnerability fails, and so does an `unsound` advisory, since a memory-safety defect is that class of problem whatever RustSec calls the row, while `unmaintained` and `yanked` stay warnings that are printed and read: neither is a defect, and an upstream maintainer stepping away must not block a PR that changed a comment. **180 of the 217 findings were fixed, not silenced.** The largest block by far is 102 nested `if`s that edition 2024 lets collapse into let-chains, which is why the analyzer, the transformer and `context.rs` lose a level of indentation in a lot of places; the machine-applicable ones were applied by `clippy --fix` and the result checked the one way that matters for a repository this commented — the multiset of comment lines the diff removes is byte-identical to the one it adds, so nothing was dropped, only reflowed. The rest of the machine-applicable set rode along with it — needless borrows and derefs, `bool::then` closures, a hand-written `Default` impl that is a derive, `map(..).flatten()`, a single-character `push_str` — and one of those is a small find in its own right: an `if !compiling_std {}` in the analyzer's std loader, empty since July, the residue of the `gate_library_imports` call the platform-coloring engine moved out of that function, sitting in the pipeline ever since with nothing to report it. The remainder was hand-fixed: `&PathBuf` and `&mut Vec` parameters that wanted slices, three `Default::default()`-then-assign blocks that are now struct literals, three `let`-`else`s that are `?`, two `loop`/`match`/`break`s that are `while let`, a `.then().unwrap_or()` that is an `if`, and a doc comment in `parsing.rs` whose 21-item chumsky statement order was a paragraph markdown read as a broken list and is now the list it always was. **The exceptions are collected in one place with one reason each** — the root `Cargo.toml`'s `[workspace.lints.clippy]`, which every crate opts into with `[lints] workspace = true`, and which each of the four entries earns by being a decision about the shape of this codebase rather than about one site: `too_many_arguments` (the compiler threads explicit context through its entry points; the tree already carried **22** per-site allows for this one threshold, and those 22 are deleted, because that was one decision written down 22 times), `type_complexity` (a return tuple in the compiler IS the documentation of what a phase yields — two more per-site allows go the same way), `only_used_in_recursion` (the recursive walkers are methods because they belong beside their siblings), and `large_enum_variant` (boxing a hot AST variant trades a memcpy nobody measured for a pointer chase in every match). Three findings are per-site judgments and keep their allow at the site with a `reason`, each recording something worth knowing: `platform_color.rs`'s `to_vec` ends a `self.graph` borrow before `walk` takes `&mut self` and does not compile without it, `interpreter.rs`'s `to_js_string` takes `&mut self` because `self` is the interpreter and the subject is the parameter, and `tests/support/boot.rs` reaps its child through a `try_wait` loop that `zombie_processes` cannot follow. Denying warnings also inherits rustc's, which is how the dead code surfaced: `Document::expr_references_definition` and `Document::use_in_entry_or_generated` — reported as pre-existing by three separate lanes across two orders, and called by nothing — are deleted; `Document::references`/`rename_edits` and `SessionTrace::total_requests`/`stat` are real API that only the pins drive (the server answers through the `_across` union), so they are `#[cfg(test)]` and no longer shipped in the binary; and `tests/parse_expr_fixtures.rs` moved to `tests/parse_expr_regression/fixtures.rs`, since cargo makes a test target out of every `tests/*.rs` and that one had been compiling as a binary containing no tests, whose entire output was four "never used" warnings against the arrays the file beside it consumes. The audit leg is green on arrival: zero vulnerabilities and zero informational advisories across 137 dependencies, so no version moved and `Cargo.lock` is untouched. Wiring both legs into `check` was caught by an existing pin doing exactly its job — `ci_ignored_pins.rs` asserts `check`'s needed jobs LINE BY LINE, so that a non-blocking leg cannot drift into the required status context and strand a PR — and its expected list is updated deliberately, with a note in the failure message, because two senses of "advisory" now meet in that file: the RustSec `audit` job blocks on purpose, while `ignored-pins.yml` is the advisory leg the pin exists to keep out. `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` gain the local ritual beside the `cargo fmt` rule, so the command a lane runs is the command CI runs. The appendix had no equivalent at all (F12): nothing checked that a curated message kept its entry, or that an entry still named something the compiler prints — five flagship messages had none, and six entries quoted sentences the compiler stopped printing. `crates/vilan-cli/tests/diagnostics_ledger.rs` closes both, over a committed index (`diagnostics-ledger.tsv`) that carries one line per ledger row, since the proposals repository the prose lives in is not present in a CI checkout. Three properties over the index: every row's key still appears in the tree, fixed-string, with Rust's string-literal line continuations normalized away first (the artifact that made the two previous mechanical re-keys hand-triaged work); every diagnostic the compiler builds at one of two enumerated anchors — `Error { .. msg: <literal> }` in the compiler crates, `errors.push(<literal>)` in `manifest.rs` — is described by some row's key; and the index is well formed, with each keyless or fragment-less row recorded by number and reason rather than skipped. Three more hold the appendix: every entry's quoted head still names a live message, every entry opens with one (a head that names a CONDITION instead is recorded), and every row the index marks `flagship` is quoted by some entry — so dropping an entry, or rowing a new flagship message without writing one, is red. The appendix now states in its own header what it is: a curated subset by three criteria, not a catalogue. What the gate deliberately does not check is written into its header beside what it does — no verdict, pin, span or anchor is verified, helper-built messages and std's runtime refusals are held by the key check alone rather than enumerated, and `Note` sites are skipped because a C3 note belongs in its primary's row. Regeneration is deliberately not automated: a new message is meant to cost its author a row and a verdict, and a `--fix` flag is how the record went stale in the first place. Both directions are plant-proven red (a reworded message, a new unrowed one, a reworded appendix head, a dropped entry).

**Spec §3's normative grammar is gated too, and the gate found four things wrong with it.** `grammar_sync.rs` has held the two syntax-HIGHLIGHTING grammars to the compiler's word tables for releases, and the anchors golden pins the book's headings, but nothing read the EBNF itself — which is how `extern-args` went three forms stale, and one form WRONG, across two releases with nothing red (N34, the smalls lane's finding). `crates/vilan-cli/tests/grammar_ebnf.rs` checks four things and says plainly in its header that it is not a parser-equivalence check: every `lexing::KEYWORDS` word is spelled as a terminal somewhere in the EBNF and every identifier-shaped terminal the EBNF quotes is a word the compiler knows (contextual words recorded with what each is); every `KNOWN_ATTRIBUTE_MARKERS` name appears, asserted on its own because that is the D15 rot site; the `extern-args` production offers exactly the form words `extern_binding_from_args` matches on, read from the parser's own source rather than from a second table, with `retains` in trailing position as the flag it is; and the grammar is internally closed — every rule a production names is one some production writes or a token class §2 declares, and every production is reached from another or is the start symbol. Bringing it green fixed four real gaps: `operator-expr` was named and never written, so `await` and `is` appeared nowhere in the normative grammar (only in §3.7's precedence table); `place` and `literal` were referenced with prose definitions alone; `struct-init` was written and reached by nothing, although §3.8's own prose makes it an operand; and the `if`/`for`/`match` productions said `secondary-expr` where §3.8 says those three positions parse `condition-expr`. Red-proven on all three axes: a form word the parser gains and the grammar does not, a keyword the grammar drops, a production naming a rule nobody writes.

<!-- family: tooling -->
**An empty subdirectory under a declared hook input woke a `--watch` round that then did nothing, because the watcher and the freshness stamp read the same directory differently.** The watcher inserts an entry per nested directory — N30's rule, which is why a declared directory *appearing* is visible at all — and the stamp's walk pushed files and symlinks only. So `mkdir icons/empty` produced `change detected, re-running` followed by `Fresh   gen`: a round that reliably does nothing. That is the safe failure direction, a spurious round rather than a missed one, and it is still a defect, because the two consumers of one declaration were reading it two ways and the freshness gate was answering about a tree the thing that woke it does not share. **The stamp learns directory rows, rather than the watcher unlearning its entries**, and the argument is N30's own: a directory appearing is a change that nothing about its (absent) files can express — which is precisely why the watcher gained the root's own entry — and a nested directory is that same rule one level down, so the reading to keep is the one already settled. It is also the reading `inputs = ["src/static"]` looks like it has: `cp -r`, `tar` and `rsync` all carry an empty directory, and a copy hook that stopped re-running when one appeared would be the silent-stale-artifact class, where the extra round is merely cheap. N30's own pin is untouched and green — the watcher did not change at all. While the row was being added, **each row gained its KIND** (`file <digest>`, `link <digest of the target path>`, `dir`) rather than the directory getting a digest of no bytes, which would be the exact row an empty *file* at that key produces: a generator replacing a directory of parts with a single file is not an exotic edit, and a stamp that cannot see it is a hook that never runs again. The kind row is pinned by planting the digest-of-nothing alternative — the kind-swap pin goes red on it and the empty-directory pin stays green, which is what makes the two rows distinct rather than merely present. One upgrade note: a hook whose declared directory input contains subdirectories re-runs once on the first build after this change, because its recorded tree now describes more of the tree than it did. Three pins, two of them red first, and the third the end-to-end one that gives the item its shape — a `--watch` session where `mkdir` under the declared input both starts the round and re-runs the hook, measured before the fix at `rounds.txt` 2, `ran.txt` 1 for the whole liveness bound. (backlog G16, audit run 5's F4; docs `guide/dev-loop.md`)

<!-- family: tooling -->
**A `[[build.hook]]` whose declared directory input is a *symlink* re-ran the hook on every build, forever, and said nothing.** The declaration has two consumers and the whole design of it is that they read it the same way — the freshness stamp and `--watch`'s wake-up set — and on a link they did not. The watcher resolved the declared path through the link (`fs::metadata`) and watched the tree behind it; the stamp stat'd the link itself (`symlink_metadata`), so a link to a directory was not `is_dir()`, fell through to the file path, got `EISDIR` from the read, and digested as *unreadable* — which is never fresh and is never recorded, so the hook ran on every single build. Nothing reported it: the `Fresh` line you were promised simply never appeared, and an expensive generator paid full cost forever. A link to a FILE hid the split completely, because reading one follows it — which is exactly why the code comment beside the watcher claimed the two already matched, and that comment is fixed with the code. Measured on the item's repro: three builds over `inputs = "linked_static"` ran the hook three times where the same tree declared by its real name ran it once. It is the silent-forever-loop class the generated root closed two slices ago, at a different door. The fix is that the declared path resolves through the link, exactly as the watcher resolves it — a link is one of the ordinary ways a static tree gets its name in a package, and hashing what the declaration *reaches* is what "one reading of the manifest" means. **Inside a tree nothing changes and nothing may:** a link found under a declared directory still hashes as its own target path and is never followed, because following one could walk out of the declared tree or into a cycle, and that fence is pinned against a re-planted follow (a re-pointed link at a byte-identical file must still be a change, which is invisible to a walk that follows it). One reading falls out of the same resolution: **a link with no target is MISSING**, not unreadable — the answer the watcher already gives it — which is a real improvement in both positions. A broken input link used to be the same forever-loop one level down; it is now recorded as missing, is fresh on the next build, and invalidates when the target appears. A broken *output* link used to be neither recorded nor reported, so the hook re-ran silently — the precise failure the "did not write it" note exists to prevent — and is now named, by hook and by path. Four pins, three of them red first on the unfixed tree and the fourth proven by planting the follow it forbids; they are `cfg(unix)` like every other symlink pin in the tree, since Windows does not grant link creation by default. (backlog G15, audit run 5's F3; docs `guide/dev-loop.md`)

<!-- family: tooling -->
**The editor now knows what a `css` block is: property names and condition heads paint as themselves, completion offers CSS instead of your scope, three refusals ship with the fix that answers them, and the two spellings convert into each other.** This is the arc's last slice, and its whole shape was decided two slices ago. Element syntax reached its own LSP slice and found *"the desugar's scaffolding spans were the real fix"* — the generated wide spans had painted `<div` as a function and attribute names as methods — which was repair work in S5 for a decision made in S2. So the css desugar cut zero-width anchors for every accessor it generates and carried the property-name, value and per-declaration spans from its first commit whether or not it used them, and the gate on the whole arc was that **S5 must require no S2 rework**. It required none: `crates/vilan-core/src/css.rs` is byte-identical after this slice, and every span this needed was already there. **Semantic tokens** come from a raw re-parse, which is the same machinery the markup tokens ride and for the same reason — `Node::Css` is retired before analysis, so property names and condition heads exist in no analyzed program — and the one accessor that deliberately KEPT a real span (the outer `style()`, at the `css` keyword, so a missing `import std::style::style` underlines the word that asked for a `Style`) is suppressed here exactly as `<div`'s is, or the keyword would light up as a function. A property paints as a property, a condition head as the method it lowers to; the two are the precise form of the TextMate rule's two regex approximations, one parse serving both sub-languages. **Completion** answers the four positions the design named — property, custom property, dotted, hole: an undotted item offers CSS property names except at a `--` custom property, whose name is the author's and gets nothing; a dotted one offers the condition combinators; a `{…}` hole is ordinary expression ground; and value position offers nothing by design (the design's own exclusion), since a binding's NAME is what would land on the sheet. The part that matters is where the vocabulary comes from — E67 refused to invent an HTML attribute list on the ground that it "would be a second source of truth with nothing to gate it", and this clears that objection on a real disanalogy rather than an exception: every property offered is a slot some `Style` method already writes, read out of the canonical-order table's own `properties` column, which six gates in `style_table_sync.rs` hold to `style.vl`'s method bodies. It is std's surface, not a list. A value position offering the enclosing scope would be worse than offering nothing, because a value is source text — a binding's NAME is what would land on the sheet — and value completion proper needs a property→enum map that does not exist. All of it lands in the editor and the playground at once, because it lives in `vilan-ide` and needed no new completion kind to reach either. **Three quickfixes** join the two a block already inherited. `#` and `@` cannot lex at all — lexing is context-free and finishes before the parser exists, so a block cannot make them lex there either — which means each diagnostic is one column wide and each fix reads its subject off the line: `color: #336699` becomes `color: {Color::hex("#336699")}`, and `@media (min-width: 768px) {` becomes `.md {`, with the breakpoint chosen by the query's own min-width and an arbitrary one becoming `.media("900px")` rather than no fix at all. That width map is not a fourth copy of std's breakpoints: it sits beside the condition table and a fifth `style_table_sync.rs` gate holds each row to the `self.media("768px", inner)` the method actually delegates with. `!important` removes itself, space included. Each fix declines where it cannot be faithful — a `#` that is not a colour (3, 4, 6 or 8 hex digits, and the run must end there) keeps the rule and gets no edit, and the three at-rules with no combinator spelling get none either. **And the two spellings now convert into each other**, which is the estate's migration path and the first `refactor.rewrite` action the server has ever offered: the cursor in a block offers "Convert to a `style()` chain", the cursor in a `style()` chain offers "Convert to a `css` block", and on everything they accept the two are inverses — a block converted and converted straight back comes out byte-identical, nesting included. They are mechanical because the lowering is total and one-to-one: a declaration is a `.raw` link, a nested rule is a combinator link carrying the inner chain as its final argument, and there is no third row. Which is also why the inverse is PARTIAL, and says so by not being offered: `.padding(space(4))` writes its slot through `with_length`, which is not the node `padding: {space(4)};` lowers to, so a chain carrying a typed property method has no block spelling this refactor is entitled to invent. Two more refusals, both about meaning rather than shape: a **comment** anywhere inside the construct stops the conversion, because its attachment is not recoverable across the reshape — the same refusal `vilan fmt` makes when it declines to reorder a commented block — and so does a value carrying a **backslash**, because a chain's string literal has its escapes processed at emission and a block's token run does not, so the two spellings would quietly stop meaning the same thing. A quoted value is fine: escaping a `"` into the literal round-trips exactly. Twenty-three pins, each red first and the refusals each proven by re-planting the guard they rest on; nothing in the desugar, `class_hash` or any emission path was touched, and no corpus golden moves. (proposal/css-block.md §7 and §11's S5; docs `appendix/editor.md`)

**One platform-coloring mistake now draws one diagnostic.** Constructing a `@process` resource in a browser build — `let file = File::open("data.txt")` — reported twice: the construction's rejection, and a second one for the compiler-inserted teardown, anchored inside `std`'s own `File::drop` at a position in a file the user cannot edit. `Database` showed it identically, so it was the resource class rather than `File`. Two causes, both general. The synthetic destruction edge (`destruction.md` §8) carried no site at all — the teardown is inserted by the transformer and has no spelling in the source — so its diagnostic fell back to the offending node's own definition, which is by construction inside the library that seeded the requirement. The edge now carries the CONSTRUCTION it answers to: the initializer behind a `let`, the assignment behind an overwrite, the argument behind an early `drop(x)`, the expression itself for an owning temporary, and the owner's site for a member reached through the drop glue. And coloring had no dedup at all: violations now collapse on `(anchor, layer, what the chain hangs from)`, and one raised beneath a teardown edge is dropped when the construction it answers to is already rejected for the same cause — which is what closes `Option::Some(File::open(p))`, the sanctioned container, where the rejected `open` sits *inside* the construction rather than at it. The same dedup fixes a third instance nobody had filed: a fence over a FAMILY is checked against every host in it, so `[platform("@process")]` reaching browser-only code drew three identical diagnostics differing only in which host was named — one broken promise, now reported once, with the fence still quoted so the family is not lost. Distinct mistakes still each report, which is the other half of the claim and pinned as such: two off-platform calls in one function, two fences broken the same way, and a resource whose only off-platform surface is its `Drop` standing beside an unrelated call. (backlog E98, found by Order 17's fs-handles lane)

**A `[[build.hook]]`'s declared `inputs` now wake `--watch`, not just the freshness stamp.** The declaration had two consumers and only one of them was reading it: the stamp re-ran a hook the moment a declared input's bytes moved, while the watch loop polled `.vl` sources and nothing else — so editing a file the manifest names in `inputs` produced **zero rounds**, and the hook re-ran only when some unrelated `.vl` save happened to wake the session (measured on 0.39.0 with a lucide icon pipeline: three edits to declared inputs, no round each time, the banner cheerfully reporting `watching . for .vl changes`). The wake-up set now extends to every declared input, resolved against the manifest's own directory the way the stamp resolves them — so an input outside the watch root is watched exactly as it is stamped — and a declared **directory** means its tree, which is already what the stamp reads it as: adding a file under `inputs = ["icons"]`, or editing one inside it, starts a round. One reading of the manifest, both consumers. This is the recorded-inputs doctrine `markdown.md` §11 settled for `const asset::read`, and it is literally the same mechanism: hook inputs join the set the compile's read inputs already join, rather than a parallel one. Declared `outputs` are deliberately left out — watching what a hook writes would let a build trigger the round that ran it, which is the invariant only `.vl` tracking has protected so far, and the negative is pinned. The session banner now says what it watches, too: it read `watching . for .vl changes` while already polling recorded `asset::read` inputs beside the scan, and that understatement is how the defect came to be diagnosed backwards (the banner looked truthful, so the stamp looked guilty). Pinned by three bounded `--watch` sessions (an edited file input rounds; an added file under a declared directory rounds; an undeclared file does not, on a session proven still alive), the first two proven red first: both waited out the full liveness bound against the unfixed tree. (backlog G10; `build-hooks.md` §9's owed watch-round pin; docs `guide/dev-loop.md`)

<!-- family: tooling -->
**A build hook that generates Vilan and `vilan fmt` were undoing each other forever — a package can now declare where its generated sources live, and the formatter leaves them alone.** The loop was live and silent in both directions. A `[[build.hook]]` names the module it writes in `outputs`; freshness digests declared outputs by content; so a `vilan fmt` that reformatted that file re-staled the hook, the next build re-ran the generator, the generator wrote the file unformatted again — a generator emits what its templates produce, not what the formatter would — and the next format rewrote it. Neither tool is doing anything wrong from where it stands, nothing reports a loop, and with format-on-save the whole cycle runs on a file you only opened to read. It also defeats the freshness gate exactly where that gate was aimed: the `Fresh <name>` line you were promised never appears, and an expensive generator pays full cost on every build after every format. The fix is one manifest key, `[package] generated = "src/icons"` (and the same key on `[library]`), naming the directory that holds the package's *products*: `vilan fmt` and `vilan fmt --check` leave every source file under it byte-identical, and say so once per run with a count and the root's name — a dim `note:`, never a warning, with the exit code unchanged, because skipping a product is the right answer rather than a degraded one. The exclusion is deliberately unconditional, holding even when you name the file on the command line, and it is one predicate in the compiler rather than a filter in the CLI's directory walk — which is what lets your editor's format-on-save honor exactly the same rule, since it reaches a file by its exact path and nothing else. A rule expressed as a walk filter could not have covered the case that most needed covering. The key is validated where the other layout keys are, with four named refusals: it must be relative and free of `..` (lexically, before any filesystem look, the way `asset::read` already refuses an escape), it may not name the package directory itself, and it may not be the source `root` — pointing it there would silently stop formatting every hand-written module in the package, so the message names both keys. A root that does not exist yet is fine; before the first build it usually doesn't, and validation never touches the disk. A declaration that *is* refused excludes nothing, so a typo fails towards formatting too much rather than towards a formatter that has quietly switched off. Nothing else reads the key: module resolution is untouched, and a generated module still resolves where it always did — `src/icons/lib.vl` is `pkg::icons`, which is the configuration that makes the whole thing useful today. The escape is the manifest rather than a flag: if a file should be formatted it isn't a product, so move it out of the root or drop the key, and either way the change lands in review. Pinned end to end — the loop, dead, across a build → format → build cycle, and the same cycle with the key absent kept as the record of the defect it closes. (proposal/build-hooks.md §12, slice S6, on the owner's Q5 ruling; the loop was found by Order 19's lucide evidence run; docs `guide/dev-loop.md`, `appendix/cli.md`, `tour/projects.md` and `spec/platform.md` §11.4)

**A parse error in an imported module now anchors where it is, instead of at line 1 in prose.** The same syntax error rendered at its true position in the ENTRY file and at 1:1 in a module: the loader rendered `line N, column M` into the message and pushed an EMPTY span, so everything a span buys was gone — the caret in the terminal, the squiggle in the editor, the position an editor can jump to, and the file-then-position order the diagnostic sort imposes. Generated code made the cost acute rather than cosmetic: one bad character out of a generator produced **798 errors, every one of them at line 1 of an 18k-line file, in an order nothing determined**. The span was never missing — `render_at` had `error.span` in hand at the moment it threw it away — so the fix is to stop discarding it: a loaded module carries `(span, reason)` pairs the way the entry has always carried the parser's own error, and the module's `SourceId` (which the loader already attributed) is what gives the span a file. Both loader paths change together — the process-global cache and the analysis-owned overlay path the language server uses — so an error reads the same however it reaches you. `vilan build` now points at `util.vl:2:11` with the source line under a caret where it used to name the file in a sentence. One consumer keeps the old shape deliberately: `vilan check <library>` walks a package's modules without registering any of them as a source and renders messages only, so with no file to hang a span on the position stays in the text. Pinned per case: the true line and the exact token spanned, several errors in one module keeping distinct spans in source order, the module error being the parser's own message and span unaltered, the library-contract path keeping its prose, and the end-to-end terminal rendering — each red on the unfixed tree, where the multi-error module reported `[1, 1]`. (backlog E100, measured by the lucide evidence run)

<!-- family: tooling -->
**`vilan build --explain` — every `dist/` file names what put it there.** The const channel scatters its contributions across files *by construction* — that scatter IS import-driven composition — so "where did this output come from?" was a grep, and for an accumulated kind a grep over every `emit` site in the program. The compiler held the answer the whole time and never said it out loud: each channel call knows its `const` site, the flush knows which kind each line landed in, the copy knows what file it carried, and the hook runner knows what ran and what was `Fresh`. The new flag builds — exactly as `vilan build` does, because explaining a stale tree would describe whatever the last build happened to leave — and then prints one block per file it wrote: an accumulated kind lists the `const` sites that contributed to it (`emitted  src/theme.vl:9`), a bundled copy its source and the site that named it with the spelling used (`named  src/client.vl:17 (asset::bundle_as)`), a hook's declared output the hook and this build's verdict (`hook  icons (Fresh)`), and the build's own files their role in the words the build already uses to refuse a resource that tries to take one of their names — `compiled bundle`, `build manifest`, `route chunk`. Then one block per tracked input — `read`/`read_dir`/`read_dir_all`/`digest`, a bundle's source read, a `[[build.hook]]`'s declared `inputs` — with an `invalidates` line per output a change to it would move. That last join is read off the records rather than reasoned about: a const input moves its leg's compiled bundle (the channel's inputs are sources to the compile, which is why editing one starts a `--watch` round — so a `digest` whose value reaches no file but the bundle still gets a true answer) plus the flushes and copies of the sites that read it, and a hook input moves that hook's declared outputs; the build manifest is left out on purpose, because every build of a browser leg rewrites it and naming it under every input would be true and would say nothing. The verb READS and SAYS: no second source of truth, and the only record extension is a `const` site's location beside each channel fact — needed because the operational halves are deduplicated and sorted precisely so a build's bytes are a function of the SET of contributions and never of call order, which is the property that erases who contributed. Every output line is written by the same call that writes the file, so a build that stops producing something stops explaining it. A site is the enclosing `const` expression rather than the `emit` call inside it, which is the granularity the record keeps (the const evaluator runs a lowered tree whose frames carry function names and no spans) and the one a const-eval *error* already points at. The shape is line-oriented and a contract — fixed keys, paths spelled as the build's own `Compiled`/`Emitted`/`Bundled` lines spell them — so `grep '^output'` lists a `dist/` and two builds diff cleanly; it is the refusal doctrine's cousin, a build that can refuse by name being able to explain by name. `--stdout` is refused with it: that flag prints a bundle, not a build, so there is nothing to explain and a report would corrupt the one stream it exists to produce. A plain `vilan build` prints not one line of any of it.

**The raw table under `Map` and `Set` now refuses a resource, closing a use-after-free nothing public could reach.** `NativeMap::insert(&mut self, key: Hash, value: V)` declares its value BARE, and a bare parameter is a loan: with C11's temporary predicate back at its ruled width, the caller destroys the value it hands over *at the insert statement* while the table goes on holding it. Measured, not inferred — `drop r`, then `after`, on a program the compiler accepted, with the host map still pointing at a freed value. It is B153's third sibling, and the one that sweep left open because the obvious fix is the wrong one: declaring `own value: V` closes it by buying a redundant deep copy on EVERY `Map` and `Set` insert in the language — twelve corpus goldens move — to fence a module the standard library documents as not public surface, imports in exactly two places (`std::map`, `std::set`), and no docs page mentions. The zero-cost fix is that R10 already refuses a resource argument to `List`, `Map`, `Set`, `Shared`, `Context`, `Promise` and `Task`, and the internal head simply was not in the list. It is now, so no resource ever reaches `insert` and the bare declaration is honest again. The key position stays bare and is pinned as such: a `Hash` is a non-generic external struct nothing can declare `resource`, so no destructor can ever hang on it. **Reachability is the reason this is hardening rather than a miscompile you might have hit:** `Map<K, resource>` and `Set<resource>` are refused at their own heads and always were, so the only route to the defect was importing `std::native_map` directly, which is why the ruling took the free fix over the language-wide one. Adding the head opened a diagnostic question worth more than the head itself. `Map<K, V>` stores a `NativeMap<(K, V)>` and `Set<T>` a `NativeMap<T>`, so a `Map<str, Database>` now offends at BOTH heads — and reported at both, the second one anchored inside `std`'s own `Map::new` at a line the user cannot edit. One mistake is one diagnostic, and the collapse is general rather than a name check: the per-instantiation body scan exists for the container a generic builds out of its own `T` and never hands back (`fun stash<T>(own value: T) { let items = [value]; }`, where no type the caller holds is a `List<Guard>`), so it now stands down exactly when the callee's own instantiated SIGNATURE is refused and the caller has already been told — the offense is the type they wrote, and the storage inside it is not a second thing to fix. That is E98's shape reused: a consequence is dropped when the thing it is a consequence of is already rejected. "Already told" is asked of the reported set rather than assumed, so a refusal nobody saw can never silence the body's account of it, and the other half of the claim is pinned too — `stash` still reports. Every `Map` and `Set` diagnostic in the tree is byte-identical to before. Nine pins: the ignored one from B153 un-ignored and passing (it compiled cleanly on the unfixed tree), the measured use-after-free program, a `NativeMap` of a non-resource still compiling and running, the bare `Hash` key still readable after the insert it was passed to, `Map` and `Set` each reporting exactly once, neither construction naming the `NativeMap` inside it (both red first, on the head fix without the collapse), and the generic-body container the caller cannot see still reported. (backlog B154, found by Order 20's b153 lane and audit run 4; docs `spec/memory.md` R10)

<!-- family: tooling -->
**A `--watch` round whose action fails is retried once, instead of losing the change that started it.** The loop consumed a snapshot difference BEFORE it ran the round — `snapshot = next; action()` — so a round that failed for a transient reason could never re-fire: the difference was spent, and the session sat healthy and silent until some OTHER file happened to move. That is the right design for a compile error, whose fix IS the next edit and whose retry would spin on a broken tree; it is a silently lost round for a `cmd` hiccup on a loaded runner, a hook racing something outside the tree, or any other flake, and it is what a Windows CI leg had already been diagnosed as once. The ruling is a restored difference and ONE retry: a failed round leaves the old snapshot in place, so the next poll sees the same difference and runs the round again — and a second consecutive failure consumes the difference and goes back to waiting for the next change, which is the posture the loop has always had, now the fallback rather than the whole policy. The guard is once, and once is what makes it safe to apply to failures the loop cannot classify: a broken tree retried once compiles-fails a second time and then rests, one extra compile per broken save, where anything unbounded would hammer a tree nothing but an edit can fix. Nor can it spin — a retry is an ordinary round riding the poll interval, and a change landing *during* a pending retry is folded into that retry rather than refreshing its budget, so "at most two runs per difference" holds however edits are timed. The reason this could not be done before is that the verdict was invisible: `run_or_watch` took an action returning `ExitCode` and discarded it, and `ExitCode` is write-only — it is built from a verdict and handed to the process, and nothing can read the verdict back out of it. So the three commands a watch session drives (`build`, `check`, `test`) now report a `RoundOutcome` the loop can read, and the exit code is minted at the one boundary that needs one; every fallible step beneath them already answered with `ExitCode::FAILURE` and nothing else, so no code carried information the verdict does not. `run --watch` deliberately keeps today's posture, and the reason is recorded at the code rather than assumed: that path has no honest failure signal to thread — an HMR round and a plain restart round both answer with an `Option<ManagedChild>`, where `None` means "no Node child to hold" (which a browser-only workspace produces on a perfectly good round) and a failed round hands back the previous child, alive — while `WatchState::failed` is the classifier's recompile-everything flag rather than a verdict, and the failure it would carry is the compile error the ruling declines to retry, at the price of a second full recompile of every leg and a second error overlay per broken save. Inventing a signal there would have bought the one retry nobody asked for. The session says which round is which: a retry announces itself, the first failure says it will retry on the next poll, and the second says it is waiting for the next change — the narration a `--watch` log needs to explain itself after the fact, which is how this defect was found in the first place. Two bounded watch sessions pin it, both proven red first (each waited out the full liveness bound against the unfixed tree, its log showing one failed round and then silence): a `[build] run` command armed to fail exactly once loses NO round — the edited input's hook still runs, and the pin deliberately does not re-touch its trigger the way the positive watch pins do every 20 s, so the retry is the only thing that can produce that second run — and a command that fails every time runs exactly TWICE per change, held across a window scaled to the machine's own first round, then rounds normally once disarmed. The undeclared-file negative is untouched and still green. (tracker G14, filed by Order 20's close; docs `guide/dev-loop.md`)

**Two different errors at one offset in an imported module are both reported again.** Giving a module parse error its real span (E100) came with a new dedup — one module reaches the loader through several seams, and the cache hands each seam the same errors — but the key it chose was `(file, position)` where the code it replaced keyed the full rendered message. Position is not what makes an error distinct: a stray `"` produces two refusals over the same one character, the LEXER's (an unterminated string cannot span lines) and the PARSER's, over the tokens that survive (this statement has no `;`), and the second one silently vanished. The audit caught it as a key narrowed without the doc comment noticing the reason had been dropped. The key is now `(file, position, reason)` — all three of what an error *is* — so the dedup still collapses the same error arriving through a re-export and a direct import, and no longer collapses two errors that merely happen to land together. Pinned both ways round: the two-refusals-at-one-offset module, red before the fix with the parser's half missing, and a module reached through two seams still reporting each of its errors exactly once. **`dist/` now sweeps a bundled resource the build stopped naming — the last of the four writers sharing that directory to learn the rule.** `write_bundled` copied files and wrote nothing down, alone among its three neighbours: `sweep_stale_chunks`, `sweep_stale_sidecar` and the per-kind prune all treat their outputs as belonging to the leg's LAST build, and the per-kind prune's own doc comment states why — a stale flush in `dist/` SHIPS, which is worse than a missing file under "a built app needs nothing but `dist/`". A copy had no such counterpart, so `dist/` accumulated. The gap pre-dates the estate verbs and they made it reachable with no source edit at all and UNBOUNDED: `read_dir_all` means a DELETION out of a listed tree is invisible to the copy (the listing loses the file, the folded array loses the url, and the copy in `dist/` stays), and the `digest`-minted fingerprint recipe mints a new name on every save, so a `--watch` session orphans one copy per edit for the life of the session. `serve_build` routes from the manifest and so never serves a stray, which is exactly why nothing noticed — but `dist/` is the DEPLOY artifact, and a static host in front of it goes on answering for a `robots.txt` the source tree no longer has. The fix is the mechanism that was already there, extended: every build records the copies it carried and the next build removes a recorded copy no leg names any more. It is a SEPARATE record file (`.vilan-bundled`) beside the kind record rather than more rows in it, and that is a determination rather than a convenience: a record is a row *and* the file that row names, and the two name their files by different rules — a kind row names `<leg>.<kind>`, a bundled row names its target verbatim, so in one file `client/logo.svg` would be ambiguous between `dist/client.logo.svg` and `dist/logo.svg`, and a pruner guessing wrong deletes a file it does not own. A bundled name may also carry `/` (a subdirectory is what `bundle` keeps and what `bundle_as` may spell, and it is the sanctioned escape from a name a leg's build owns) where a kind is fenced to one segment, so one file would need two row grammars; and each record is removed with its last row so it never becomes its own stale artifact, which sharing would tie to whether the *other* mechanism had anything to say. What the two do share is the row shape and both record primitives, so there is one format and one pruning law, not two. **That law is the whole safety argument and it is G6's, unchanged: the pruner acts only on its own record.** A file placed by hand beside the copies, another leg's outputs, and anything unrecorded are untouchable however bundle-shaped the name — the general "delete whatever this build did not write" sweep is still deliberately unbuilt. Rows are keyed by leg because `dist/` is one directory every leg copies into, with the one subtlety that shape forces: a name is NOT one leg's to delete just because that leg stopped naming it, since two legs bundling one file to one url is legal and expected, so a file is removed only when the record the build is about to WRITE no longer names it at all. A resource that is already its own destination is deliberately never recorded — that is the case `same_file` exists to protect, and recording it would put the build's own source on a future build's deletion list. Six pins, each proven red first by planting the defect: the disappearance pin's missing `dist/` half (a file dropped out of a listed tree takes its copy with it), the fingerprint's orphan (the old digest's copy is gone and the new one is there), the record's exact contents, an empty record removing itself, a hand-placed file surviving the sweep that empties the record around it, and the cross-leg case — where dropping the SECOND leg's bundle is what makes the pin non-vacuous, because dropping the first one's lets the second's copy put the file back and hide a prune that had no business running. (backlog G13, audit run 4 finding 2; docs `std/misc.md`)

**Creating a declared directory that the build was waiting for now starts a `--watch` round, even when it is empty.** A directory input means its whole TREE to both the freshness stamp and the watcher — the reading G10 unified — but the watcher expanded it to its FILES and inserted nothing for the directory itself. The narrow shape is what made it easy to miss — the first file created inside the directory *did* fire, so the only silent step was the one where you create the directory and then look for what to put in it. A directory now contributes its own entry alongside its files, and each half answers exactly what the other cannot: the directory's entry makes its appearance and its membership observable, its files' entries make an edit *inside* it observable (a directory's own mtime does not move for that). Nested directories get the same treatment for the same reason — a subdirectory appearing empty is a change to the tree that no file entry can express. **A connection that closes for good now takes its client's graph with it — the terminal `Closed` disposes the `ReactiveClient` that was holding the mirrors.** A26 gave the reconnect path two honest refusals: a re-dialled server whose contract has DRIFTED, and one that answers `__contract` and then REFUSES the `__attach`. Both reach the terminal `Closed` and close the socket, because a mirror that cannot be rebound is pointed at the previous connection's dead channel ids and would never update again. What the refusal did not do was let go. The client kept every route — one deliverer per mirror, each holding that mirror's cache — and the transport kept the inbound handler `ReactiveClient::new` installed, which captures the whole client: the exact `client → transport → handler → client` retention A29 measured and gave `dispose` to cut, left standing on the one connection that can be certain it will never carry another frame. A wedged client is now a disposed one. `close_for_good` is the single line both branches take — state, then `close()`, then the client's own `dispose()` — so the honest report and the release happen together rather than one of them being remembered. The ORDER is deliberate and the pins read it: a `connection_state` observer runs inside `state.set(Closed)`, one line before the disposal, so an app watching the signal sees the state it is being told about and not a half-torn-down client. Nothing a program can call changes. A disposed client's mirrors read their last value forever, which is what they did before — the socket was closed, so nothing was going to arrive on it either way — and that is the same reason A29's repairs were unobservable. What moves is what stays reachable after the app has been told the connection is over. The negative is the load-bearing half and it is pinned as such: an ORDINARY redial disposes nothing, and neither does the third failure the same function meets — the server unreachable when the re-attach runs, which is a delay rather than a desync, because that socket keeps trying and its mirrors resync when it succeeds. Disposal belongs only where the mirrors are unrecoverable, and `reattach_mirrors`'s three arms are exactly that distinction written out. `dispose` is idempotent by construction (both lines assign an empty), which stops being incidental the moment std calls it: an app that tore its own client down before the socket gave up must not be punished for it. Four pins, each proven red first — the refused re-attach and the drift case ride A26's failure-mode-as-a-spawn-argument harness against real servers and assert the disposal on top of the existing `Closed` assertions, the resync case asserts the opposite over the same wire (removing the wiring reddens both terminals and leaves the negative green; wiring the disposal onto every reconnect reddens the negative), and the double-dispose is a unit pin reading the routes count and the handler slot across two passes. The standing heap-snapshot SCC gate is unmoved and could not have moved: its exemplar disposes its client by hand over an in-process `duplex_pair`, with no socket and no `reattach_mirrors` in reach. (backlog A30, ruled 2026-08-29; completes A26; proposal/lifetimes.md §5 V5, proposal/transport-robustness.md §2.5; docs `std/rpc.md`, `guide/services.md`)

**A second, unrelated container refusal is no longer swallowed by the first one's stand-down.** B154 gave R10's per-instantiation body scan a stand-down, and it was the right rule stated correctly — *a refusal the caller has already been told about is not repeated a layer deeper, and a refusal nobody saw never silences the body's account of it* — but it was IMPLEMENTED as a single early return over the whole instantiation, so the first refused signature type dropped every body-container report at that call, including ones that had nothing to do with it. `fun two<A, B>(a: Map<str, A>, own b: B) { let items = [b]; }` at `A := Guard, B := Other` is the case: the caller was told about `Map<str, Guard>`, which it wrote and can fix, and the `List<Other>` the body builds out of a completely different parameter — a type no caller holds, which is the entire reason the body scan exists — vanished without a word. That is the half of B154's own sentence the code was not keeping, and it is the failure direction these rules must never take: a silent accept, not a noisy one. The question is now asked **per offending type** rather than once per instantiation. A refused-and-reported signature type contributes the generic parameters its unsubstituted spelling is written in terms of, and a body container stands down only when every parameter IT is written in terms of is among them — so `Map<K, V>`'s storage collapses into the `Map<K, V>` the caller wrote exactly as before (`NativeMap<(K, V)>` traces to `K` and `V`, both covered), while `List<B>` under a signature that only refused `Map<str, A>` traces to `B`, which is nobody's consequence, and reports. A type mentioning no parameter at all is never vacuously covered. The mixed shape both halves have to agree on is pinned in the middle: one parameter refused at the signature AND that same parameter's container built in the body — `fun wrap<A>(own a: A, table: Map<str, A>) { let items = [a]; }` — stays exactly one report, because the caller made one decision and fixing `A` fixes both. Found by audit run 5 rather than by a user, and fixed inside the same order that introduced it, so the suppression lived one union-tip day and before any release carried it. **A `css` block you are still WRITING is still a `css` block: the editor offers property names inside one whose closing `}` you have not typed yet, where it used to offer `fun`, `for … in { }` and every name in scope.** The 23 pins css-block S5 shipped all describe blocks that close, and the block that matters most in an editor is the one that does not. `css_position` asks the RAW PARSE which body the cursor is in, and `parse_css_atom` declines a block that never closes — correctly, because a region with no end has no span — so there was no `Node::Css` to find, `css_position` returned `None`, and the dispatch fell through to ordinary expression ground. The code comment beside it said completion "simply does not fire there", which was the one thing that was not happening: it fired, with the wrong sub-language. **The parser is deliberately left alone.** Minting a node to end-of-input would have traded the located `unclosed `{`` the statement recovery reports at the opener — the diagnostic the author actually needs — and handed the css desugar a block nobody has finished, to answer a question the editor can answer for itself. What the fix does instead is let the LIVE LEXIS answer the first question, which is the same instrument, and the same reason, as the second: the position walk has always read the live buffer, because the character being typed is in no parse tree, and a block whose `}` has not been typed is exactly that kind of text. The parse stays the authority wherever it has an answer, so all 23 S5 pins are untouched by construction. The fallback is one pass with a stack of open brackets, each remembering whether it is a css BODY, and the two markers that decide are the grammar's own (§3): a block's own `{` is the one directly after the `css` keyword, and a nested rule's is one opened while the enclosing item has taken the `.` that commits it to a condition — so an unterminated `.md {` is a body too, and a `{…}` hole, a condition head's argument and an ordinary block are not, however css-adjacent. Comments and strings cannot plant a phantom `css {`: comments are trivia that never reach the token stream, and a string is one token. Five pins, and the negatives carry the weight — the unterminated block, its four positions (dotted, value, custom property) answering as they do in a closed one, the unterminated nested rule, an unclosed HOLE staying ordinary expression ground, and a CLOSED block not leaking past its own `}` with the enclosing function still open. Ten call sites are short tokens and are fine. The eleventh, `skip_raw_text`, folded the ENTIRE markup and handed the copy to `index_of`, once per raw-text element, so a page with five `<script>`s folded itself five times; and `index_of` here is `document.vl`'s own vilan loop, which mints a needle-length substring per position on top of that. The CHANGELOG that shipped the rename priced none of it. **The cheaper shape is the windowed compare, not the folded-once copy, and the argument is `document.vl`'s own structure.** `tags_of` is the only caller, and caching a folded copy there would allocate a second whole document, thread mutable cache state through the scan loop, and still pay `index_of`'s per-position substring for every element. Comparing `A`–`Z` to `a`–`z` in place pays neither: it allocates nothing at all, and its work is bounded by the distance to the element's CLOSING TAG rather than by the length of the document, which is the actual asymptotic change — a small script at the top of a one-megabyte page went from folding a megabyte to reading a few dozen code units. The answer is the same one because the needle is already ASCII-folded by its caller and folding `A`–`Z` preserves both length and index, which is the F14 property the old comment was there to assert. **Measured, in counts and never in milliseconds** (the item's own instruction): an 18,190-unit page carrying five `<script>` elements, with the driver's own search left uninstrumented — 182,015 strings minted and 90,950 code units read before, 5 strings and 290 units after. Those eight are now a pin, and it is red under three plants: the case fold removed (`upper` fails), the give-up value changed from the document's end to where the skip started (`swallowed` fails, which is the shape that exists to discriminate it), and the search disabled outright. No corpus golden moves — no corpus program reaches `std::document`. Audit run 6 carries "std's emitted cost" as a standing angle beside the shipped sentence, per the run-5 charter. (tracker M14, audit run 5's F7)
